Module 3 · Lesson 5

Logging in Depth:
Telemetry, Collection & the Road to the SIEM

Four lessons of evidence — network, protocol, endpoint — is worthless if it never arrives, arrives broken, or arrives too late. This lesson builds the pipeline: how logs are structured, shipped, parsed, and stored so that detection becomes possible.

LEVELBeginner DURATION45–55 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–4 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • A useful log answers when, where, who and what — and the pipeline must deliver it intact: collect → transport → parse → normalize → store.
  • Normalizing to a common schema (CIM, ECS, ASIM, OCSF) is what lets one rule watch many products.
  • Use NTP + UTC everywhere, TCP/TLS rather than UDP for evidence, and keep logs longer than attackers stay hidden.
Hands-on:Lab 6 · A real SIEM (Splunk)
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Anatomize a log entry

Name the fields every useful log needs, and tell structured from unstructured data at a glance.

Recognize the formats

Read the same event in syslog, JSON, and CEF, and understand why normalization must exist.

Design a collection path

Choose between agents and syslog, UDP and TLS, and explain what a collector actually does all day.

Respect the clock

Explain why UTC and NTP aren't pedantry — and how clock skew silently destroys correlation.

Reason about retention

Balance hot search, archive, cost, and compliance — and know why "we'll check the logs later" often fails.

Diagnose pipeline failures

Given a symptom — missing fields, silent sources, impossible timestamps — name the broken stage.

02
Orientation

Why the pipeline decides whether detection is possible

Every scenario replay so far has quietly leaned on the same hero: the moment evidence left the machine that created it. The firewall logged the connection, Sysmon recorded the process, auth.log kept the brute force — but none of that matters at 3 a.m. unless those records were collected, transported intact, parsed correctly, and stored somewhere searchable before the attacker cleared them, the disk filled, or the retention window closed.

This is the least glamorous and most consequential layer of security operations. SOCs don't usually fail because an analyst missed a clue; they fail because the clue was never collected, arrived with an empty username field, or carried a timestamp three hours adrift from every other source. Detection engineering begins with pipeline engineering.

Analogy — the courtroom

Think of logs as evidence headed for court. It must be gathered at the scene (generation), bagged and tagged (collection), moved with an unbroken chain of custody (transport), translated so the jury can read it (parsing), and archived until trial (retention). Break any link — evidence lost, mislabeled, or undated — and the case collapses no matter how good the detective is.

Where this leads. This lesson is the bridge into the SIEM modules: Lesson 6 introduces the SIEM itself, and the collection, parsing, and normalization ideas here become hands-on configuration there. Every "missing data" mystery you'll ever debug traces back to one of this lesson's five stages.

In plain words

Logs are only useful if they arrive, stay, and match up. Devices ship logs to a collector, ideally over a reliable, encrypted path (not plain UDP, which can silently drop them). Everything gets a synced clock and a common format (normalization) so you can search it all together. Bad clocks and lost logs ruin more investigations than clever hackers do.

03
Core concepts

What makes a log a log

Strip away vendors and formats, and a useful log record answers five questions: when (a precise timestamp), where (which system produced it), who (the account or process acting), what (the action and its outcome), and context (the details — IPs, ports, paths, command lines — that make investigation possible). A record missing "when" or "who" is trivia, not evidence.

Structured vs. unstructured

Unstructured logs are prose for humans — a sentence you must read. Structured logs are labeled fields for machines — src_ip=192.168.10.24 — which a computer can filter, count, and correlate at millions per second. The industry's whole trajectory is toward structure, because SIEM detection is just arithmetic on fields. When a source only speaks prose, parsing (stage four of the pipeline) converts it — fragile, essential work you'll meet shortly.

Severity: the log's own volume knob

Most logging systems tag each record with a severity. The syslog scale runs 0–7 — memorize the shape, not just the numbers: 0–2 (Emergency, Alert, Critical) mean things are on fire, 3–4 (Error, Warning) mean something's wrong, 5–6 (Notice, Informational) are routine life, and 7 (Debug) is the firehose you enable only while troubleshooting. Two traps: severity reflects the source's opinion, not security relevance — a quiet Informational 4688 can matter more than a noisy Critical disk warning — and collecting Debug everywhere will drown both your storage and your attention.

The clock is sacred. Correlation means putting events from many systems in order — impossible if their clocks disagree. Two rules, no exceptions: every system syncs time via NTP, and logs are recorded or normalized to UTC (local timezones plus daylight saving have ruined more investigations than encryption ever has). A three-minute skew can reverse cause and effect; three hours can hide an attack entirely.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five-stage pipeline

Every log travels the same road from birth to analyst. Select a stage, then use the tabs to see what it does, the design decisions it forces, and how it fails — because in the pipeline, failure modes are the curriculum.

05
Core concepts

One event, three dialects

Here is the same firewall event — the suspicious port-4444 connection from Lesson 2's challenge — as three different sources might emit it. Read all three and the case for normalization makes itself:

SYSLOG — the venerable standard: priority, timestamp, host, then free text <134>Aug 4 09:16:38 fw-01 ngfw: ALLOW TCP 192.168.10.24:51611 -> 198.51.100.7:4444 bytes 2114788
CEF — Common Event Format: a labeled header, then key=value pairs CEF:0|VendorX|NGFW|7.0|traffic|allow|3|src=192.168.10.24 dst=198.51.100.7 dpt=4444 out=2114788
JSON — the cloud-native default: fully structured, machine-first { "ts": "2026-08-04T09:16:38Z", "src_ip": "192.168.10.24", "dst_ip": "198.51.100.7", "dst_port": 4444, "action": "allow", "bytes_out": 2114788 }

Three spellings of one fact. Now imagine a SIEM receiving fifty formats from a hundred products and being asked "show every allowed connection to port 4444." That question is only answerable after normalization: parsing each dialect and mapping its fields onto one common schema, so that dpt, dst_port, and the number buried in prose all become the same searchable field. Normalization is why a single detection rule can watch an entire heterogeneous estate — and why a broken parser is a silent hole in your defenses.

The schemas you'll actually meet. Every major platform ships its own common schema: Splunk's CIM (Common Information Model), Elastic's ECS (Elastic Common Schema), Microsoft Sentinel's ASIM (Advanced Security Information Model), and the vendor-neutral open standard OCSF (Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework). Same idea, different spellings for the same source address: src (CIM), source.ip (ECS), SrcIpAddr (ASIM), src_endpoint.ip (OCSF). Portable rule formats like Sigma bridge the gap with processing pipelines that map generic field names onto each schema — you'll use one in Lesson 8 and Lab 4.

Windows speaks its own language. Windows events are structured XML under the hood (that's why Event IDs and named fields exist at all) and travel natively via Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) or an agent — no syslog required. Different dialect, same pipeline, same normalization destination.

06
Core concepts

Collection architecture: agents, collectors & what to gather first

Two ways to get a log off its source: an agent installed on the machine (reads local logs, buffers when the network drops, ships reliably — the norm for endpoints) or agentless export, where the device pushes syslog itself (the norm for firewalls, switches, and appliances that can't run your software). Either way, records usually converge on a collector — a middle tier that does the unglamorous heavy lifting:

SOURCES MIDDLE TIER DESTINATION endpoints ──agent──────┐ firewalls ──syslog─────┤──▶ COLLECTOR ── TLS / queued ──▶ SIEM (parse → normalize → index) dns / proxy ─syslog────┤ buffers · filters noise windows ──WEF / agent──┘ enriches · one egress point

The collector buffers (so a SIEM outage doesn't lose events), filters (dropping known noise before it costs storage), enriches (stamping hostnames, geo, asset tags), and gives the network team one egress point instead of five hundred. Transport from device to collector is where the classic trap lives: plain syslog over UDP 514 is fire-and-forget — under load or across a flaky link it silently drops records. For anything you'd miss in court, use TCP with TLS (typically port 6514): delivery, order, and confidentiality.

What to collect first

Volume costs money and attention, so mature programs prioritize by investigative value. A battle-tested starting order — notice it's simply Lessons 3 and 4 restated as a shopping list:

  • Authentication everywhere — Windows 4624/4625, Linux auth.log, VPN, cloud sign-ins. Who got in, from where, how.
  • Process creation with command lines — 4688/Sysmon 1. The endpoint's genealogy record.
  • DNS queries — the earliest witness to nearly everything, at modest volume.
  • Web proxy / firewall — who talked to what outside, with byte counts.
  • Email gateway verdicts — every lure that arrived, tagged or not.
  • Cloud control-plane audit — admin actions in your cloud consoles; one hijacked key can outweigh a hundred workstations.

Retention: hot, cold, and the law

Storage strategy is tiers: a hot window (commonly 30–90 days) that's instantly searchable for triage, and an archive (often a year or more) that's cheap but slower to restore for the breach discovered months late. The floor is frequently set not by engineering but by compliance — regulations and frameworks (PCI DSS being the classic example) mandate minimum log retention, which is why "how long do we keep this?" is a question for policy and capacity planning. Rule of thumb: incidents are routinely discovered long after they begin, so retention shorter than your likely detection delay is a bet you'll lose.

07
Hands-on · Simulation

You're the analyst: name the broken stage

Pipeline debugging is pattern recognition: each stage fails with its own signature. For every symptom below, name the stage that's broken. The feedback walks the diagnostic reasoning — that reasoning is the takeaway.

Pipeline triage drill

Symptom 1 / 6 · Score 0
08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

The life of a log — from wrong branch to analyst's screen

Remember Lesson 4's highest-signal record — Excel spawning hidden PowerShell? Follow that single Sysmon event through every stage of the pipeline, in the two seconds between its birth on FIN-WS-042 and the moment it can page a human.

Pipeline replay — "Two seconds, twelve steps"

GenerationThe kernel notices a process being bornEXCEL.EXE spawns powershell.exe. Sysmon's driver sees the creation the instant it happens — before the malware has done anything else.
GenerationSysmon writes Event 1, in structured XMLImage, command line, parent, user, hashes — and a UTC timestamp, because the host syncs NTP. The record exists. Now it must survive.
CollectionThe agent reads the event channelWithin milliseconds the endpoint agent tails the Sysmon log, picks up the new record, and stamps it with source metadata.
CollectionThe agent buffers — just in caseThe record sits in a local queue until delivery is confirmed. If the network blinks or the collector restarts, nothing is lost — replay, not regret.
TransportEncrypted, acknowledged deliveryTLS to the collector: confidential in transit, acknowledged on receipt. The UDP-and-hope era ends here.
CollectorFilter, enrich, forwardKnown-noise events are dropped; this one is kept and enriched — asset tag FIN-WS-042 = finance workstation, user m.haddad = finance team — then queued onward to the SIEM.
IngestionThe SIEM accepts the recordInto the ingestion queue with tens of thousands of peers per second. Order and integrity preserved; the firehose is organized, not resisted.
ParsingThe dialect is decodedThe Sysmon parser splits XML into fields: Image, CommandLine, ParentImage, User, Hashes. One vendor's format, understood.
NormalizationFields map to the common schemaParentImage becomes parent_process; UtcTime becomes @timestamp. Now this record speaks the same language as every firewall, proxy, and auth log in the estate.
StorageIndexed and searchable — hot tierWritten, indexed, and queryable in seconds; bound for the archive tier months from now. The evidence is safe even if FIN-WS-042 is wiped in the next minute.
DetectionA rule has been waiting for exactly this"Office application spawns script engine" evaluates against the normalized fields — parent_process + process + hidden flag — and matches. Alert raised, context attached.
The analystA human sees a story, not a haystackElapsed time since the process spawned: about two seconds. Every pivot the analyst now makes — user history, host timeline, hash search — is a query against this same pipeline's output.
Ready. Press Play to follow the record, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: detection latency is pipeline latency. The rule fired in two seconds only because every stage — NTP'd generation, buffered collection, TLS transport, working parser, common schema — held. Weaken any one, and the same attack becomes invisible without a single alert telling you so. That's why pipeline health is a detection in itself.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Pipeline misconceptions fail silently — which makes them the most dangerous kind. Retire these now:

Misconception

"Just collect everything — storage is cheap."

Reality

Volume costs money, ingestion licenses, and — worst — attention. Debug logs from everything bury the 4688 that matters. Mature collection is prioritized: high-value sources first, noise filtered at the collector, coverage expanded deliberately.

Misconception

"Syslog over UDP has worked for decades — it's fine."

Reality

UDP syslog silently drops records under load, exactly when attacks generate the most events. It's also unencrypted and trivially spoofable. For evidence you'd want in an incident, use TCP/TLS with buffering — "fine" isn't a delivery guarantee.

Misconception

"The logs exist on the device — we can always pull them if something happens."

Reality

Attackers clear logs (Event 1102), ransomware encrypts them, disks rotate them away in days, and the device itself may be the thing that's gone. Evidence counts only once it's off-host, in real time. You've now seen this rule save the case in three separate replays.

Misconception

"Timestamps are timestamps — the SIEM will sort it out."

Reality

Mixed timezones, daylight saving, and unsynced clocks quietly shuffle your timeline. Correlation rules with time windows simply miss, and incident narratives reverse cause and effect. NTP everywhere, UTC everywhere — it's two settings that protect every investigation you'll ever run.

Misconception

"Parsing is set-up-once plumbing."

Reality

A firmware update changes a log format and your parser starts dropping the username field — no error, no alert, just quieter dashboards. Parsers are living code: monitor for unparsed events and field-population rates, and treat a parsing drop like the outage it is.

Misconception

"A quiet log source is a healthy log source."

Reality

Silence is ambiguous: maybe nothing happened — or the agent died, the queue overflowed, or an attacker disabled logging as step one. Monitor source liveness ("last event seen") and alert on gaps. In telemetry, absence of evidence is itself evidence worth investigating.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • A useful log answers when, where, who, what, and context — and the pipeline's job is getting it to an analyst intact: generation → collection → transport → parsing & normalization → storage.
  • Structured beats prose: detection is arithmetic on fields. Syslog, CEF, and JSON are dialects; normalization to a common schema is what lets one rule watch a heterogeneous estate.
  • Severity 0–7 is the source's opinion, not security relevance — an Informational process-creation event can outrank a Critical disk warning.
  • NTP + UTC, no exceptions: clock skew silently reverses timelines and blinds correlation windows.
  • Agents for endpoints, syslog for appliances, collectors to buffer, filter, enrich, and concentrate; TCP/TLS (6514) over UDP 514 for anything you'd miss in court.
  • Collect by value: auth, process creation, DNS, proxy/firewall, email, cloud audit — Lessons 3 and 4 as a shopping list.
  • Retention = hot tier + archive, floored by compliance and by the fact that breaches are found late; and monitor the pipeline itself — a silent source is a finding.
11

Lesson 6 — What Is a SIEM? Architecture & Core Capabilities

The pipeline is built; now meet the platform it feeds. What a SIEM actually is, its architecture from ingestion to alerting, search and dashboards, and how correlation turns five lessons of telemetry into detections — the door into the heart of this series.

Start Lesson 6

SOC Foundations Module 4 — SIEM Lesson 6 — What Is a SIEM?
Module 4 · Lesson 6

What Is a SIEM?
Architecture & Core Capabilities

Five lessons of telemetry converge here. The SIEM is where a million events an hour become searchable evidence, real-time detections, and the alert queue where your analyst career begins. Time to meet the platform.

LEVELBeginner DURATION45–55 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–5 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • A SIEM centralizes and normalizes logs so cross-source attack stories become searchable and detectable.
  • Every query is filter → aggregate → present — in SPL, KQL or any dialect. The entity timeline is the workhorse pivot.
  • Rules alert, dashboards inform, and every analyst verdict must feed back into tuning.
Hands-on:Lab 5 · Browser SIEM (no install)
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Define a SIEM precisely

Explain what Security Information & Event Management platforms do, where they came from, and what they deliberately don't do.

Sketch the architecture

Trace data from collectors through ingestion, parsing, storage, and the detection engine to the analyst's screen.

Think in queries

Read and reason about SIEM searches — filter, aggregate, present — regardless of which vendor's dialect they're written in.

Explain correlation

Describe how rules turn normalized events from many sources into real-time detections — and why content needs tuning.

Navigate the alert lifecycle

Follow an alert from rule match through enrichment, triage, verdict, response, and the tuning loop that closes it.

Prioritize a queue

Rank competing alerts by severity and context — the judgment call Tier-1 analysts make all shift long.

02
Orientation

Why every serious SOC is built around one

Picture defending the company from Lessons 2–5 without a SIEM. The firewall has a console. So does the mail gateway, the DNS server, the EDR, the cloud tenant, and four hundred Windows hosts. The phishing campaign from Lesson 3 touched five of those systems in eleven minutes — to see it, an analyst would need five browser tabs, five query languages, and the luck to check them in the right order. Nobody detects anything that way. Attacks are cross-source stories; consoles are single-source windows.

The SIEM exists to fix exactly that. It centralizes every source into one searchable store, normalizes their dialects into one schema (Lesson 5's payoff), correlates events across sources in real time, alerts when patterns match, and gives analysts one place to investigate, document, and report. It is the reading room for the three ledgers — and every other ledger besides.

Analogy — air traffic control

Hundreds of aircraft each have their own radio and instruments — but safe skies require one tower seeing all of them, on one screen, in real time, with automation flagging conflicts before humans could spot them. That tower is the SIEM: it doesn't fly the planes (the firewalls still block, the EDR still quarantines) — it provides the unified picture and the early warning that make coordinated response possible.

A word on names. The market calls them Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic Security, IBM QRadar, FortiSIEM, and more. Interfaces and query dialects differ; the architecture and concepts in this lesson are common to all of them — learn these once, and every product becomes "the same machine with different buttons."

In plain words

A SIEM is the giant searchable box holding all your logs — plus the rules that raise alerts. A good correlation rule connects events into meaning (“10 failures then a success”). Too many noisy alerts cause alert fatigue, where real attacks get missed in the flood. The fix is tuning: fewer, better alerts. An alert is a lead to check, never a proven fact.

03
Core concepts

SIEM, defined — and de-mythologized

SIEM stands for Security Information and Event Management — a name that fossilizes its history: two older product categories, SIM (log storage, search, and compliance reporting) and SEM (real-time event monitoring and alerting), fused into one platform. That heritage still describes the two halves of the job: a long memory you can interrogate, and a fast reflex that watches the stream as it arrives.

Boiled down, a SIEM makes five promises: collect everything relevant into one place, normalize it into one language, detect patterns across sources in real time, enable investigation at interactive speed, and report for compliance and management. Each promise leans on the previous — which is why a broken parser (Lesson 5) quietly degrades detection, investigation, and reporting all at once.

What a SIEM is not

Three boundaries save careers' worth of disappointment. A SIEM is not a prevention tool — it observes and alerts; blocking belongs to firewalls, EDR, and mail gateways (it can trigger them, which is SOAR's territory, Lesson 19). It is not intelligent out of the box — it ships as an engine, and detection content (the rules) plus tuning (fitting rules to your environment) are ongoing human work. And it is not a replacement for analysts — it compresses a million events into a handful of leads, but judgment on those leads is the job. Yours, soon.

The compression ratio. A mid-size company might generate 50 million events a day. A healthy SIEM turns those into perhaps 50–200 alerts, of which a handful become incidents. That funnel — millions to dozens to a few — is the entire economics of the SOC, and every module ahead is about making the funnel more precise.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five capabilities

Select a capability, then use the tabs to see what it does, how an analyst actually uses it during a shift, and where it struggles — because knowing a tool's limits is half of wielding it.

05
Core concepts

Architecture: the machine, end to end

Put Lesson 5's pipeline and this lesson's capabilities together and the whole machine appears. Data flows left to right; analysts work the right edge:

FROM LESSON 5 THE SIEM PLATFORM ANALYSTS collectors ──TLS──▶ INGESTION ─▶ PARSE + NORMALIZE ─▶ INDEX & STORE (hot ▸ archive) │ │ ▼ ▼ DETECTION ENGINE ─────▶ ALERT QUEUE ◀─── triage · cases rules watch the stream │ ▼ SEARCH · DASHBOARDS · REPORTS

Three architectural truths worth internalizing. First, storage and detection are siblings fed by the same normalized stream: search interrogates the past, rules watch the present. Second, the platform scales horizontally — capacity is measured in EPS (events per second) and daily ingest volume, and big estates add nodes for indexing and search rather than one giant box. Third, the deployment model is a spectrum: self-hosted (you run everything, maximal control), cloud/SaaS (the vendor runs the platform, you run the content), and co-managed/MSSP arrangements in between. The concepts you're learning are identical across all three.

Licensing reality check. Most SIEMs charge by ingest volume or EPS — which is why Lesson 5's "collect by value, filter noise at the collector" isn't just engineering hygiene; it's budget. The person who onboards a chatty debug feed nobody queries has spent real money to make the haystack bigger.

06
Core concepts

Thinking in queries: filter, aggregate, present

Every SIEM has a query language — SPL, KQL, EQL, Lucene — and they all express the same three-step grammar. Learn the grammar and the dialects become vocabulary. The examples below use a generic pseudo-syntax; read the shape, not the punctuation:

1 · FILTER — carve the haystack down to candidate events (fields + time window) source=proxy dst_port=4444 earliest=-30d → every proxy event to port 4444 in the last 30 days — Lesson 2's challenge, fleet-wide
2 · AGGREGATE — turn events into an answer (count, group, sum) source=auth action=failure earliest=-1h | stats count by src_ip | sort -count → "who is failing logons the most this hour?" — brute force floats to the top row
3 · PIVOT — during triage: everything one entity did in one window host=FIN-WS-042 earliest=09:00 latest=10:00 | sort @timestamp → the host's full timeline across every normalized source — DNS, proxy, Sysmon, auth, in one view

Notice what makes query three possible at all: normalization. Because every source shares field names and UTC timestamps, "one host, one hour, all sources" is a single line instead of five consoles. That query — the entity timeline pivot — is the most-typed search in incident response, and you already understand every layer beneath it.

The same three questions in real dialects

Here are the filter, aggregate and pivot queries above in the two languages you're most likely to meet first: Splunk's SPL and Microsoft's KQL (Sentinel and Defender XDR). Same grammar, different spelling — and different field names, because each platform normalizes differently (Lesson 5).

# 1 · FILTER
index=proxy dest_port=4444 earliest=-30d

# 2 · AGGREGATE
index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 earliest=-1h
| stats count by src
| sort - count

# 3 · PIVOT (entity timeline)
host="FIN-WS-042" earliest="08/04/2026:09:00:00" latest="08/04/2026:10:00:00"
| sort 0 _time

Field names here follow Splunk's Common Information Model (src, dest_port); your index names and parsing may differ. sort 0 means “no row limit”.

// 1 · FILTER (firewall/proxy events arriving as CEF)
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort == 4444

// 2 · AGGREGATE
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize Failures = count() by IpAddress
| sort by Failures desc

// 3 · PIVOT (Defender XDR advanced hunting tables)
union DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents, DeviceFileEvents
| where DeviceName startswith "fin-ws-042"
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-08-04 09:00) .. datetime(2026-08-04 10:00))
| sort by Timestamp asc

KQL starts from a table and pipes downward; summarize is its stats. Elastic speaks its own languages too (ES|QL, EQL, KQL-for-Kibana) — the three-step grammar never changes.

Practice the grammar now. Lab 5 is a SIEM sandbox inside this page: eight challenges on a synthetic day of telemetry, each with the KQL equivalent of your answer.

Dashboards are saved questions. A dashboard panel is just a query on a refresh timer with a chart on top — "failed logons by office, last 24h" drawn as a bar chart. Useful for trends and health (remember Lesson 5's source-liveness board); never confuse a pretty dashboard with a detection — rules alert, dashboards inform.

07
Hands-on · Simulation

You're the analyst: which capability do you reach for?

A shift is a stream of tasks, and speed comes from routing each one to the right capability without thinking. For each request below, pick the SIEM feature that solves it. The feedback explains the routing logic.

Capability-routing drill

Task 1 / 6 · Score 0
08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

An alert's day in court — one pass through the whole machine

Lesson 5 followed a log to the SIEM's front door. Now walk the other half: the same Excel→PowerShell event arriving, matching a rule, becoming an alert, surviving triage, and — this is the part beginners miss — improving the system on its way out.

SIEM replay — "From stream to verdict"

IngestionThe stream never stopsTens of thousands of normalized events per second flow in — among them, one Sysmon Event 1 from FIN-WS-042 with a familiar parent-child pair.
Detection engineEvery rule reads every eventHundreds of correlation rules evaluate the stream continuously. Most events match nothing and settle quietly into the index. This one has an appointment.
Rule match"Office spawns script engine" firesparent_process ∈ office apps AND process ∈ script engines AND window=hidden. Normalized fields made this one line of logic — and that line just earned its keep.
Alert createdSeverity: highThe match becomes an alert object: rule name, the triggering events, timestamps, and a severity set by the rule's author. Not an incident yet — a lead.
EnrichmentContext attaches itselfAsset DB: finance workstation. Identity: m.haddad, finance team. Recent related alerts on this host: one, last month. The analyst will start with answers, not lookups.
QueueInto the triage queue, rankedIt lands among the shift's other alerts, sorted by severity and age. On a healthy SIEM it sits near the top instead of drowning — tuning is why.
Triage beginsAn analyst opens a caseOwnership recorded, clock started, notes begun. From here every finding lands in the case — the institutional memory that outlives the shift.
InvestigationThe pivot you already knowhost=FIN-WS-042, one-hour window, all sources: the doc download in proxy, the spawn in Sysmon, the C2 in firewall, the drop in file events. One query, whole story.
VerdictTrue positiveLineage, hidden window, encoded command, external connection — the evidence converges. The alert was right. Severity holds; escalation criteria met.
ResponseAction beyond the SIEMHost isolated via EDR, credentials reset, hash swept fleet-wide — executed by other tools, coordinated from the case. The SIEM observes; the stack acts.
DocumentationThe case closes, completeTimeline, evidence, actions, verdict — written while fresh. Next quarter's auditor, next month's similar incident, and next week's handover all read this record.
Tuning loopThe alert improves the systemReview: rule fired correctly, but enrichment missed the file hash — added. A sibling rule that stayed silent gets a fix. Today's incident just made tomorrow's detection sharper.
Ready. Press Play to run the alert lifecycle, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: the lifecycle is a loop, not a line. Alerts that end in verdicts and tuning make the funnel more precise every week; alerts that end in "closed, no notes" teach the system nothing. The difference between those two SOCs is culture, not products — and it's set by how Tier-1 analysts close their cases.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

SIEM misconceptions are expensive — some cost budgets, some cost breaches. Retire these before your first shift:

Misconception

"Deploy the SIEM and it starts catching attacks out of the box."

Reality

A SIEM ships as an engine, not a detective. Vendor rule packs are generic starting points; real detection comes from content engineering — rules built for your environment — and continuous tuning. An untuned SIEM is a very expensive log archive.

Misconception

"More alerts means more security."

Reality

Past the analysts' capacity, more alerts mean less security: alert fatigue trains people to skim, snooze, and miss the real one buried at position 3,847. The metric that matters is precision — the fraction of alerts worth raising — and tuning is how you buy it.

Misconception

"With a good SIEM, you barely need analysts."

Reality

The SIEM compresses millions of events into dozens of leads; judgment on leads is human work — context, intent, business impact, the phone call to ask "did you mean to do that?". Automation (SOAR, later modules) removes toil around the judgment, not the judgment.

Misconception

"The SIEM didn't alert, so nothing happened."

Reality

No alert means no rule matched what was collected. Coverage gaps (no rule for that behavior), pipeline gaps (Lesson 5's silent sources, broken parsers), and attacker tradecraft below thresholds are all invisible by definition. Absence of alerts is not evidence of absence — that's why hunting exists.

Misconception

"Buying the SIEM is the project. Then we're done."

Reality

The purchase is the cheapest part. The real program is people and process: onboarding sources, writing and tuning content, staffing triage, feeding lessons back. A modest SIEM with a disciplined team beats a flagship one running on defaults, every time.

Misconception

"Look at our dashboards — we'd definitely see an attack."

Reality

Dashboards are saved questions on a timer — superb for trends and pipeline health, but nobody stares at one at 3 a.m. Rules alert; dashboards inform. If a behavior matters, it needs a correlation rule with a severity and a queue, not a chart hoping to be noticed.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • SIEM = Security Information and Event Management: SIM's long memory plus SEM's fast reflex — one platform that collects, normalizes, detects, investigates, and reports.
  • Its reason to exist: attacks are cross-source stories, and only a centralized, normalized store can read them — five consoles can't.
  • Architecture in one breath: collectors → ingestion → parse/normalize → index & store (search the past) + detection engine (watch the present) → alert queue → analyst.
  • Every query is filter → aggregate → present; the entity-timeline pivot (one host, one window, all sources) is the workhorse of incident response.
  • Correlation rules turn normalized fields into real-time detections; dashboards are saved questions — rules alert, dashboards inform.
  • The alert lifecycle is a loop: match → enrich → triage → verdict → response → tuning. Closing cases without feeding the loop wastes the incident.
  • A SIEM is not prevention, not smart out of the box, and not a substitute for analysts — the funnel from 50 million events to a handful of incidents is built by people, content, and tuning.
11

Module 5 · Lesson 7

Data Onboarding:
Bringing Sources into the SIEM

You know the machine; now feed it. Onboarding is where blind spots are born or prevented — the disciplined path from "we should collect that" to a source the SOC can actually trust, one acceptance check at a time.

LEVELBeginner DURATION45–55 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–6 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • Start from the detection use case, then work backwards to the source and the exact fields it needs.
  • “Connected” isn't “usable”: prove liveness, timestamps, field population, coverage — and that a test alert fires.
  • Keep watching: upgrades break parsers and tokens expire silently. A silent source is a finding.
Hands-on:Lab 6 · Onboard logs into Splunk
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Plan use-case first

Start from the detection you want and work backwards to the data it needs — instead of drowning in "collect everything."

Connect the big five

Know how Windows, Linux, network devices, cloud platforms, and business applications each get their logs into the SIEM.

Run the onboarding lifecycle

Walk a source through six stages — define, scope, connect, map, validate, operate — without skipping the ones that hurt later.

Apply the acceptance checklist

Prove a source is usable, not just connected: liveness, timestamps, field population, coverage, and rule visibility.

Write validation queries

Use the query grammar from Lesson 6 to hunt missing hosts, empty fields, and clock skew before they hunt you.

Diagnose onboarding failures

Given a broken source, name which lifecycle stage was skipped or botched — and what would have caught it.

02
Orientation

Why "connected" and "usable" are different words

Here is the quiet scandal of many SOCs: the SIEM proudly lists three hundred connected sources, and a painful fraction of them are decorative. Events arrive but the username field is empty, so no rule matches. Timestamps run three hours ahead, so correlations miss. Forty servers in the fleet never actually reported, and nobody counted. Every one of those sources was "onboarded" — and every one is a blind spot wearing a green status light.

Onboarding is the discipline that prevents this. It treats each new source as a small engineering project with a defined purpose, an estimated cost, a connection plan, a field mapping, an acceptance test, and an owner. Done well, it's boring paperwork. Skipped, it becomes the incident review sentence nobody wants to write: "the data we needed was never actually being collected."

Analogy — hiring a witness

Onboarding a source is hiring a witness for future trials. You don't hire at random — you ask what testimony you'll need (the use case), check the witness can actually see the scene (coverage), confirm they speak a language the court understands (parsing), verify their watch is set correctly (timestamps), and then check in on them regularly (liveness). A witness hired without those checks shows up on trial day with nothing usable — and you find out exactly when it matters most.

Where this sits. Lesson 5 built the pipeline in theory; Lesson 6 showed the platform it feeds. This lesson is the practical bridge: the repeatable process that turns "we bought a SIEM" into "we can see our estate." It's also classic Tier-2/engineering work you'll assist with early and own later.

In plain words

Getting a new log source in is a careful process, not a checkbox. For each device you decide what to collect, how it travels, how it's parsed, and — crucially — you validate that it's actually arriving and give it an owner. The scary failure is a silent log source: it quietly stops sending, your detections keep “passing” against nothing, and you're blind without knowing it. If you can't see a system, you can't defend it.

03
Core concepts

Use-case first: work backwards from the detection

The single most important onboarding principle fits in one sentence: start from the detection you want, and work backwards to the data it requires. "Detect brute-force logons" needs authentication events with source IP and outcome. "Catch Office spawning script engines" needs process creation with command lines and parent info. "Spot C2 beacons" needs proxy or firewall events with destination, port, and bytes. The use case tells you which source, which event types, and which fields must survive parsing — everything downstream inherits from this decision.

The alternative — onboarding whatever is easiest or loudest — produces the estate from section 02: maximum license spend, minimum detection coverage. Remember Lesson 6's economics: most SIEMs charge by ingest, so every gigabyte of purposeless debug logging is money spent making the haystack bigger.

Prioritizing the queue: value ÷ (volume × effort)

You can't onboard everything at once, so sequence by return: investigative value divided by data volume and integration effort. That arithmetic is why Lesson 5's priority list looks the way it does — authentication and process creation are high-value, moderate-volume, well-supported; full packet capture is high-value but crushing volume; that custom legacy app is valuable but weeks of parser work. Mature programs keep an explicit onboarding backlog, ranked and re-ranked as detections demand new data.

The trap of the green checkmark. Every SIEM has a sources page full of reassuring status indicators. Those indicators usually mean "a connection exists" — not "fields parse," not "all hosts report," not "a rule could fire." This entire lesson is the difference between that green light and the truth. Trust acceptance tests, not dashboards.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five source families

Nearly every onboarding request falls into one of five families, each with its own collection method, its own must-have events, and its own classic mistakes. Select a family, then work the tabs — the gotchas tab is tuition other teams already paid.

05
Core concepts

The onboarding runbook: six stages, no shortcuts

Every source — a single firewall or a three-hundred-server fleet — walks the same six stages. Here's the runbook, written as the record you'd keep for one source:

SOURCE ONBOARDING RECORD — SRC-1204 1 DEFINE use case: detect outbound C2 from server VLAN → needs dst_ip, dst_port, action, bytes_out 2 SCOPE source: FW-02 (VendorX NGFW 7.0) · est volume: ~400 eps · license impact: approved 3 CONNECT syslog → collector-01 over TLS 6514 · firewall egress rule change: CHG-8817 4 MAP parser: vendorx-ngfw v7.x · fields verified against schema: src_ip dst_ip dst_port action bytes 5 VALIDATE acceptance checklist run: see section 06 · issues found: 1 (timestamp offset) · fixed & re-run 6 OPERATE owner: network team · liveness monitor: alert if last_event > 15 min · review: quarterly

Two stages deserve emphasis because they're the ones teams skip. Stage 2, scope, is where you estimate events-per-second and check the license before connecting — the alternative is discovering a budget problem in production. Stage 6, operate, is what keeps the source alive after the ticket closes: a named owner (sources outlive their onboarding engineers), a liveness monitor (Lesson 5's silence-is-a-signal, now standard practice), and a review cadence, because vendors change formats and tokens expire whether you're watching or not.

Fleets are sources too. "Onboard Windows" isn't one connection — it's a policy deployed to hundreds of hosts. The runbook is identical, but stage 5's coverage check becomes the star: the question isn't "are events arriving?" but "are events arriving from every host in the inventory?" A fleet at 87% coverage is 13% blind spot, distributed randomly across your estate.

06
Core concepts

The acceptance checklist: proving "usable"

Stage 5 is a battery of concrete tests. A source passes all of them or it isn't done — and each test is just a Lesson 6 query with a purpose:

  • Liveness — events are arriving now, and a monitor will notice if they stop.
  • Timestamps — event time is UTC and matches ingest time within seconds; no skew, no lag.
  • Field population — the fields the use case needs are parsed and non-empty at ~100%, not buried in a message blob.
  • Volume sanity — observed EPS is near the estimate; far under means missing data, far over means noise or a loop.
  • Coverage — every host in scope appears in the data; count against the asset inventory, never assume.
  • Rule visibility — a test detection actually fires on a simulated event; searchable is not the same as detectable.
  • Documented — owner, parser version, transport path, and monitor recorded where the next engineer will look.

Three of those checks as validation queries — read the shape, it's the filter → aggregate grammar you already own:

COVERAGE — who in the fleet has NOT spoken? (compare result count to inventory) source=linux_auth earliest=-24h | stats count by host → 260 hosts returned, inventory says 300 → forty servers are silent. Finding, not sign-off.
FIELD POPULATION — is the field the rule needs actually filling in? source=fw02 earliest=-1h | stats count, count(dst_port) as parsed → count=41,882 but parsed=0 → events arrive, parsing doesn't. The rule that queries dst_port is blind.
CLOCK SKEW — does the source's watch agree with reality? source=fw02 earliest=-15m | eval lag = _ingest_time - _event_time | stats avg(lag) → avg lag ≈ -10,800 s: events claim to be from three hours in the future → local timezone, not UTC. Fix at the source.

Validation never really ends. Firmware upgrades change formats (Lesson 5's silent parser break), API tokens and certificates expire, fleets grow past their collection policy. The acceptance checklist runs in full at onboarding — and its automated skeleton (liveness, parse rate, volume band) keeps running forever. That's the difference between a source you checked once and a source you can trust tonight.

07
Hands-on · Simulation

You're the analyst: which stage was botched?

Every onboarding failure traces back to a lifecycle stage that was skipped or rushed. For each incident below, name the stage where the mistake was made — not where the pain showed up. The feedback walks the trace-back reasoning.

Onboarding post-mortem drill

Case 1 / 6 · Score 0
08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

Onboarding FW-02 — from ticket to trusted source

Walk the runbook for real: one firewall, six stages, and — pay attention around step eight — a genuine defect that only the acceptance checklist stood any chance of catching before production.

Onboarding replay — "SRC-1204, end to end"

1 · DefineThe use case writes the shopping listGoal: detect outbound C2 from the server VLAN. Backwards from that: firewall traffic events with dst_ip, dst_port, action, bytes_out. Those four fields are now the contract.
2 · ScopeCost before connectionFW-02, VendorX NGFW 7.0. Estimated ~400 eps from similar units. License headroom confirmed, volume band recorded — the number step 10 will test against.
3 · ConnectChange request, not cowboy configFirewall configured to ship syslog to collector-01 over TLS 6514 via change CHG-8817. Lesson 5's transport rules applied by default: encrypted, acknowledged, buffered.
3 · ConnectFirst events landThe collector's intake shows FW-02 speaking — a few hundred events per second flowing to the SIEM. On many teams, this is where someone declares victory. Not here.
4 · MapParser assigned — by vendor AND versionThe vendorx-ngfw parser for the 7.x format family is applied. Version matters: the 6.x parser "mostly works" on 7.0 output — the most dangerous phrase in onboarding.
4 · MapContract fields verified against the schemasrc_ip, dst_ip, dst_port, action, bytes — each mapped to the common schema and spot-checked on live events. The C2 rule from step 1 will query exactly these names.
5 · ValidateChecklist begins: liveness and fields passEvents arriving steadily; field-population query shows the contract fields at 99.7%. Two boxes ticked. Then the timestamp check runs.
5 · ValidateDefect: events from three hours in the futureEvent-time vs ingest-time shows a clean -10,800 second offset. FW-02 is logging local time, not UTC. Every correlation window involving this source would silently miss.
5 · ValidateFix at the source, then re-run everythingNTP and UTC configured on the firewall; skew query re-run — lag now under two seconds. The checklist restarts from the top: a fix invalidates prior passes.
5 · ValidateVolume and coverage check outObserved 380 eps against the 400 estimate — inside the band. Single device, so coverage is 1 of 1. The estimate from step 2 just earned its keep.
5 · ValidateRule visibility: a test detection firesA benign connection to a test IP on port 4444 is generated; the C2 rule matches it within seconds. Searchable was never the goal — detectable is. Final box ticked.
6 · OperateOwner named, monitor armed, source trustedNetwork team owns it; liveness alert set at 15 minutes of silence; parser version and transport path documented. SRC-1204 closes — and stays honest without you.
Ready. Press Play to run the onboarding, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: the timestamp defect at step 8 would have been invisible on the sources dashboard — events flowing, status green — and devastating in production: three hours of skew quietly breaks every cross-source correlation this firewall touches. It was caught because a checklist item compared two clocks on purpose. Acceptance testing isn't bureaucracy; it's the only step whose whole job is finding what green lights hide.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Onboarding mistakes are slow-motion incidents — invisible for months, then decisive. Retire these now:

Misconception

"Events are arriving — the source is onboarded."

Reality

Arrival is one of seven acceptance checks, and the weakest. A source can stream events all day with empty fields, skewed clocks, and a third of its fleet missing. Connected is a cable; usable is a checklist.

Misconception

"Onboard everything on day one — we'll figure out what's useful later."

Reality

That's how license budgets die and haystacks grow. Use-case-first sequencing gets detection coverage per gigabyte: each source earns its ingest by feeding a named rule. The backlog can hold everything; the pipeline should hold what's justified.

Misconception

"The default parser will be fine."

Reality

Parsers are version-specific. The old-version parser on new-version output often "mostly works" — extracting some fields, silently dropping the ones your rule needed. Match parser to product and version, then prove it with a field-population query. "Mostly works" is a blind spot with good manners.

Misconception

"Documentation can wait — the ticket's closing."

Reality

Sources outlive their engineers. In eighteen months, someone will need the parser version, the transport path, and a human to call — during an incident, at speed. Undocumented sources become archaeology; documented ones become five-minute fixes.

Misconception

"We validated it at onboarding — it's good."

Reality

Sources drift: firmware upgrades change formats, API tokens and certificates expire, fleets outgrow their policies. Onboarding validation is a snapshot; liveness, parse-rate, and volume monitors are the movie. A source you checked once is not a source you can trust tonight.

Misconception

"Three hundred sources connected — look at our coverage!"

Reality

Source count is a vanity metric. Coverage is use cases fed with validated data: fields populated, clocks true, fleets complete, rules demonstrably firing. Fifty honest sources beat three hundred decorative ones — and only acceptance testing tells you which you have.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • Use-case first: start from the detection, work backwards to the source, event types, and the exact fields that must survive parsing — that's the contract everything downstream serves.
  • Sequence the backlog by value ÷ (volume × effort) — ingest licensing makes purposeless collection a real cost, not just clutter.
  • Five source families, five methods: Windows (agent/WEF, mind the channels), Linux (agent on auth/syslog/auditd), network (syslog over TLS), cloud (API pull, tokens expire), applications (custom parsers, budget the effort).
  • The lifecycle is six stages — define → scope → connect → map → validate → operate — and the skipped ones (scope, operate) are where future incidents hide.
  • The acceptance checklist proves "usable": liveness, timestamps, field population, volume sanity, coverage, rule visibility, documentation — each check is one purposeful query.
  • Coverage counts against inventory — 260 of 300 hosts reporting is a finding, not a sign-off; and searchable is not detectable — prove it with a test alert.
  • Validation never ends: liveness, parse-rate, and volume monitors are the standing guard against drift — upgrades, expiring tokens, and growing fleets don't announce themselves.

Eight questions, mixed formats. Onboarding judgment is checklist thinking — the scenarios test whether the checklist has become reflex.

Detection Engineering 101:
From Use Case to Correlation Rule

Seven lessons built the telemetry; now it starts hunting. Rule anatomy, thresholds and time windows, backtesting against history before anything pages a human — and the tuning discipline that decides whether your queue is a weapon or a wasteland.

LEVELBeginner DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–7 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • Every rule has scope, logic, threshold & window, severity and response metadata — plus a one-sentence use case.
  • The lifecycle is use case → data check → author → backtest → silent mode → production & review. Nothing pages a human untested.
  • Write rules as code (Sigma → SPL / KQL), test them against recorded attacks, and judge them by precision and recall.
Hands-on:Lab 4 · Write & test a detectionLab 5 · Browser SIEMLab 7 · Attack simulation
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Dissect a rule's anatomy

Name the parts every detection rule shares — scope, logic, threshold, window, severity — and read unfamiliar rules by their skeleton.

Choose the right rule type

Match a detection need to signature, threshold, sequence, anomaly, or intel-driven logic — each catches what the others miss.

Run the rule lifecycle

Take an idea from use case through backtesting and silent deployment to production — without paging anyone prematurely.

Reason about precision

Balance false positives against false negatives deliberately, using thresholds, windows, and documented exceptions.

Judge rules by metrics

Read fire rate, true-positive percentage, and time-to-triage per rule — and know when a rule needs tuning or retirement.

Spot spraying vs brute force

Recognize how attackers shape their behavior to slip under thresholds — and how detection logic adapts in response.

02
Orientation

Why rules are the SOC's memory made executable

Every rule in the SIEM is a lesson someone learned, written down so a machine can apply it forever. "Office spawning a script engine is rarely innocent" — an incident taught somebody that, and now a rule checks it fifty thousand times a second without coffee or sleep. The rule set is the SOC's institutional knowledge, compiled and running. A SOC with three analysts and three hundred sharp rules out-detects a SOC with thirty analysts staring at raw logs, every single time.

Which is also the warning. Rules are the faucet that fills Lesson 6's alert queue — and the queue's quality is set here, at authoring and tuning time, not at triage time. Every sloppy rule taxes every future shift: a rule firing two hundred times a day at one percent true-positive doesn't just waste its own alerts, it trains analysts to skim, and skimming is how the real one gets missed. Detection engineering is writing checks that Tier-1 has to cash.

Analogy — the smoke detector wall

A building's detectors are placed deliberately: heat sensors in the kitchen (steam would false-alarm a smoke sensor), smoke sensors in bedrooms, each with a threshold chosen so burnt toast doesn't evacuate the tower but a real fire triggers in seconds. Nobody installs four hundred random detectors and hopes; and every false alarm gets investigated and the detector adjusted. Your rule set deserves the same architecture: right sensor, right place, right threshold — and relentless adjustment.

Where this sits. Lesson 7 validated the data; this lesson turns it into detections; Lesson 9 will teach the triage of what these rules produce. You're now on the authoring side of the alert lifecycle you replayed in Lesson 6 — including the tuning loop that closes it.

In plain words

A detection is a rule that turns raw logs into an alert — and you build it like software. You write it (often in Sigma, a portable format), map it to a known attacker technique (MITRE ATT&CK), and test it by replaying real attack data. Then you tune it to cut false alarms without going blind. A rule you never tested is just a guess.

03
Core concepts

Rule anatomy: five parts, every rule, every product

Vendors dress them differently, but every detection rule has the same skeleton. Learn it once and you can read any rule in any SIEM:

Scope

Which data it watches — source, event types, sometimes an asset group. "Windows process-creation events" or "proxy traffic from server VLANs." Narrow scope is free precision.

Logic

The condition that must match — field comparisons over normalized data: parent_process is an Office app AND process is a script engine. This is where Lesson 7's field contract gets cashed.

Threshold & window

How many, how fast — "more than 50 in 5 minutes." The pair that separates one typo from an attack, and the primary tuning dial you'll turn for the rest of your career.

Severity

Triage, decided in advance — the rule author ranks the queue before the alert exists. Severity inflation ("everything is HIGH") is queue poison; discipline here is kindness to future analysts.

Response metadata

What the analyst needs on arrival — a description of why this matters, the triage runbook link, known false-positive causes, and tags mapping the rule to attacker techniques.

…and a use case

Not a field in the rule — the reason it exists. Every rule should answer "what attack does this catch?" in one sentence. If it can't, it's noise with a version number.

The fidelity spectrum

Detections live on a spectrum. At one end, high-fidelity signatures: a known-bad hash executes, event 1102 fires — nearly always real, trivially evaded by an attacker who changes one byte. At the other, behavioral logic: "Office spawns a script engine," "many accounts, few attempts each" — harder to evade because it targets what attackers must do rather than what tools they use, but demanding careful tuning because legitimate activity sometimes rhymes with attacks. A mature rule set deliberately covers both ends: signatures for speed and certainty, behavior for resilience. Neither alone is a strategy.

The community shelf. Open rule collections — the Sigma project is the flagship — encode thousands of detections in a portable format. They're superb starting points and terrible final states: field names, thresholds, and exclusions must be fitted to your environment and proven by backtest. Deploying community rules unchanged is how you inherit someone else's false positives at industrial scale.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five rule types

Five kinds of logic cover nearly every detection you'll ever write — and each has a worked example and a characteristic way of failing. Select a type, then work the tabs; the failure modes are how attackers think about your rules.

05
Core concepts

The rule lifecycle: nothing pages a human untested

A rule is software with an on-call rotation attached — so it gets an engineering lifecycle. Here's a rule definition in a portable, Sigma-flavored pseudo-format, annotated part by part:

RULE DEFINITION — R-2041 (pseudo-format; every SIEM has an equivalent) title: Password spraying — many accounts, few attempts, one source status: monitor # silent mode: records matches, pages nobody — yet logsource: authentication # SCOPE — the data it watches detection: selection: action=failure # LOGIC — what counts condition: distinct(username) > 20 by src_ip # THRESHOLD — how many timeframe: 30m # WINDOW — how fast level: high # SEVERITY — triage decided in advance falsepositives: vulnerability scanners, password-audit tooling runbook: KB-118 · spray triage # RESPONSE METADATA — what the analyst gets

The lifecycle wrapped around that definition has six stages. Use case: one sentence naming the attack. Data check: confirm the fields exist and populate — Lesson 7's acceptance work is the prerequisite; a rule over ghost fields matches nothing, silently. Author: write the logic against the schema. Backtest: run it over weeks or months of history — every hit is either an incident you missed or a false-positive source you must handle now, before deployment. Silent deployment: run in monitor mode against live data, generating records but no pages, until the fire rate and precision are known. Production & review: enable paging, then track per-rule metrics forever — fire rate, true-positive percentage, time-to-triage — because those numbers, not opinions, decide what gets tuned or retired.

The backtest is not optional. History is the only free preview of a rule's behavior. A rule that fires 400 times across 90 days of history will fire 400 times a month in production — except in production, each one interrupts a human. Ten minutes of backtesting routinely saves a rollback, an apology to the night shift, and the quiet credibility damage of a noisy launch.

06
Core concepts

Precision, recall & the tuning discipline

Two ways a rule can be wrong, forever in tension. A false positive fires on innocence — it costs analyst minutes and, in bulk, attention itself. A false negative stays silent on an attack — it costs the breach. In analyst terms: precision is "when it fires, how often is it real?" and recall is "of the real attacks, how many does it catch?" Every threshold you raise buys precision by spending recall; every exception you add does the same. Tuning is choosing that trade deliberately, per rule, with eyes open — the mistake isn't making the trade, it's making it by accident.

The dials, in the order you should reach for them: narrow the scope (server VLANs instead of everything — free precision), adjust threshold and window (the spraying rule's 20-in-30m came from backtest data, not vibes), and add exceptions — the vulnerability scanner that legitimately fails logons across every host. Exceptions are where discipline lives or dies: every one must be specific (that scanner's IP, not "internal ranges"), documented (why, who approved, when), and reviewed (attackers who learn your exceptions operate from inside them). An undocumented exception is a blind spot with no expiry date.

TUNING CHANGELOG — R-2041 (the rule's memory; every change is a decision on record) v1.0 backtest 90d: 3 hits — 2 = vuln scanner 10.20.8.14, 1 = unexplained (escalated) v1.1 exception: src_ip=10.20.8.14 (scanner; approved SEC-441; review quarterly) v1.2 silent mode 14d: fired 2, both true → precision est. 100%, fire rate ~1/wk v1.3 status: production · severity high · runbook KB-118 attached v1.4 quarterly review: 6 fired / 5 TP (83%) · threshold holds · exception still valid

Per-rule metrics close the loop: fire rate (alerts per day), precision (TP percentage from analyst verdicts — this is why Lesson 6 insisted verdicts feed back), and time-to-triage (expensive alerts reveal missing enrichment or unclear runbooks). And rules can retire: the product it watched was decommissioned, or a better rule supersedes it. A rule set that only ever grows becomes sediment; review cadence keeps it an arsenal.

Zero false positives is a smell, not a triumph. A rule that never false-fires is often a rule tuned so narrow it would miss the real thing too — precision bought with recall nobody agreed to spend. Perfect silence deserves the same scrutiny as constant noise: test it against a simulated attack (you proved you could in Lesson 7) and find out which kind of quiet it is.

07
Core concepts · From pseudo-code to production

Real rules: Sigma, SPL, KQL & detection-as-code

R-2041 above was written in pseudo-format on purpose: the anatomy matters more than the punctuation. But on day one of the job you'll read and write real syntax. Here is the same rule three ways — the portable Sigma source, the Splunk search a converter generates from it, and a hand-written Microsoft Sentinel query. Notice that scope, logic, threshold, window and the documented exception survive every translation.

title: Failed Windows logon (R-2041 base)
id: 0e95725d-7320-415d-80f7-004da920fc11
name: failed_logon
status: test
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4625
  filter_scanner:
    IpAddress: '10.20.8.14'   # SEC-441 approved scanner, review quarterly
  condition: selection and not filter_scanner
level: informational
---
title: Password spraying - many accounts, few attempts, one source (R-2041)
id: 3b2a7c90-51f4-4d0e-a6c2-7e19d4f08b22
status: test
tags:
  - attack.credential-access
  - attack.t1110.003
correlation:
  type: value_count
  rules:
    - failed_logon
  group-by:
    - IpAddress
  timespan: 30m
  condition:
    field: TargetUserName
    gt: 20
falsepositives:
  - Vulnerability scanners and password-audit tools
level: high

Two documents: a base rule that selects single events (failed logons, minus the documented scanner), and a correlation rule (Sigma's v2 specification) that counts distinct usernames per source IP over 30 minutes. The attack.t1110.003 tag maps it to ATT&CK Password Spraying — that tag is what coverage maps are built from.

source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4625 NOT IpAddress="10.20.8.14"
| bin _time span=30m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) as value_count by _time IpAddress
| search value_count > 20

This is the exact output of sigma convert -t splunk -p splunk_windows r2041.yml (sigma-cli with the Splunk backend). Field names like TargetUserName and IpAddress assume Windows events parsed by the Splunk Add-on for Windows; in a CIM-normalized estate you'd write user and src. That gap is Lesson 7's field contract — and why the pipeline step (-p) exists.

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventID == 4625
| where IpAddress != "10.20.8.14"   // SEC-441: approved scanner, review quarterly
| summarize Accounts = dcount(TargetUserName), Attempts = count()
    by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| where Accounts > 20

KQL (Microsoft Sentinel / Defender) reads top to bottom like a pipeline: table, filters, summarize (KQL's stats), then the threshold. Saved as a scheduled analytics rule with a query frequency and look-back, it becomes a production detection.

Fixed buckets leak. bin cuts time into fixed 30-minute slots. A 24-account spray running 10:20–10:40 splits across two buckets — about 12 accounts in each — and never crosses 20. Platforms counter this with scheduled rules whose look-back is longer than the window, or with sliding-window correlation engines. Your backtest is where you discover which one your rule needs.

Detection-as-code: rules are software, so ship them like software

Mature teams keep detections in a Git repository and give them the same discipline as production code. Every change is a pull request a second engineer reviews; a pipeline validates and tests it; deployment is automated and reversible; and the history answers “who changed this threshold, and why?” years later.

detections/
├── rules/windows/credential_access/r2041_password_spray.yml
├── tests/r2041/
│   ├── tp_spray_26_accounts.json        # recorded attack events  → must fire
│   └── tn_scanner_sec441.json           # approved scanner        → must NOT fire
├── docs/r2041.md                        # ADS write-up (below)
└── .github/workflows/detections.yml     # CI: validate → convert → test → deploy
The pipeline, step by step
  1. Validate — syntax and required fields (sigma check or your platform's linter).
  2. Convert — to every target SIEM (sigma convert).
  3. Test — run against recorded true-positive and true-negative samples; a rule that stops firing on its own attack sample fails the build.
  4. Deploy — via API, in monitor mode first (section 05's silent deployment).
  5. Promote & review — production after silent-mode metrics; every change versioned and revertable.
Document with ADS

Palantir's open Alerting & Detection Strategy framework gives every rule the same write-up: goal · ATT&CK categorization · strategy abstract · technical context · blind spots & assumptions · false positives · validation · priority · response. “Blind spots” is the section that keeps a team honest: R-2041 cannot see a spray spread across many source IPs.

Test with emulation, not hope

Purple-team exercises are rare; Atomic Red Team tests are free and run in minutes — small scripts that reproduce one ATT&CK technique each. Run the atomic, confirm the rule fires, and keep the run's events as a regression sample in tests/. (Lab 7 walks you through it.)

Measure coverage honestly

ATT&CK tags let you paint your rules onto the matrix in the ATT&CK Navigator. Count a technique as covered only when a tested rule exists for the data you actually collect — a tagged-but-untested rule is a hope, and an all-green heatmap is a vanity metric (Lesson 20).

Do it, don't just read it. Lab 5 lets you build R-2041 query by query in a SIEM sandbox inside this page. Lab 4 writes a Sigma rule and runs it with a real engine against your own telemetry, and Lab 7 validates a rule with an Atomic Red Team test and maps your coverage.

08
Hands-on · Simulation

You're the engineer: pick the rule type

Six detection requests from the backlog. For each, choose the logic type that fits — the feedback explains why, and why the neighboring types would fail. Routing requests to logic types is the first reflex of detection engineering.

Rule-type routing drill

Request 1 / 6 · Score 0
09
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

Birth of a rule — R-2041, from gap to production

Follow one rule through its entire lifecycle: a purple-team exercise exposes a blind spot, and twelve steps later a tested, tuned, documented detection stands watch. Note how many steps happen before anyone gets paged — that's the discipline.

Detection replay — "R-2041: password spraying"

The gapA purple-team exercise walks right past the rulesRed team sprays two attempts against each of 200 accounts. The brute-force rule — 50 failures per account — never stirs. Nobody planned for an attacker who read the thresholds.
Use caseOne sentence, written down"Detect password spraying: many distinct accounts, few attempts each, from a single source." The inverse of brute force — and invisible to per-account counting.
Data checkDo the fields even exist?The logic needs action, username, and src_ip from authentication events — all validated at 99%+ population during Lesson 7's onboarding. The contract holds; authoring may proceed.
AuthorLogic drafted against the schemaaction=failure, grouped by src_ip: more than 20 distinct usernames within 30 minutes. Thresholds are guesses at this point — the backtest will correct them.
Backtest90 days of history, interrogatedThree hits. Two trace to the vulnerability scanner at 10.20.8.14 — a false-positive source found before it ever paged anyone. The third has no innocent explanation.
BacktestThe third hit becomes an incidentA real spray from six weeks ago, undetected at the time. Escalated for investigation on the spot — backtests routinely find history you missed, which is reason enough to run them.
TuneException: specific, documented, reviewablesrc_ip=10.20.8.14 excluded — that host, not a range; approval SEC-441 recorded; quarterly review scheduled. The changelog starts keeping the rule's memory.
Silent modeDeployed with the pager unpluggedStatus: monitor. Live data flows through the logic for two weeks; matches are recorded, nobody is interrupted. The rule earns trust before it spends attention.
Silent modeThe numbers come in cleanTwo fires in fourteen days, both true positives against a test spray and a red-team rerun. Estimated precision: high. Fire rate: comfortably sane. Evidence, not hope.
PackageSeverity and runbook attachedLevel: high — a spray in progress is minutes from a valid credential. Runbook KB-118 linked: what to check, who to call, how to contain. The analyst will arrive equipped.
ProductionThe pager goes live — and earns its first saveEleven days in, R-2041 fires on a real spray against the VPN. Caught at account 23 of what the attacker planned as 400. Triage to containment: nine minutes.
ReviewQuarterly, by the numbersSix fires, five true — 83% precision; threshold holds; the exception is still justified. The rule joins the arsenal's permanent rotation. Somewhere, a red team updates its playbook.
Ready. Press Play to run the rule lifecycle, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: the rule paged a human for the first time at step 11 — after a backtest, a discovered incident, a documented exception, and two weeks of silent metrics. Compare the anti-pattern: draft logic at 4 p.m., enable HIGH severity at 5, flood the night shift by midnight. The lifecycle isn't bureaucracy slowing detection down; it's what makes the queue trustworthy enough that a HIGH actually means something.

10
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Detection engineering mistakes are paid for by other people — the analysts working the queue. Retire these before writing rule one:

Misconception

"More rules means more coverage."

Reality

More tuned rules means more coverage. Untuned rules are negative coverage: they flood the queue, burn analyst attention, and bury the alerts from good rules. Fifty maintained detections beat five hundred abandoned ones — the queue does the math either way.

Misconception

"Community rules are plug-and-play — someone already did the work."

Reality

Someone did half the work: the logic. Field names must map to your schema, thresholds must fit your volumes, and exclusions must match your environment — then a backtest must prove it. Community rules are excellent drafts and terrible deployments.

Misconception

"The rule works — set it and forget it."

Reality

Environments drift: new software rhymes with old attacks, upgrades rename fields (Lesson 5's silent parser break now silently breaks your logic), attackers adapt to known thresholds. Rules need review cadence and per-rule metrics — a detection nobody maintains is a detection nobody can trust.

Misconception

"When unsure, mark it HIGH — better safe than sorry."

Reality

Severity inflation destroys the only ranking the queue has. When everything is HIGH, nothing is — analysts re-triage from scratch, which is the queue failing at its one job. Severity is a promise about urgency; keep it honest or lose it entirely.

Misconception

"False positives mean the rule is bad."

Reality

False positives mean the rule is alive — behavioral detections trade some noise for evasion resistance, and tuning that noise down is the job, not a defect. The suspicious extreme is the other one: a rule that never false-fires may be too narrow to catch the real thing. Judge rules by precision and recall, never one alone.

Misconception

"Just enable it in production — we'll see how it behaves."

Reality

You will — through the night shift's suffering. History and silent mode exist precisely so a rule's behavior is known before it can interrupt a human: backtest for the past, monitor mode for the present, production only when the numbers are in. Nothing pages a human untested.

11
Consolidate

What to remember

  • Every rule shares one skeleton: scope, logic, threshold & window, severity, response metadata — plus a one-sentence use case naming the attack it catches.
  • Five logic types cover the field: signature (known-bad, fast, evadable), threshold (N in T), sequence (A then B, across sources), anomaly (deviation from baseline), intel-driven (match against feeds) — mature coverage mixes them deliberately.
  • The fidelity spectrum: signatures are precise but brittle, behavior is resilient but noisy — cover both ends, because attackers pick whichever end you left open.
  • The lifecycle is use case → data check → author → backtest → silent mode → production & review — and nothing pages a human until history and silent metrics say it's ready.
  • Precision vs recall is a deliberate trade: scope first, thresholds second, exceptions last — every exception specific, documented, reviewed.
  • Judge rules by metrics, not vibes: fire rate, true-positive percentage from analyst verdicts, time-to-triage — and retire what no longer earns its place.
  • Attackers read thresholds too: spraying (many accounts, few attempts) exists to duck the brute-force rule — which is why detection engineering never finishes, only iterates.
12
