Module 7 · Lesson 9

Alert Triage & Investigation:
The Analyst's Core Loop

Eight lessons built the machine that raises alerts. This one puts you in the chair that answers them: the triage questions that sort real from noise in minutes, the pivots that turn a lead into a story, and the verdicts that make the whole system smarter.

LEVELBeginner DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–8 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • Triage is a fixed protocol: what is claimed → is it true → is it active → scope → verdict, under a timebox.
  • Severity ranks the queue; it isn't evidence. Validate the rule's claim against raw data every time.
  • TP, FP and benign-TP verdicts drive different fixes; escalate with a package — summary, evidence, actions, a clear ask.
Hands-on:Lab 9 · Run a full triage
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Work a queue methodically

Apply the five triage questions to any alert, in order, without skipping the ones that feel obvious.

Validate before believing

Confirm what the rule claims against what the data shows — severity is a promise, not a verdict.

Pivot with purpose

Run the standard investigation moves — entity timeline, who-else, prevalence, before/after — knowing what question each answers.

Call clean verdicts

Distinguish true positive, false positive, and benign true positive — and know why the third category exists.

Escalate like a professional

Know when to hand off, and package the handoff so Tier-2 starts running instead of re-investigating.

Write notes that count

Document as you go, in UTC, separating what you observed from what you infer — evidence hygiene under time pressure.

02
Orientation

Why methodology beats heroics

Triage is the SOC's heartbeat: the repeating loop where a human looks at what the machine flagged and decides what's real. It's where every previous lesson converges — the rule fired (Lesson 8) on normalized data (5–7) describing network and endpoint behavior (2–4), and now the queue (6) is waiting. Most of an analyst's shift is this loop, and the SOC's actual detection rate is set here: a perfect rule whose alert gets skimmed and bulk-closed detected nothing.

The case for methodology over instinct is brutal arithmetic. You'll triage thousands of alerts a year; the one that matters will look, at first glance, much like the hundreds that didn't. A fixed sequence of questions is what keeps alert four-hundred-and-seven getting the same scrutiny as alert one — and it's what makes your verdicts consistent enough to feed the tuning loop that Lesson 8 built. Heroic intuition has a bad habit of taking nights off; checklists don't.

Analogy — the emergency department

An ER triage nurse doesn't diagnose everyone fully — they run a fixed rapid assessment on each arrival: vitals, chief complaint, severity, then route — treat here, admit, or call the specialist. Speed comes from the protocol, not from rushing; and the notes travel with the patient so the specialist never starts from zero. Swap patients for alerts and you have Tier-1 triage exactly: assess fast, route correctly, document so the next person runs.

Where this sits. You replayed an alert's lifecycle in Lesson 6 and authored the rule behind one in Lesson 8. This lesson is the human middle of that lifecycle — the triage-and-verdict stage — done properly. Lesson 10 picks up where a confirmed incident leaves Tier-1's hands.

In plain words

Triage is the fast first look at an alert: is it real, how bad, what next? You compare it to what's normal (baseline), follow the evidence sideways (pivot), and lay out everything one user or machine did in order (an entity timeline). Then you decide — escalate or close — and write down why. The written reasoning matters as much as the verdict.

03
Core concepts

The five questions, and the three verdicts

Every alert, regardless of rule or severity, gets the same five questions in the same order:

1 · What is claimed?

Read the alert properly: which rule, why it exists, what entities, what severity and why. The runbook and false-positive notes (Lesson 8's response metadata) are the author talking to you — listen first.

2 · Is the claim true?

Validate the trigger against raw data: did 23 distinct accounts really fail from that IP, or did a parsing quirk inflate a count? Rules can be wrong about their own evidence — check before building on it.

3 · Is it active?

Ongoing changes everything: an attack in progress needs containment in minutes; a historical match needs investigation in hours. One time-bounded query answers it — ask early.

4 · What's the scope & impact?

Pivot outward: what else did this entity touch, did anything succeed, what is the asset worth? A spray that failed everywhere and a spray with one success on a service account are different emergencies.

5 · Verdict & action

Call it, with confidence stated; then act — close with reason, escalate with a package, or trigger response. And write the verdict down: it's the datapoint Lesson 8's precision metrics are made of.

…under a timebox

Not a question — a discipline. Tier-1 triage has a time budget (commonly 15–30 minutes). Hitting the wall isn't failure; it's an escalation criterion. Queues die when analysts marinate.

The verdict vocabulary

Three verdicts, and the third one is where beginners stumble. True positive (TP): the detected activity happened and is malicious — the alert did its job. False positive (FP): the alert misrepresents reality — the activity didn't happen as described (a geo-lookup artifact "moved" a VPN user to another country; a parsing quirk double-counted). Benign true positive (BTP): the activity happened exactly as detected — but it's authorized. The vulnerability scanner really did fail five hundred logons; the sysadmin really did clear that log during a decommission. BTP matters because the fix differs: FPs mean the rule's logic misreads data; BTPs mean the rule needs a documented exception. Mislabel them and you tune the wrong dial.

Severity is not a verdict. The HIGH on an alert is the rule author's estimate of urgency if true — it ranks the queue, nothing more. HIGHs are false sometimes; LOWs are real sometimes. The moment "it says HIGH so it's probably real" creeps into your reasoning, the attacker who triggers MEDIUMs owns your estate.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five triage phases

The five questions become five working phases at the desk. Select a phase, then work the tabs — the "where it goes wrong" tab is a catalog of the exact shortcuts that get real intrusions closed as noise.

05
Core concepts

The investigation toolkit: five pivots, one notebook

Investigation is a small set of reusable moves — each a Lesson 6 query shape with a purpose. Learn what question each pivot answers and you'll never stare at an alert wondering what to type:

  • Entity timeline — one host or user, bounded window, all sources, sorted by time. Answers: what's the story around this alert? The workhorse; you've known it since Lesson 6.
  • Who-else — pivot on the indicator: which other hosts touched this IP, hash, or domain? Answers: is this one machine's problem or the fleet's?
  • Before / after — widen the window around the trigger: what led here, what followed? Answers: cause, and consequence — the difference between a download and a breach.
  • Prevalence check — how common is this process, domain, or behavior across the estate? Answers: is this weird? Ubiquitous means probably-fine; first-ever-seen means keep digging.
  • Reputation lookup — the external indicator against intel: known-bad, known-good, or unknown? Answers: has the world seen this before? Treat "unknown" as unknown — not as innocent.

And the notebook. Notes are written as you go, not reconstructed after — memory under adrenaline is a liar. Three habits make notes evidence-grade: timestamps in UTC on every entry (your notes must interleave cleanly with the logs), observation separated from inference ("23 distinct accounts failed from 203.0.113.77" is observation; "this is a spray" is inference — both belong, labeled), and queries recorded verbatim, so anyone can re-run your steps. Here's what that looks like at speed:

CASE 2041-118 — triage notes (analyst: you · all times UTC) 09:07 alert received: R-2041 spray sev=HIGH src=203.0.113.77 ← observation 09:09 ran: source=auth action=failure src_ip=203.0.113.77 -30m → 23 distinct accounts confirmed ← observation + query on record 09:11 pattern consistent with password spraying ← inference, labeled as such 09:13 ran: same src action=success → 1 hit: svc-vpn01 09:05 ← the finding that changes everything

Absence of evidence needs a health check. Before "no results" becomes "didn't happen," verify the telemetry: is the source alive, are the fields populated, does the window cover the right time? You spent Lessons 5 and 7 learning every way a pipeline lies by silence — triage is where that knowledge cashes out. An empty result from a broken source is not an FP; it's a second finding.

06
Core concepts

Escalation: when, and how to hand off clean

Escalation is the system working, not the analyst failing — Tier-1's job is to sort, and sorting includes routing upward. Four triggers make the call for you: confirmed TP with real impact (a success on that spray, code execution on an endpoint); scope beyond your authority (containment decisions, crown-jewel assets, anything touching executives or production payments); the timebox expired and the verdict is still unclear; and you found something the alert wasn't about — the second finding that smells worse than the first.

What separates a professional escalation from a hot potato is the package. Tier-2 should start running, not re-investigating — which means your handoff carries four things: a two-line summary (what happened, why it matters), the key evidence with UTC timestamps and the queries that produced it, the actions already taken (so nothing is duplicated or missed), and a clear ask — what decision or capability you need from them. Compare the anti-pattern: forwarding an alert ID with "looks bad, pls check."

ESCALATION — CASE 2041-118 → Tier-2 (09:16 UTC) SUMMARY Password spray from 203.0.113.77, ongoing since 08:52. 1 successful auth: svc-vpn01 @ 09:05 — service account, VPN infra. EVIDENCE 23 distinct accounts, failures continuing (queries in case notes 09:09–09:13) ACTIONS none taken — containment beyond T1 authority; session NOT yet terminated ASK approve: block src IP at perimeter + kill svc-vpn01 sessions + credential reset

Notice the last line does Tier-2's first three minutes of thinking for them. That's the standard: every handoff should shorten the incident, not just relocate it. And when the case closes — whoever closes it — the verdict flows back to the rule's metrics, the exception list, or the enrichment backlog. You saw that loop from the engineer's side in Lesson 8; now you're the one feeding it.

07
Hands-on · Simulation

You're the analyst: call the verdict

Six alerts, investigated to the point of decision. For each, call it: true positive, false positive, benign true positive — or admit the data isn't there yet. The feedback explains the category logic, which is the real lesson.

Verdict-calling drill

Alert 1 / 6 · Score 0
08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

Nine minutes — one triage, queue to escalation

Lesson 8 ended with R-2041 catching a live spray and "nine minutes to containment." Here are those nine minutes, from the analyst's side of the screen — every phase, every pivot, every note, in real time.

Triage replay — "Case 2041-118"

09:07 · QueueThe alert lands on topR-2041, HIGH, password spraying from 203.0.113.77. Severity and age rank it first; the case opens, the clock starts, and the notes file gets its first UTC timestamp.
Phase 1 · ReadThirty seconds with the authorRule intent: many accounts, few attempts, one source. Known FPs: vuln scanners (excluded already). Runbook KB-118 open in a tab. The alert's claim is now precisely understood.
Phase 2 · ValidateThe claim survives contact with raw dataQuery: failures from that IP, last 30 minutes — 23 distinct accounts, alphabetical username pattern, ~2 attempts each. The rule read the data correctly. Noted, with the query verbatim.
Phase 3 · Active?Still happening — right nowSame query, last 2 minutes: fresh failures. This is an attack in progress, not history. The timebox mentally halves; containment questions move to the front.
Phase 4 · ScopeThe pivot that changes the nightSame source, action=success: one hit. svc-vpn01 authenticated at 09:05 — two minutes before the alert even fired. The spray isn't attempted access anymore; it's achieved access.
Phase 4 · ImpactAsset context multiplies the stakesEnrichment answers instantly: svc-vpn01 is a service account on VPN infrastructure — a credential that opens the front door from anywhere. Who-else pivot: no other sources, no lateral movement yet. Yet.
Phase 4 · TimelineBefore / after locks the story downThe account's history: datacenter subnet only, for months — until 09:05 from an external IP. Post-success activity: session established, no commands yet visible. The window for cheap containment is open, and closing.
Phase 5 · VerdictTrue positive, high confidence — in writingObservation: spray confirmed, one success, anomalous source for the account. Inference, labeled: active credential compromise. Verdict recorded at 09:14. No attribution theater — just what the evidence supports.
EscalateThe trigger is automaticConfirmed TP + real impact + containment beyond Tier-1 authority: three escalation criteria at once. This stopped being a solo case at step 5; now the handoff makes it official.
The packageSummary, evidence, actions, askTwo-line summary; queries with timestamps; "no actions taken — beyond T1 authority"; ask: block the IP, kill the sessions, reset the credential. Tier-2's first three minutes of thinking, pre-done.
09:16 · HandoffTier-2 starts running, not readingIP blocked, sessions terminated, credential reset — nine minutes from alert to containment. The handoff package is why the response began at 'act', not at 'wait, what happened?'.
Close the loopThe verdict becomes fuelTP recorded → R-2041's precision metric improves. One gap noted: enrichment didn't flag svc-vpn01 as a service account automatically — backlog item filed. The case made the system smarter on its way out.
Ready. Press Play to run the triage, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: nothing in these nine minutes was improvised. Five phases in order, three pivots you already knew, notes in UTC, a handoff with a clear ask — the speed came from the methodology, not despite it. The analyst never wondered what to do next; the protocol always knew. That's what "trained" means at 3 a.m.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Triage habits form fast and calcify faster. These are the ones to refuse from day one:

Misconception

"A fast analyst is one who closes the most alerts."

Reality

Throughput without verdict quality is worse than useless — wrong verdicts poison the tuning metrics and bulk-closing is how the real one dies at position 3,847. The measure that matters is correct verdicts per shift, at protocol speed. The checklist is fast enough.

Misconception

"It's marked HIGH — it's probably real."

Reality

Severity is the author's urgency estimate if true — a queue-ranking device, not evidence. HIGHs false-fire; LOWs catch intrusions. Validation (phase 2) exists precisely because the rule's claim and the data's truth are separate things until you check.

Misconception

"I searched, found nothing — false positive, closed."

Reality

Empty results have three explanations: nothing happened, your query was wrong (window, field, typo), or the telemetry is broken — and Lessons 5 and 7 taught you how often it's the third. Verify the source is alive and the fields populate before absence of evidence becomes a verdict.

Misconception

"I'll write the notes after I've figured it out."

Reality

After-the-fact notes are memoirs, not evidence — timestamps get reconstructed, queries get paraphrased, and the inference you made at 09:11 quietly becomes something you 'observed'. Note as you go, UTC, queries verbatim. Your notes should let a stranger replay your investigation keystroke by keystroke.

Misconception

"Escalating means I couldn't handle it."

Reality

Escalation is Tier-1's product — the whole design assumes leads get sorted and routed. A confirmed TP escalated in nine minutes with a clean package is the system working perfectly. The actual failure mode is its opposite: sitting on a live intrusion to avoid 'bothering' Tier-2.

Misconception

"The activity really happened, so it's a true positive."

Reality

Not if it was authorized — that's a benign true positive, and the distinction drives the fix: FPs mean the rule misreads data (fix the logic); BTPs mean the rule reads correctly but needs a documented exception (fix the scope). Collapse the categories and you'll tune the wrong dial, forever.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • Triage is a fixed protocol, not a vibe: what is claimed → is it true → is it active → scope & impact → verdict & action, every alert, under a timebox.
  • Severity ranks the queue; it is not evidence. Phase 2 validation — checking the rule's claim against raw data — is never skippable, especially when the alert "obviously" looks real.
  • Five pivots cover most investigations: entity timeline, who-else, before/after, prevalence, reputation — each answers one named question.
  • Three verdicts, three fixes: TP (respond), FP (the rule misread data — fix logic), BTP (real but authorized — documented exception). Mislabeling tunes the wrong dial.
  • Notes are evidence: as-you-go, UTC timestamps, queries verbatim, observation labeled apart from inference. A stranger should be able to replay your work.
  • Escalate on any of: confirmed TP with impact, beyond-authority scope, expired timebox, or a second finding — and hand off a package: summary, evidence, actions taken, clear ask.
  • "No results" is a hypothesis, not a verdict — check the pipeline before trusting silence; and every verdict you record feeds the tuning loop that keeps tomorrow's queue honest.

Module 8 · Lesson 10

Incident Response Fundamentals:
From Escalation to Recovery

Your nine-minute escalation just landed on Tier-2's desk. Now learn what happens next: the incident lifecycle, containment decisions and their trade-offs, evidence that survives the response, communication under pressure — and the review that turns pain into detections.

LEVELBeginner DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–9 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • An incident is a validated event with real or likely impact that needs a coordinated response.
  • Order matters: prepare → identify & scope → contain → eradicate → recover → learn — and capture evidence before you change anything.
  • NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (2025) maps IR onto the CSF 2.0 functions; the six phases remain the working vocabulary.
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Define an incident precisely

Draw the line between event, alert, and incident — and know what "declaring" one actually changes.

Walk the IR lifecycle

Run the six phases — prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, learn — and explain why the order is load-bearing.

Reason about containment

Weigh isolate-vs-watch, business impact, and coordinated containment — the hardest trade-offs in the whole discipline.

Preserve evidence under fire

Know what to capture before remediation destroys it — and why "wipe it now" is the most expensive sentence in IR.

Communicate like a responder

Route the right information to the right people at the right cadence — through channels the attacker can't read.

Close the loop

Run a lessons-learned that produces detections, fixes, and policy — the phase that pays for all the others.

02
Orientation

Why response is decided before the incident starts

An incident is the moment security stops being a monitoring function and becomes an operation: multiple teams, business impact, executives asking questions, and an adversary who may still be inside, watching you respond. Every skill from Lessons 1–9 remains in play — the pivots, the evidence hygiene, the pipeline knowledge — but the stakes change shape: decisions now cost money, downtime, and sometimes legal exposure, and they must be made fast, with incomplete information, in the right order.

Here's the uncomfortable truth the lifecycle encodes: most of an incident's outcome is determined before it begins. Whether logs were forwarded (Lesson 5), whether the fleet had coverage (Lesson 7), whether a runbook existed, whether anyone knew who could authorize killing a production server at 3 a.m. — preparation is the phase nobody sees and everybody feels. Teams that respond well aren't faster thinkers; they've simply already made the hard decisions, calmly, in advance.

Analogy — the fire department

Firefighters don't debate hose technique at the burning building — hydrant maps, roles, and protocols existed before the alarm. On scene there's one incident commander, a disciplined comms channel, and a fixed priority order: life, containment, extinguish, then investigate the cause so the next building doesn't burn the same way. Notice what they also don't do: bulldoze the site before the fire investigator arrives. Every part of that maps onto IR — including the bulldozer.

Where this sits. Lesson 9 ended with a four-part escalation package about a compromised VPN service account. This lesson follows that exact case through Tier-2's hands — and Lesson 9's evidence discipline (UTC notes, observation vs inference) is about to matter more than ever, because incident records get read by auditors, insurers, and occasionally lawyers.

In plain words

Incident response is the organized way to handle a confirmed attack. The steps: prepare, identify, contain (stop the bleeding), eradicate (remove the attacker everywhere at once), recover, and learn. Move too early and the attacker digs in deeper; too slow and damage spreads. One person, the incident commander, runs the show, and every action is documented.

03
Core concepts

Incidents, the lifecycle, and who's in charge

First, the vocabulary ladder you've been climbing all course: an event is anything observable (a log line); an alert is a rule's claim that events match a suspicious pattern (a lead); an incident is a validated event or series with confirmed or likely impact, requiring coordinated response beyond routine triage. Declaring an incident is a formal act with consequences: it starts the clock on response obligations, activates roles, opens the incident record, and often triggers notification requirements. Incidents get their own severity classification — typically by impact and scope (a single workstation vs. the payment platform) — which drives who gets woken up.

The lifecycle: six phases, one loop

Framework currency check (2025). NIST withdrew SP 800-61 Rev. 2 — the source of the famous four-phase lifecycle — in April 2025. Rev. 3 no longer draws a lifecycle diagram; it maps incident response onto the six CSF 2.0 functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. The phases below remain the working vocabulary of most IR teams, runbooks, and interviews — just cite Rev. 3 when you name NIST, and know that preparation now lives under Govern / Identify / Protect.

The industry-standard working model (you'll see it as SANS's PICERL; the classic four-phase lifecycle from NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 compresses the same ideas): Preparation — runbooks, roles, tooling, and the telemetry groundwork of Lessons 5–7, all done in peacetime. Identification — confirm the incident and, critically, scope it: every foothold, every account, every host, using the pivots you already own. Containment — stop the bleeding without destroying evidence or tipping your hand prematurely. Eradication — remove the attacker's access and artifacts: malware, persistence, stolen credentials. Recovery — restore services, then watch: heightened monitoring until you trust the environment again. Lessons learned — the structured review that converts the incident into rules, fixes, and policy. Then the loop closes: those outputs are next incident's preparation.

The ordering is load-bearing in one non-obvious way: eradication before complete identification is how attackers survive response. Clean one host while a second foothold exists, and you've told the attacker exactly what you can see — they'll return through the door you didn't know about, quieter this time. Scope fully, then contain broadly, then eradicate everything at once.

Roles, briefly. Real incidents run with an incident commander (owns decisions and priorities — not necessarily the most technical person), responders (investigation and remediation hands), and a communications lead (the single mouth through which status flows). Tier-1's place in this structure: you're often the intake that started it, a responder running pivots, and always the person whose case notes the IC is reading. Small SOCs collapse the roles into fewer people; the functions still exist.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the response phases

Select a phase, then work the tabs — "in practice" is the responder's checklist, and "classic failures" is a museum of how incidents get worse during the response. Eradication and recovery share a card; in practice they share a weekend.

05
Core concepts

Containment: the hardest decisions in the room

Containment is where IR earns its reputation, because every option costs something. The core tension: act immediately and stop the damage — but tip off the attacker and possibly lose sight of their other footholds — or watch briefly and scope completely, accepting risk while the adversary still has access. There's no universal answer; there's a decision, made deliberately by the IC, based on what's at stake: active data exfiltration says act now; a quiet foothold on a low-value host may justify hours of watching to map the full intrusion first.

Two more dimensions every containment decision carries. Business impact: isolating a workstation is free; isolating the VPN gateway logs out three hundred remote workers, and killing a production database "to be safe" can cost more than the attack — which is why containment authority sits above Tier-1, and why the IC exists. Evidence preservation: containment and remediation actions destroy volatile evidence — memory contents, active sessions, running processes vanish at the first reboot. The discipline: capture before you change — memory snapshot, disk image, session listing — because scope, root cause, and any future legal or insurance process all depend on evidence that only exists right now.

CONTAINMENT SHEET — INC-0042 (svc-vpn01 compromise) · IC decision, 09:2x UTC OPTION STOPS COSTS block 203.0.113.77 @ perimeter attacker's src IP trivial — approved kill svc-vpn01 sessions live access none — approved disable svc-vpn01 account re-entry via cred VPN health checks fail → IT notified — approved isolate VPN-GW-01 entirely everything 300 remote workers offline — held: not yet justified SEQUENCED AFTER EVIDENCE: memory + disk snapshot of VPN-GW-01 captured 09:24, BEFORE changes

Note the shape of that sheet: options priced, one deliberately not taken, and evidence capture sequenced first. Also worth naming: short-term vs long-term containment. Blocking an IP and disabling an account are short-term — fast, reversible, buying time. Long-term containment (network segmentation, credential rotation at scale, rebuilt trust boundaries) happens once scope is known, and it's the bridge into eradication.

The coordinated strike. When identification finds multiple footholds, containment and eradication should hit all of them in one coordinated window — not one-by-one as each is discovered. Sequential cleanup is a running commentary to the attacker on what you can see; a synchronized strike gives them nothing to adapt to. This is the single most common way sophisticated intrusions survive response.

06
Core concepts

Communication: the incident inside the incident

Post-mortems of badly-handled incidents converge on the same finding: the technical response was adequate; the communication failed. The discipline has four rules. One voice: status flows through the incident commander or comms lead — parallel narratives breed contradictory decisions and leaked speculation. Right information, right audience: executives need impact, status, and decisions-needed in plain language; responders need technical detail; legal needs facts and timestamps — nobody needs your working theories. A cadence, kept: updates at agreed intervals even when the update is "no change" — silence gets filled with rumor. Facts, labeled: Lesson 9's observation-vs-inference rule, now with an audience of lawyers; "we have confirmed X; we are investigating Y" survives scrutiny, "it's probably ransomware from <country>" does not.

STATUS UPDATE #3 — INC-0042 · 11:00 UTC · next update 13:00 CONFIRMED spray from external IP; 1 service account compromised 09:05–09:16; attacker session active ~11 min; persistence attempt found & captured CONTAINED source blocked · sessions killed · account disabled (09:16–09:26) ONGOING scoping: fleet-wide hunt for the persistence artifact — 60% complete, no further hits NEEDED approval window tonight 22:00 for credential rotation (affects VPN users) no customer data systems in scope as of this update · single source of truth: this channel

Two hard-won specifics. First, the out-of-band rule: if there's any chance the attacker has email or chat access, coordination moves to a channel outside the compromised environment — planning the response inside a mailbox the adversary reads is handing them your playbook in real time. Second, external obligations are real: depending on data and jurisdiction, regulators, partners, and affected individuals may be legally owed notification on a clock. That call belongs to legal and leadership — but it's fed entirely by the quality of the facts and timeline the responders maintain. Your notes, again.

The timeline is the deliverable. Throughout the incident, one document accumulates every event, action, and decision with UTC timestamps — attacker activity and responder activity interleaved. It drives the daily response, the final report, the lessons-learned, the insurance claim, and the regulator's questions. Incidents are remembered exactly as well as their timeline was kept.

07
Hands-on · Simulation

You're the responder: name the phase

Six moments from real responses. For each, name the lifecycle phase you're operating in — knowing where you are is how you know what must already be done and what must wait. The feedback explains the phase logic.

Phase-recognition drill

Moment 1 / 6 · Score 0
08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

INC-0042 — Tier-2's twelve hours

The escalation package from Lesson 9 arrives at 09:16. Here is the incident it becomes — twelve steps from declaration to a closed loop, including the one decision deliberately not taken and the evidence captured before anything changed.

Incident replay — "INC-0042: the svc-vpn01 compromise"

09:16 · IntakeThe package lands — and worksSummary, evidence, actions-taken, ask. Tier-2 approves the ask inside two minutes: block the IP, kill the sessions, disable the account. The handoff shortened the incident, exactly as designed.
09:20 · DeclarationINC-0042 exists — formallyConfirmed credential compromise on infrastructure: incident declared, severity HIGH, incident commander assigned, record opened, comms channel established. The clock and the obligations both start now.
09:24 · Evidence firstSnapshot before changeMemory and disk of VPN-GW-01 captured while the machine still remembers everything: sessions, processes, the attacker's artifacts. Every remediation step after this would have destroyed some of it.
09:26 · ContainmentShort-term measures — priced and sequencedIP blocked, sessions killed, account disabled. Full gateway isolation considered and held: 300 remote workers offline isn't justified by current scope. Someone wrote that decision down, with reasons.
IdentificationWhat did eleven minutes buy the attacker?Session forensics from the snapshot: reconnaissance commands, a directory listing of VPN configs — and one persistence attempt: a scheduled task planted at 09:11. The intrusion had a plan beyond the credential.
ScopingThe whole blast radius, before any cleanupFleet-wide hunt for the task's artifact and hash: no other hosts. All 23 sprayed accounts flagged; no other successes. Lateral movement checks from VPN-GW-01: clean. One foothold, fully mapped — now eradication may proceed.
EradicationEverything, in one coordinated passScheduled task removed, artifacts deleted, svc-vpn01 credential rotated, the 23 sprayed accounts force-reset as a precaution — one synchronized window, nothing sequential, nothing for the attacker to learn from.
Comms disciplineStatus update #3, on cadenceConfirmed / contained / ongoing / needed — two hours apart, one channel, facts labeled. Executives learn impact and decisions-needed; nobody learns speculation. The approval for tonight's rotation window is requested here.
RecoveryService restored — harder than beforesvc-vpn01 re-enabled with new credentials and MFA enforced (the gap that made the spray viable). VPN service validated. The environment returns to work, but not to its old trust level.
Validation watchRecovered is a hypothesis; watched is a fact48 hours of heightened monitoring: auth patterns on the rotated accounts, the persistence artifact's signature, the attacker's infrastructure. No re-entry. Only now does "contained" become past tense.
Lessons learnedThe blameless hour that pays for everythingFindings on record: service accounts lacked MFA; enrichment didn't flag service accounts (noted in Lesson 9's triage); detection caught the spray but not the persistence technique. Three gaps, named without blame.
OutputsThe incident becomes infrastructureTwo new rules (scheduled-task persistence; service-account geo anomaly), MFA policy extended to service accounts, enrichment fix shipped. INC-0042 closes — and next quarter's attacker meets a harder target because this one existed.
Ready. Press Play to run the incident, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: trace what made each step possible. The two-minute containment approval came from Lesson 9's package. The session forensics came from a snapshot taken before remediation. Eradication waited for scoping — and hit everything at once. And the whole incident's last act was manufacturing its own successor's defenses. IR done well is Lessons 1–9, executed in the right order, under pressure, with the evidence kept alive.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

IR mistakes are made under adrenaline and defended in post-mortems. Pre-decide against these:

Misconception

"Malware found — wipe and reimage, right now."

Reality

The reflex destroys the two things you need most: evidence (memory and disk state that establish root cause and scope) and knowledge (how did it get there? where else is it?). Capture first, scope fully, then eradicate everything at once. Reimaging one host of a three-host intrusion just teaches the attacker to be quieter.

Misconception

"Containment means isolate everything instantly, always."

Reality

Containment is a priced decision, not a reflex: active exfiltration says act now; a quiet foothold may justify watching long enough to map the intrusion. And isolation has business costs the IC must own — killing the VPN gateway "to be safe" can hurt more than the attacker did. Deliberate beats fast-and-blind.

Misconception

"Incident response starts when the incident does."

Reality

Response quality is mostly preparation: the telemetry forwarded in peacetime (Lesson 5), the coverage validated (Lesson 7), the runbooks written, the authority questions pre-answered. A team improvising these at 3 a.m. isn't responding — it's rehearsing, expensively, in production.

Misconception

"Keep everyone updated on everything — transparency!"

Reality

Uncontrolled comms breed contradictory narratives, leaked speculation, and — if the attacker reads your email — a live feed of your response. The discipline: one voice, right audience, kept cadence, facts labeled, out-of-band if compromise of comms is plausible. The opposite sin is real too: hiding incidents from legal and leadership creates obligations violations. Disciplined ≠ secretive.

Misconception

"Services restored — incident over."

Reality

Recovery ends with a validation watch, not a restart: heightened monitoring on the rotated credentials, the attacker's indicators, and the affected systems until re-entry is ruled out. Attackers routinely return within days through the foothold scoping missed. Recovered is a hypothesis; watched is a fact.

Misconception

"Lessons learned is paperwork for the compliance binder."

Reality

It's the phase with the highest return: the incident already paid its tuition — the review collects the education. Run it blameless (punished honesty produces silence, and silence produces repeat incidents) and demand concrete outputs: rules, fixes, policy changes, each with an owner. An incident without lessons learned will be attended again.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • The ladder: event → alert → incident — an incident is validated, has confirmed or likely impact, and requires coordinated response. Declaring one starts clocks, roles, and records.
  • The lifecycle: prepare → identify & scope → contain → eradicate → recover → learn — and the order is load-bearing: eradication before complete scoping is how attackers survive response.
  • Containment is a priced decision: isolate-vs-watch, business impact, short-term vs long-term — owned by the incident commander, written down with reasons.
  • Capture before you change: memory, disk, sessions — volatile evidence dies at the first remediation step, and scope, root cause, and legal all depend on it.
  • Multiple footholds get a coordinated strike — one synchronized containment/eradication window, never sequential cleanup that narrates your visibility to the attacker.
  • Comms: one voice, right audience, kept cadence, facts labeled, out-of-band if needed — and the UTC timeline is the deliverable that feeds the report, the review, and the regulator.
  • Recovery includes a validation watch, and every incident ends by manufacturing defenses: blameless review, concrete outputs, owners — the loop that turns pain into preparation.

Module 9 · Lesson 11

Threat Intelligence Fundamentals:
IOCs, TTPs & the Pyramid of Pain

INC-0042's artifacts — that IP, that hash, that scheduled-task trick — are someone else's early warning, and theirs are yours. This lesson is how defenders share memory: what intelligence actually is, why indicators age but behaviors endure, and the framework that gives the whole field one language.

LEVELBeginner DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–10 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • Intelligence is data plus the context and analysis that let it support a decision.
  • Pyramid of Pain: hashes trivial, IPs easy, domains simple, artifacts annoying, tools challenging, TTPs tough.
  • MITRE ATT&CK names tactics (why) and techniques (how); keep intel feeds honest with confidence and expiry.
Hands-on:Lab 7 · ATT&CK coverage
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Tell data from intelligence

Explain what turns a raw indicator into intelligence — and why a feed of naked IPs is neither.

Work all three levels

Distinguish strategic, operational, and tactical intelligence — and route each to the audience it serves.

Climb the Pyramid of Pain

Rank indicators by the cost they impose on attackers — and explain why TTP detections outlive every blocklist.

Speak ATT&CK

Use MITRE ATT&CK's tactics and techniques to map incidents, rules, and coverage in the field's shared language.

Consume feeds responsibly

Apply feed hygiene — confidence, context, expiry — so intel sharpens detection instead of flooding the queue.

Produce as well as consume

Turn your own incidents into intelligence — the loop that makes every defender's pain everyone's preparation.

02
Orientation

Why defenders share memory

Every lesson so far has defended with what your estate can see. Threat intelligence adds everyone else's eyes: the attacker who hit you last night probably hit three other organizations last week, and somewhere a defender wrote down the infrastructure, the tooling, and the behavior. Consumed well, that record means you block infrastructure before it touches you, recognize tooling on first contact, and hunt behaviors you've never personally suffered. Intelligence is how detection stops being autobiographical.

It's also two-directional, and INC-0042 makes it concrete: the IP you blocked, the hash you hunted, the scheduled-task technique you eradicated — packaged with context, those artifacts are an early warning for every peer the attacker visits next. The SOC that only consumes intel is drafting behind the community; the SOC that produces it is part of why the community works.

Analogy — the neighborhood watch

One burglary teaches a street three different things. The victim's report — "red van, plate XYZ-123" — is tactical: watch for exactly this, useful tonight, stale when the van is repainted. The pattern across ten streets — "they enter through unlocked garage side-doors, weekday mornings" — is operational: it survives the repaint, because changing method is expensive. And the annual crime report shaping where the city funds patrols is strategic. Same event, three altitudes — and notice which one the burglar can escape cheapest.

Where this sits. You've already used intel without naming it: Lesson 8's intel-driven rules, Lesson 9's reputation-lookup pivot, Lesson 10's fleet hunts for attacker artifacts. This lesson gives those moves their theory — and hands you the vocabulary (IOC, TTP, ATT&CK) that the entire industry runs on.

In plain words

Threat intelligence is organized knowledge about attackers, used to make alerts smarter. An IOC (a bad IP or file hash) is concrete but easy for attackers to change. Their TTPs — how they behave — are much harder to change, so detections built on behavior last longer. That's the Pyramid of Pain: aim higher to hurt attackers more. Scores from feeds are inputs to your judgment, never the verdict.

03
Core concepts

What intelligence is — and the ladder it lives on

Start with a distinction that sounds pedantic and decides everything: data is a raw observable — 203.0.113.77. Information is data with a fact attached — "this IP performed password spraying on 2026-08-05." Intelligence is information analyzed into something that supports a decision: "infrastructure linked to a campaign targeting VPN service accounts across our sector this month; high confidence; block and hunt for these related behaviors." The difference is context and actionability — a feed of naked indicators is data wearing intelligence's badge, and treating it as intelligence is how queues drown.

Three altitudes, three audiences

Tactical intelligence is machine-speed: IOCs — indicators of compromise — the concrete observables of malicious activity: file hashes, IP addresses, domains, URLs, email artifacts. It feeds enrichment and detection directly, and it ages in days-to-weeks. Operational intelligence describes campaigns and actors: their TTPs — tactics, techniques, and procedures — the behaviors that persist across infrastructure changes. It feeds detection engineering and hunting. Strategic intelligence is trend-level — which sectors are targeted, how the threat landscape is shifting — and it feeds leadership decisions about risk and investment. Tier-1 lives mostly at tactical altitude, but the operational layer is where careers and detections both level up.

The intelligence lifecycle

Real intel work runs a loop you'll recognize by shape: direction (what do we need to know? — priority intelligence requirements), collection (gather from feeds, incidents, sharing communities), processing (normalize into usable records), analysis (turn it into judgments with confidence levels), dissemination (deliver to the people and systems that act), and feedback (did it help? — refine direction). It's Lesson 8's rule lifecycle wearing a different badge: nothing ships unvalidated, and the loop never closes for good.

Indicators decay; behaviors endure. An IP is abandoned in days, a domain in weeks, a hash the moment the malware is recompiled. A technique — spraying, Office-spawns-script, scheduled-task persistence — takes retraining and retooling to abandon. This single asymmetry drives the entire next section, and most of modern detection philosophy with it.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the Pyramid of Pain

David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain ranks six indicator types — hashes, IPs, domains, network/host artifacts, tools, TTPs — by one question: how much does it hurt the attacker when you detect and deny this? Bottom levels are trivial for them to change; the top forces them to relearn their trade. Select a level (bottom = cheapest for the attacker, top = most painful), then work the tabs.

05
Core concepts

MITRE ATT&CK: the field's shared map

MITRE ATT&CK is a public, curated knowledge base of real-world attacker behavior, organized on two axes. Tactics are the why — the attacker's goals, arranged roughly as an intrusion unfolds: initial access, execution, persistence, privilege escalation, credential access, lateral movement, exfiltration, and so on. Techniques are the how — the specific methods that achieve each goal, each with a stable ID (like T1059, Command and Scripting Interpreter) and sub-techniques for the variants. The genius is the shared vocabulary: when a report, a rule, a red-teamer, and a vendor all say T1053.005, everyone means exactly "persistence via Windows scheduled task" — no translation, no ambiguity.

Here's INC-0042 mapped, which is exactly how mature SOCs write incident reports:

INC-0042 → ATT&CK MAPPING (tactic ← technique) Credential Access ← T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying — the 23-account spray Initial Access ← T1078 Valid Accounts — svc-vpn01 login at 09:05 Discovery ← T1083 File and Directory Discovery — the config listing Persistence ← T1053.005 Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task — planted at 09:11

Once incidents and rules speak ATT&CK, the SOC gains three capabilities. Coverage assessment: map every detection rule to its techniques and the gaps become visible — INC-0042's review found exactly this (spraying covered, scheduled-task persistence not). Prioritized engineering: operational intel says which actors target your sector and which techniques they favor; you build detections for those first. Frictionless communication: red teams report in technique IDs, intel reports arrive in them, and your rules tag them — one language across the whole conversation about attacker behavior.

A heatmap is a map, not a scorecard. The famous ATT&CK coverage matrix tempts teams to chase green in every cell. Resist: hundreds of techniques exist, many irrelevant to your environment, and shallow coverage everywhere loses to deep coverage of the techniques your actual threats use. The matrix's job is to make choices visible — not to gamify completeness.

06
Core concepts

Feeds, hygiene & the three uses of intel

Intelligence reaches the SOC as feeds — from commercial providers, open-source projects, and sharing communities (sector-based ISACs, where peers exchange what's hitting them). Standards like STIX (a structured format for describing threats) and TAXII (the transport for exchanging it) make feeds machine-consumable — Lesson 5's normalization story, replayed for threat data. Whatever the source, an indicator arriving without context is a liability; a usable IOC record looks like this:

IOC RECORD — what separates intelligence from a naked indicator indicator: 203.0.113.77 type: ipv4 context: C2 / credential-attack infrastructure — VPN-targeting campaign first_seen: 2026-07-29 last_seen: 2026-08-05 confidence: high (3 independent ISAC reports + internal incident) source: sector ISAC · INC-0042 expires: 2026-09-05 ← indicators age out by design related: T1110.003 · task artifact hash · 2 sibling IPs

The SOC puts intel to work three ways, in ascending ambition. Enrichment: every alert's indicators are checked against intel automatically, so context arrives pre-attached — Lesson 9's reputation pivot, industrialized. Detection: Lesson 8's intel-driven rules match the stream against feeds in real time. Hunting: operational intel — "this actor uses these techniques" — becomes hypotheses to search for proactively, which is Lesson 12's entire subject.

What keeps all three honest is feed hygiene: confidence scoring (one anonymous sighting ≠ three corroborated reports), aging and expiry (that IP was a C2 in March; in August it's someone's reassigned cloud instance), deduplication across overlapping feeds, and scoped action — high-confidence fresh indicators can auto-block; low-confidence ones should enrich and inform, never page. An unhygienic feed is just Lesson 8's noisy rule with better marketing.

Benign infrastructure is the classic feed injury. Malware talks to public DNS resolvers, cloud providers, and CDNs — so those addresses show up in "malicious traffic" datasets constantly. Push them to blocking and you've outaged your own company with an intel feed. Every candidate block gets the question: what legitimate traffic also touches this?

07
Hands-on · Simulation

You're the analyst: rate the pain

Six defensive wins from the INC-0042 saga and beyond. For each, place it on the Pyramid of Pain — which level of indicator does the defense operate on? The feedback explains what it actually cost the attacker.

Pyramid-placement drill

Win 1 / 6 · Score 0
08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

One incident's artifacts, everyone's armor

INC-0042 is closed. Watch its remains travel the full intelligence lifecycle — out into the community, into a stranger's SOC at the worst possible moment for the attacker, and back to your own perimeter when they return wearing new infrastructure.

Intelligence replay — "the afterlife of INC-0042"

DirectionThe questions come firstBefore collecting anything, the team writes its priority intelligence requirements: Is this actor still targeting us? What infrastructure and techniques do they run? Which of our peers are seeing them? Intel without direction is a hoard, not a program.
CollectionThe incident is minedFrom INC-0042's evidence: the source IP, the task artifact's hash, the task name, the config paths touched — and the behaviors: spray pattern, valid-account entry, scheduled-task persistence. Artifacts and TTPs, kept separate on purpose.
ProcessingRaw evidence becomes recordsEach observable is normalized into an IOC record: type, context, first_seen, confidence, source, expiry. The naked indicator 203.0.113.77 becomes a structured claim someone else's SIEM can consume. Lesson 5's parsing story, at intel altitude.
AnalysisThe pattern outgrows the incidentCross-referencing the ISAC: three peer organizations report the same infrastructure family, same VPN-targeting spray, same persistence trick. Judgment formed, confidence high: an active campaign against the sector — not a one-off visit.
Dissemination · internalIntel goes to work at homeIOCs enter the enrichment and blocking feeds with expiry dates set. Two new detection rules ship, each tagged with its ATT&CK technique — T1110.003, T1053.005. The heatmap's gap from the incident review turns green where it matters.
Dissemination · externalThe sanitized report shipsIndicators, TTP profile, ATT&CK mapping — scrubbed of anything identifying — shared to the ISAC. It costs an hour of write-up. Somewhere, a stranger's SOC just received your incident's education without paying its tuition.
The payoff · elsewhereA peer's quiet saveA member organization loads the feed, blocks the infrastructure — and their enrichment flags an alert from last week that had been closed as noise. Re-opened with context: an active intrusion, same actor, caught mid-foothold. Your artifacts, their save.
The counter-moveThe attacker pays the cheap costsBurned, the actor rotates: new IPs, new domains, recompiled tooling with fresh hashes. Total cost: an afternoon and some cryptocurrency. Every bottom-of-pyramid defense just expired at once — exactly as the pyramid predicts.
The pyramid proves outThe behavior comes back — into the new ruleWeeks later, your VPN sees it: many accounts, few attempts, one unfamiliar source. New infrastructure, same technique — and the T1110.003 behavioral rule fires on first contact. They changed everything cheap; the expensive thing is what you were watching.
Routine triageNine boring minutesThe alert lands enriched: campaign context, ATT&CK tag, runbook attached, prior-incident links. Tier-1 validates, scopes, closes the door — no success this time, MFA held. The most anticlimactic paragraph in this course, which is the point.
FeedbackThe loop critiques itselfDid the intel help? The behavioral rule: decisively. The IOC blocks: bought two quiet weeks, then aged out on schedule. PIRs updated — track the actor's technique drift, not their disposable infrastructure. Direction sharpens for the next cycle.
The bigger loopMemory, compoundingYour incident armed four organizations; a peer's save validated the sharing; the actor's return validated the TTP focus. Every SOC in the circle now detects this campaign better than any of them could alone. That's threat intelligence — collective memory, with a feedback loop.
Ready. Press Play to run the lifecycle, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: follow what survived the attacker's rotation. The IPs died, the hashes died, the domains died — the technique detection and the shared behavioral profile are what caught the return. Tactical intel bought weeks; operational intel bought the win. Spend accordingly.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Intel programs fail in predictable ways — usually by confusing volume with value:

Misconception

"More feeds means better intelligence."

Reality

Feeds overlap, contradict, and decay — ten unhygienic sources produce duplicate alerts, stale blocks, and enrichment noise that lowers analyst trust. One curated, confidence-scored, expiring feed beats ten raw ones. Intel is judged by decisions improved, never by indicators ingested.

Misconception

"We consume IOC feeds, so we have a threat intelligence program."

Reality

Naked indicators are data. Intelligence requires context (what campaign, what behavior), confidence, and analysis that supports decisions — plus direction: knowing what questions you're trying to answer. An IOC pipe with no analysis layer is a blocklist subscription, which is fine — as long as nobody calls it intelligence.

Misconception

"We blocked the hash and the IP — that threat is handled."

Reality

You've imposed the two cheapest costs on the pyramid — a recompile and an infrastructure swap, an afternoon's work. The threat is the actor and their techniques, and those just moved. Bottom-of-pyramid blocking is worth doing precisely because it's cheap for you too — but 'handled' begins where TTP detection starts.

Misconception

"Threat intel is for big SOCs with dedicated analysts."

Reality

A two-person SOC consuming a free sector ISAC feed with expiry hygiene, tagging rules with ATT&CK IDs, and reading one campaign report a week is doing threat intelligence. The lifecycle scales down gracefully; what doesn't scale down is skipping the hygiene and drowning a small team in stale indicators.

Misconception

"An indicator that was malicious stays malicious."

Reality

Infrastructure is rented and recycled: March's C2 is August's legitimate cloud instance, and yesterday's compromised website is patched today. Indicators without expiry dates become false-positive generators and — worse — outage risks when benign infrastructure lingers in blocklists. Aging out is a feature, not data loss.

Misconception

"Our goal is ATT&CK coverage — green in every cell."

Reality

Hundreds of techniques, many irrelevant to your stack, and 'coverage' claims that are a single shallow rule deep — the all-green heatmap is a vanity metric. The matrix exists to make choices visible: deep detection for the techniques your threat model and your intel say matter, and honest gray everywhere you've consciously deprioritized.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • Data → information → intelligence: the upgrades are context, analysis, and actionability. A naked indicator feed is data wearing intelligence's badge.
  • Three altitudes, three audiences: tactical (IOCs, machine-speed, short-lived), operational (campaigns and TTPs — detection engineering's fuel), strategic (trends, for leadership).
  • The Pyramid of Pain ranks defenses by attacker cost across six levels: hashes trivial, IPs easy, domains simple, network/host artifacts annoying, tools challenging — and TTPs tough: they force attackers to relearn their trade.
  • Indicators decay; behaviors endure — block the bottom of the pyramid because it's cheap, but invest detection engineering at the top, where the attacker can't afford to follow.
  • MITRE ATT&CK = tactics (the why) × techniques (the how, with stable IDs): one shared language for incidents, rules, red teams, and reports — and a map for choices, not a scorecard to fill.
  • Intel serves the SOC three ways — enrichment, detection, hunting — and stays honest through feed hygiene: confidence, expiry, deduplication, scoped action, and the benign-infrastructure check.
  • The lifecycle — direction, collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, feedback — runs both ways: consume the community's memory, and produce for it from your own incidents.
11
Assessment

The feed review

Five IOC records are queued for tonight's push to the perimeter blocking list. Four belong there. One, pushed to blocking, would hurt your own organization more than any attacker. Click the record you'd pull.

Lesson 12 — Threat Hunting Fundamentals: Assume Breach, Then Prove It

Detection waits for rules to fire; hunting doesn't wait. How hypothesis-driven hunts turn operational intel and ATT&CK techniques into proactive searches, why "assume breach" changes what you look for, and how every hunt ends — finding something, or manufacturing the rule that will.

Threat Hunting Fundamentals:
Assume Breach, Then Prove It

Every lesson so far waited for something to fire. Hunting doesn't wait. This is the discipline of forming a falsifiable hypothesis about an attacker already inside, searching the data your rules aren't watching — and ending every hunt with either a finding or the rule that would have found it.

LEVELBeginner-plus DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–11 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • Assume breach: hunting looks proactively for what rules didn't catch — including back through history.
  • A good hypothesis is specific and falsifiable: “if technique X happened, evidence Y exists in source Z.”
  • Every hunt ends in an output: an escalation, a new rule, a telemetry fix, or a documented clean result.

01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Adopt the assume-breach mindset

Explain why mature defense operates as if compromise already happened — and what that changes about where you look.

Write real hypotheses

Turn intel, ATT&CK techniques, and crown-jewel thinking into specific, testable, scoped hunting hypotheses.

Run the hunting loop

Walk a hunt from hypothesis through scoping, search, and investigation to a concrete output — every time.

Apply core techniques

Use baselining, stacking, and lineage analysis — the three moves that power most real-world hunts.

Convert hunts to detections

Prioritize under constraint

02
Orientation

Why defenders stopped waiting

Detection has a structural blind spot, and you've already met it twice. A rule only sees what it was written to see, only from the day it was deployed, only if the telemetry feeding it exists. INC-0042's review said it plainly: the spray was caught, but the scheduled-task persistence had no rule at all until after the incident. Whatever happened before that rule shipped — wherever else that technique was used — no alert will ever fire for it. Retroactively, detection is blind by design.

Threat hunting is the answer to that blindness: a proactive, human-driven search through existing data for attacker activity that current detections miss. Its founding assumption is called assume breach — operate as if an attacker is already inside, because industry dwell-time studies keep finding intrusions that sat undiscovered for weeks or months. The question shifts from "will we be compromised?" to "where is the compromise we haven't found yet?" — a question you can actually go answer with the query skills, telemetry knowledge, and intel you've built across eleven lessons.

Analogy — the smoke detector and the inspector

Smoke detectors are superb at what they're pointed at — and silent about everything else: the wiring smoldering inside a wall, the gas leak with no smoke, the fire that predates the detector's installation. So buildings also get inspectors: humans with a checklist of known failure modes, walking the structure on a schedule, looking for trouble that never tripped an alarm. The inspector doesn't replace the detectors — every problem found becomes a spec for a better one. Detection is your smoke detectors. Hunting is the inspection.

Where this sits. Hunting is where the whole course converges: Lesson 6's search syntax is your instrument, Lesson 7's coverage map tells you where you can even look, Lesson 8 receives your outputs, and Lesson 11's operational intel and ATT&CK techniques supply the hypotheses. Tier-1 analysts rarely own hunts on day one — but hunt findings land in your queue, and contributing to hunts is the classic path off the queue.

In plain words

Hunting is actively searching for attacks your alerts missed. You start from a hypothesis (“if an attacker did X, I'd see Y”), then go look in the logs — no alert required. You especially watch for normal system tools being abused (LOLBins like PowerShell). The goal is to shrink dwell time: how long an attacker operates before you catch them.

03
Core concepts

Hypotheses: the difference between hunting and browsing

Strip the mystique: hunting is hypothesis-driven search. Not scrolling logs hoping something looks weird — that's browsing, it doesn't scale, and it finds nothing reproducibly. A real hunt starts with a falsifiable claim: "If an attacker used technique X in our environment, evidence Y would exist in data source Z." That single sentence forces three honesties at once: a specific behavior (X), an observable trace (Y), and a place you actually have telemetry (Z — Lesson 7's coverage map suddenly matters again). Then you go look. Either you find Y, or you've proven something about your environment — both are wins, as we'll see.

Where hypotheses come from

Four reliable sources, in rough priority order. Operational intel: "this actor targets our sector using T1053.005" — the ISAC report from Lesson 11 is a hunting to-do list. ATT&CK coverage gaps: the techniques your heatmap honestly marks undetected — hunting is how you check them manually until a rule exists. Crown-jewel reasoning: start from your most damaging outcome (payment systems, domain controllers, the VPN gateway) and ask what an attacker's path there would leave behind. Environmental anomalies: things that made an analyst squint during triage — Lesson 9's "noted for the hunt team" line lands here.

Structured vs unstructured — and the loop

Hypothesis-first hunts are structured. There's also unstructured hunting — starting from a weird artifact and pulling the thread — and it's legitimate, but even it graduates into a hypothesis fast ("if this artifact means X, then Y should also exist"). Either way the work runs the same loop you'll explore next: hypothesis → scope the data → search and analyze → investigate what surfaces → convert the outcome into something durable → feed what you learned into the next hypothesis. One more honest note: hunting assumes decent telemetry and search skills exist — a SOC that can't yet see its endpoints (Lesson 7) fixes that first. Hunting maturity grows in steps, and step one is always visibility.

The retroactive superpower. A detection rule watches forward from its deploy date. A hunt searches backward through everything retention holds. That asymmetry is why hunting exists as a discipline: it's the only way to answer "did this technique already happen here before we could detect it?" — the exact question INC-0042 left hanging.

Explore the hunting loop

05
Core concepts

The three moves that power most hunts

Underneath most real hunts sit three analytical techniques, all runnable with Lesson 6's search skills. Baselining: establish what normal looks like for an entity or behavior, then surface first-time deviations — "service accounts authenticate from servers; show me any authenticating from a workstation for the first time." Normal is boring; new is interesting. Stacking (frequency analysis): count occurrences of a value across the whole environment, sort, and read the rare end — malicious things tend to be nearly unique in a fleet of conformity. Lineage analysis: Lesson 4's parent-child discipline weaponized at scale — search history for process relationships that should never exist, like Office spawning script engines, or a web server process spawning a shell.

Here's stacking doing its signature trick — one query, the whole fleet, and the answer sitting quietly at the bottom:

HUNT QUERY — stack scheduled task names, fleet-wide, 90 days search events type=task_created | stats count by task_name, dc(host) | sort count asc ─── output (bottom of stack — the rare end) ─── GoogleUpdateTaskMachine count=412 hosts=402 ← fleet-wide conformity: boring Adobe_Acrobat_Update count=398 hosts=395 BackupAgent-Nightly count=61 hosts=61 ← all servers: boring WindowsDiagnosticSvc count=1 hosts=1 ← unique in the fleet · plausible-sounding name rare + system-sounding + user-writable binary path = investigate the host, not the task

Two notes that separate practitioners from tourists. First, rare ≠ malicious — the bottom of every stack is mostly legitimate one-offs (that one engineer's tool, that one legacy job); the skill is triaging the rare end with Lesson 9's judgment, fast. Second, these techniques compound: a stacking hit becomes a baselining question ("has this host ever created tasks before?") becomes a lineage question ("what process created it?"). And a special mention for LOLBins — living-off-the-land binaries, legitimate system tools (PowerShell, certutil, schtasks) doing attacker work — which are nearly invisible to hash-and-IOC thinking but light up beautifully under lineage and baseline hunts. Top-of-pyramid detection, once again.

Hunt where the attacker must walk. The best hunting grounds are choke points — behaviors an intrusion can rarely avoid: authentication, persistence creation, process spawning, outbound beaconing. Techniques change; the need to run code, survive reboots, and phone home doesn't. Aim the three moves at those four grounds and you cover a startling amount of ATT&CK.

06
Core concepts

Every hunt ends in an artifact

The iron rule that keeps hunting a program instead of a hobby: no hunt ends in a shrug. Four legitimate endings, all of them deliverables. An intrusion found — the headline outcome: escalate into Lesson 10's lifecycle, and note with pride that hunting found it without an alert. A detection shipped — the most common valuable ending: your hunt query, once tuned, is a draft rule for Lesson 8's pipeline; now the machine watches this hypothesis forever. A gap documented — the hunt couldn't run because telemetry was missing: that's a Lesson 7 onboarding request with evidence attached. Clean, and documented — the hypothesis was tested honestly and nothing was found: coverage proven, baseline captured, and the next analyst doesn't re-hunt it blind.

HUNT REPORT — HUNT-007 · closed 2026-08-05 HYPOTHESIS If T1053.005 persistence was used on servers, task-creation events will show tasks executing from user-writable paths SCOPE 90 days · server fleet · task_created events COVERAGE 198/200 hosts METHOD stack task names → triage rare end → lineage on survivors FINDINGS 1 confirmed persistence (HR-WS-117 → INC-0043) · 2 benign one-offs OUTPUTS rule drafted: R-2077 (task exec from user-writable path) telemetry gap: 2 hosts silent → onboarding ticket baseline doc: normal task population, server fleet every line above outlives the hunt — that's the point of writing it

Notice what the report card enforces: the hypothesis is quoted (so its logic can be challenged), scope and coverage are stated (so "clean" means something), and every finding became a tracked artifact. A hunt documented like this compounds — the next hunter starts from your baseline, your query, your gaps. A hunt that lives only in a terminal history and an analyst's memory evaporates by Friday.

The notebook graveyard. The most common failure in real hunting programs isn't bad hypotheses — it's good hunts whose findings never left the hunter's notes. If the ending isn't a rule, a ticket, a report, or an escalation, the organization didn't hunt; one person just had an interesting afternoon.

08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

HUNT-007: the alert that never fired

INC-0042's review left one question hanging: the persistence rule now exists — but it watches forward. Was the technique already used somewhere, before there was a rule to see it? Twelve steps of the hunt that went looking.

Hunt replay — "the intrusion nothing detected"

DirectionThe question INC-0042 left behindThe updated PIR reads: has this actor's tradecraft been used against us anywhere detection wasn't watching? The persistence rule deploys forward-only. Everything before it is dark — unless someone goes and looks.
HypothesisFalsifiable, scoped, testable"If T1053.005 persistence was used in the last 90 days, task-creation events will show tasks executing binaries from user-writable paths." Technique named, evidence predicted, data source confirmed to exist. HUNT-007 opens.
ScopeCheck the ground before hunting on itCoverage check first, Lesson 7 style: 198 of 200 in-scope hosts are reporting task events. Two silent hosts are noted immediately — whatever this hunt concludes, it concludes about 198, and says so.
Search · stackingCount everything, read the bottomEvery task name in 90 days, counted and sorted. The top is fleet-wide conformity: updaters, backup agents. The rare end holds five entries — four explain themselves in minutes. One doesn't: WindowsDiagnosticSvc, count of one.
AnalyzeRare, plausible-sounding, wrongly placedThe unique task lives on HR-WS-117 — a workstation, in a server-focused hunt's peripheral vision. System-sounding name, but the binary runs from a user-writable temp path. Lineage check: created by a PowerShell process. Squint harder.
The cold partCreated three weeks BEFORE INC-0042The task's creation timestamp predates the VPN spray entirely. This isn't INC-0042's cleanup miss — it's a separate, older foothold that no rule ever saw, because no rule existed yet. The hunt just reached somewhere detection structurally couldn't.
Pivot · lineageHow did it get there?Entity timeline on HR-WS-117 around creation time, Lesson 9's pivots verbatim: Outlook → browser download → Excel opens "salary_bands_2026.xlsm" → Excel spawns PowerShell → PowerShell creates the task. A phishing chain, start to finish, sitting in cold storage.
EscalationThe hunt becomes INC-0043Findings packaged Lesson 9 style — summary, evidence, ask — and declared. Same actor? The tooling artifacts match the ISAC profile. The spray wasn't their first visit; it was their second. Assume breach just stopped being a slogan.
ResponseLesson 10, executed calmlySnapshot before change. Scope: the task beaconed to a dormant domain — no lateral movement found, credentials on the host rotated anyway. Coordinated eradication. The quiet foothold dies quietly, three weeks after it was planted.
Output · ruleThe hunt query becomes R-2077The winning search — task execution from user-writable paths — is tuned against the fleet baseline the hunt just built, exceptions documented, and enters Lesson 8's pipeline. This hypothesis is now watched by the machine, forever, for free.
Output · everything elseThe report card fills inTelemetry gap → onboarding ticket for the two silent hosts. Baseline doc → the normal task population, archived for the next hunter. Intel update → the actor's earlier phishing entry, shared to the ISAC. Nothing stays in the notebook.
FeedbackThe loop turnsHUNT-007 closes with one intrusion, one rule, one ticket, one baseline, one intel report — from one sentence of hypothesis. The next PIR is already obvious: hunt the phishing entry technique fleet-wide. Which is precisely where this course goes next.
Ready. Press Play to run the hunt, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: count what one hypothesis produced — an intrusion detection never saw (planted before the rule existed), a new rule, a telemetry ticket, a fleet baseline, and shared intel. Then notice the machinery: every single step was a prior lesson's skill. Hunting isn't a new toolset; it's the offensive use of everything you already know.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Hunting attracts more mythology than any other SOC discipline. Clear these before they cost you:

Misconception

"Hunting means browsing logs until something looks suspicious."

Reality

Browsing is unfalsifiable, unscoped, and unrepeatable — it ends when the analyst gets tired, proves nothing when it finds nothing, and can't be handed to anyone else. A hunt starts from a hypothesis naming a technique, a predicted trace, and a data source. The sentence is the discipline.

Misconception

"A hunt that finds no intrusion failed."

Reality

A clean hunt with honest scope proved coverage: the technique was tested against 90 days of data and isn't present — that's an evidence-backed claim most organizations can't make. It also built a baseline, validated telemetry, and often shipped a rule anyway. The only failed hunt is an undocumented one.

Misconception

"Hunting is for elite teams with dedicated hunters and exotic tooling."

Reality

HUNT-007 used a search bar, a count-and-sort, and Lesson 9's pivots. One structured hypothesis-driven hunt per month, documented, beats a fantasy program that never starts. What hunting genuinely requires is telemetry (Lesson 7) and query skills (Lesson 6) — both of which small SOCs can own.

Misconception

"Once hunting matures, it replaces detection."

Reality

They're a cycle, not competitors: detection handles the known continuously and at machine speed; hunting probes the unknown episodically with human judgment — and every good hunt feeds detection a new rule. A SOC that hunts but doesn't ship rules re-hunts the same hypothesis forever; one that only detects never sees behind its own deploy dates.

Misconception

"Hunt broadly — cast the widest possible net."

Reality

Hunting hours are scarce and hypotheses are infinite. Prioritize like the intel-informed defender you now are: techniques your actual threats use (Lesson 11's operational intel), aimed at your crown jewels, at the choke points attackers can't avoid — authentication, persistence, process spawning, beaconing. Wide nets catch fatigue.

Misconception

"The new platform hunts for you."

Reality

Tools accelerate hunts brilliantly — they stack, baseline, and visualize at scales no human can. But a hypothesis is a judgment about your environment, your threats, and what evidence would look like — and anomaly dashboards without that judgment are just prettier browsing. The analytics are the instrument; the hunter supplies the question.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • Assume breach: operate as if an attacker is already inside, and go look for the evidence — because detection only sees what it was told to watch, from the day it was told.
  • Hunting is hypothesis-driven search: "if technique X was used, evidence Y exists in data source Z" — specific, falsifiable, scoped. Everything else is browsing.
  • Hypotheses come from operational intel, ATT&CK gaps, crown-jewel reasoning, and triage anomalies — and hunting's superpower is retroactive reach through everything retention holds.
  • The loop: hypothesis → scope → search → investigate → output → feedback — and scope means checking coverage first, so "clean" is a claim about known ground.
  • Three moves power most hunts: baselining (first-time deviations), stacking (count, sort, read the rare end), lineage (impossible parent-child pairs) — aimed at choke points: auth, persistence, process spawning, beaconing.
  • No hunt ends in a shrug: an intrusion escalated, a rule shipped, a gap ticketed, or a clean result documented with its baseline — the notebook graveyard is the discipline's real enemy.
  • Hunting and detection form a cycle: hunts probe what rules can't see, then become the rules — the machine watches yesterday's hypothesis while the hunter writes tomorrow's.

Phishing Analysis Fundamentals:
Dissecting the Initial Access Workhorse

HUNT-007 traced its intrusion to one email and a salary-themed spreadsheet. Most breaches start exactly this way. This lesson makes you dangerous to phishing: reading headers as provenance evidence, dissecting lures and links safely, and running the pipeline that turns one user's Report click into a fleet-wide save.

01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Read headers as evidence

Walk the Received chain, spot From/Return-Path games, and treat headers as the email's provenance record.

Interpret SPF, DKIM & DMARC

Know what each authentication check actually proves — and the crucial thing a "pass" does not prove.

Dissect the lure

Recognize the psychology — urgency, authority, curiosity, fear — and the spectrum from mass spam to targeted spear-phish and BEC.

Defang, expand, detonate — extract verdicts from hostile links and files without ever endangering your own machine.
