02
Orientation

Why email is still the front door

Year after year, incident statistics tell the same story: the majority of intrusions begin with a message to a human. Not because email technology is uniquely broken, but because email is the one channel where strangers are allowed to deliver content and instructions directly to your least-monitored attack surface — people. Every firewall lesson, every hardened server, every detection rule can be bypassed by one convincing sentence and one click. INC-0043 proved it in this very course: the actor who needed a password spray to breach the VPN walked into HR-WS-117 through a spreadsheet named salary_bands_2026.xlsm.

For a Tier-1 analyst, phishing is bread and butter: user-reported emails are one of the highest-volume queues in any SOC, and one of the highest-leverage — a single well-triaged report can expose an entire campaign before anyone clicks. It's also where your judgment is most visible: verdict too slow and the second recipient clicks; verdict wrong and either a real threat gets deleted as spam, or the finance team loses access to a legitimate invoice. The craft is speed and rigor, on the same artifact.

Analogy — the forged letter

A letter arrives on convincing bank stationery. The content — logo, tone, signature — is whatever the forger wanted it to be; judging authenticity by how official it looks is exactly the mistake the forger planned for. Investigators instead read the envelope and postmarks: where was it actually mailed from, which post offices handled it, does the return address match the claimed sender? Email is identical: the body is the forger's canvas, the headers are the postmarks — and the postmarks are much harder to fake.

Where this sits. Everything converges here again: Lesson 3's protocol literacy (SMTP's trusting design is why spoofing exists), Lesson 9's triage discipline, Lesson 11's indicator thinking, and Lesson 12's hunt — whose finding is about to become this lesson's live scenario, from the other end of the timeline.

In plain words

Phishing is the fraudulent message that starts most attacks. It tricks people into clicking, opening, or paying. You investigate by reading the email's real headers, checking links and attachments safely in a sandbox (detonation), and using the mail gateway logs to find everyone else who got it. Scoping the whole campaign matters more than saving one inbox.

03
Core concepts

The spectrum of phish — and the game being played

"Phishing" covers a spectrum, and the analyst's response scales with where a message sits on it. Mass phishing: thousands of identical credential-harvest or malware lures, sprayed broadly — low effort, caught largely by filters, dangerous in volume. Spear phishing: crafted for a specific organization or role — your brand, your projects, your org chart — like a salary spreadsheet sent precisely to finance staff. BEC (business email compromise): the pure social-engineering end — often no link and no attachment at all, just an authority figure's identity and an urgent financial instruction, which is exactly why filters struggle with it. And credential phishing vs malware delivery cuts across all of these: the lure either wants your password on a fake page, or wants you to run something.

Under every variant, the same psychological levers: urgency ("expires today"), authority ("from the CEO"), fear ("suspicious activity on your account"), curiosity and reward ("salary bands", "bonus schedule", "package delivery"). The lever's job is to make the target act before thinking — which is worth internalizing, because the same levers get aimed at analysts: an email screaming urgency is trying to rush your triage too.

The artifact and its two layers

An email is two things stapled together. The body — everything the recipient sees: text, branding, links, attachments — is entirely attacker-controlled, a forger's canvas. The headers — the metadata stack prepended by every server that handled the message — are the envelope and postmarks: the Received chain written by infrastructure the attacker mostly doesn't control, the authentication results stamped by your receiving servers, the addressing fields where claims and reality can be compared. Analysis lives in the gap between the two layers: what the message claims versus what its provenance proves. The next section gives you the full toolkit for both.

Safe handling is rule zero. A reported phish is live ordnance. It gets analyzed in the mail gateway's preview, a sandbox, or an isolated analysis VM — never by opening links or attachments on your own workstation "just to check." Indicators get defanged when written down — hxxps://evil[.]example — so a stray click in your own case notes can't detonate. The analyst who becomes patient zero while investigating patient zero is a genre of post-mortem nobody wants to star in.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five examination points

Every phishing investigation walks the same five stations. Select one, then work the tabs — "analyst moves" is the practical checklist, and "attacker tricks" is what the adversary does to beat a lazy version of that station.

05
Core concepts

Reading the postmarks: a header walk

Here are the load-bearing headers of the very email that started INC-0043 — the one HUNT-007 found the aftermath of. Read bottom-up for the Received chain (each server prepends, so the bottom Received is the origin), and watch the gap between claim and proof:

HEADERS — "Updated salary bands FY2026" · reported by USR-4471 (read Received bottom-up) Received: from mx-in-01.company.example by mailstore … ← our edge, trustworthy Received: from vps-1023.bulkhost.example (203.0.113.88) ← true origin: a rented VPS by mx-in-01.company.example; Tue, 05 Aug 2026 08:37:02 +0000 From: "HR Compensation" <hr-team@cornpany-hr.com> ← lookalike: rn ≈ m Reply-To: hr-comp-desk@cornpany-hr.com Return-Path: <bounce-8817@cornpany-hr.com> Authentication-Results: spf=pass (domain of cornpany-hr.com) dkim=pass dmarc=pass (policy of cornpany-hr.com) ← passes — FOR THE WRONG DOMAIN Subject: Updated salary bands FY2026 — confidential

Three lessons live in that block. First, the Received chain is written by the servers themselves — the origin VPS at the bottom is evidence the attacker can't easily erase, only push deeper. Second, the lookalike domain: cornpany-hr.com is registered, real, and fully attacker-controlled — one glyph from trusted. Third, and most important: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all pass, because the attacker configured them correctly for their own domain. Authentication answers "did this really come from the domain it claims?" — it says nothing about whether that domain is friendly. A pass for cornpany-hr.com is a perfectly authenticated message from the enemy.

What the three checks actually prove: SPF — the sending IP is on the domain's published list of authorized senders. DKIM — a cryptographic signature confirms the message wasn't altered and was signed by the domain's key. DMARC — the domain's published policy for handling failures, plus alignment: the From header domain must match the domain that passed. Where they shine defensively: a message claiming to be @company.example that fails DMARC is near-certain spoofing of your domain — that's the smoking-gun pattern. Where they're silent: lookalikes, freemail senders, and compromised legitimate mailboxes, which authenticate flawlessly.

The analyst's header reflex, in order: Where did it really come from (bottom Received)? Do From, Reply-To, and Return-Path agree — and with which domain? What do Authentication-Results say, and about whose domain? Claim versus provenance, every time.

06
Core concepts

From Report click to fleet-wide save

A user report is the start of a pipeline, and speed matters at every stage. Triage: headers, sender, lure, URLs, attachments — the five stations, run in minutes with the explorer's discipline. Verdict: malicious (phish or malware), spam (unwanted but not hostile), or benign (the legitimate invoice someone found suspicious — it happens constantly, and misjudging it has real cost too). Then the part teams skip under pressure: a confirmed phish is never about one mailbox. The immediate questions are who else received this (search the gateway for the sender, subject pattern, URL, attachment hash — Lesson 9's who-else pivot, in mail form) and who interacted — clicked, opened, entered credentials — from proxy logs, endpoint telemetry, and auth records.

RESPONSE — campaign "salary bands FY2026" · verdict: targeted phish · T1566.001 SCOPE gateway search: sender OR subject OR attachment-hash → 7 recipients proxy + EDR: 2 clicked link · 1 opened attachment · auth: no cred entry yet CONTAIN purge message from all 7 mailboxes · block sender domain + URL at gateway/proxy quarantine attachment hash fleet-wide USERS 2 clickers: sessions revoked, credentials reset as precaution 1 opener: host isolated pending endpoint review ← blameless, fast, factual LOOPS IOCs → intel records (expiry set) · lure TTP → detection request reporter thanked within the hour ← reporting is a behavior you feed

Two culture notes that decide whether this pipeline works. Blameless, always: the user who clicked and reported is your early-warning system functioning — punish or embarrass clickers and reports stop, and the next campaign runs uninterrupted. Thank reporters visibly and quickly, even when the verdict is benign; you are training a sensor network. And phishing response feeds every loop you know: indicators to intel (Lesson 11), lure patterns to detection engineering (Lesson 8), "how many more like this already got through?" to hunting (Lesson 12) — which is precisely the question the scenario section now answers in the other direction.

The clock on credentials. If evidence shows a user submitted credentials to a harvest page, reset-and-revoke starts immediately — attackers commonly use stolen credentials within minutes to hours, and a reset an hour late is a Lesson 10 incident instead of a Lesson 13 save. Sessions too, not just passwords: a live token survives a password change.

08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

08:42 — the Report button

Three weeks after HUNT-007 exposed the actor's phishing entry, the same campaign returns for a second wave — and this time, the defenses it helped build are waiting. Twelve steps from one user's click on Report to a closed loop.

Response replay — "the wave that hit a prepared SOC"

08:42 · ReportA finance analyst hesitates — then clicks Report"Updated salary bands FY2026" from HR Compensation. Something about the sender felt off. The report lands in the phishing queue with headers intact — the single most valuable click of the quarter.
08:45 · HeadersClaim versus provenanceBottom Received: a rented VPS, not any HR system. From, Reply-To, Return-Path all agree — on cornpany-hr.com, one glyph from home. Auth results: pass, pass, pass — for the attacker's own lookalike domain. The postmarks tell the story in three minutes.
08:49 · URL & attachmentDefang, expand, detonateThe link, defanged and traced through its shortener, lands on a credential-harvest page skinned as the company SSO. The attached .xlsm goes to the sandbox: macro spawns PowerShell, creates a scheduled task. Both artifacts documented, neither ever touched the analyst's own machine.
08:56 · VerdictTargeted phish — and a familiar signatureSalary-themed lure, finance recipients, macro-to-task tradecraft: this matches INC-0043's entry technique and the ISAC campaign profile. Verdict: targeted phishing, T1566.001, same actor. Fourteen minutes from report to attribution-grade verdict.
08:58 · ScopeWho else — and who interactedGateway search on sender, subject, and attachment hash: seven recipients, all finance. Proxy logs: two clicked the link. EDR: one opened the attachment. Auth logs: no credential submissions yet. The blast radius, mapped before nine a.m.
09:02 · The rule firesR-2077 catches the opener's host mid-actOn the machine that opened the attachment, the macro's scheduled task creation trips the very rule HUNT-007 shipped. The alert arrives pre-enriched with campaign context. Last quarter this was an invisible three-week foothold; today it's a nine-minute-old alert.
09:05 · ContainPurge, block, isolate — in one passMessage purged from all seven mailboxes. Sender domain and harvest URL blocked at gateway and proxy. Attachment hash quarantined fleet-wide. The opener's host isolated pending review. The campaign's second wave ends before its first credential.
09:09 · UsersPrecautionary resets, blameless handlingThe two clickers: sessions revoked, credentials reset — no evidence of submission, but tokens are cheap to rotate and expensive to trust. All seven users get a factual heads-up. Nobody is named, shamed, or quizzed. The reporter gets a thank-you before 09:30.
09:20 · The hunt reflex"How many more like this?"Lesson 12 thinking kicks in unprompted: gateway history searched for the lure's pattern family across 90 days. One earlier wave found — the one that built INC-0043 — and nothing else. The campaign's full footprint in this estate is now known, not assumed.
10:00 · Intel outThe wave becomes everyone's warningLookalike domain, harvest URL, attachment hash, VPS origin — packaged as IOC records with context and expiry, pushed to enrichment, and shared to the ISAC within the morning. Three peer SOCs block the domain before their own finance teams hear from "HR."
10:30 · Detection askThe lure pattern becomes a rule requestOne gap noted honestly: the gateway had no detection for lookalike-domain registration patterns against the company brand. Filed to detection engineering with this campaign as the test case — Lesson 8's intake, fed by Lesson 13's morning.
The loop, visibleEvery lesson, one morningA hunt built a rule; the rule caught the phish's payload; triage craft scoped the wave; response contained it; intel armed the neighbors; and one user's Report click started all of it. Fifty-three minutes, no incident declared. That's what foundations are for.
Ready. Press Play to run the response, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: compare this morning to HR-WS-117 three weeks earlier — same actor, same lure family, same technique. The difference wasn't smarter analysts; it was accumulated loops: a hunt that became a rule, an incident that became intel, a reporting culture that produced the 08:42 click. Prepared SOCs aren't lucky; they're compounding.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Phishing triage runs on reflexes, so wrong reflexes are expensive. Recalibrate these now:

Misconception

"SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all pass — so the email is legitimate."

Reality

Authentication proves the message genuinely came from the domain it claims — including when that domain is the attacker's own lookalike, configured with perfect SPF and DKIM in five minutes. A pass answers "is the sender who they say?" — never "is who they say friendly?" The INC-0043 lure passed everything.

Misconception

"Phishing is easy to spot — typos, bad grammar, ugly logos."

Reality

That heuristic died years ago. Modern lures are cloned from real corporate mail, fluently written (increasingly machine-written), and pixel-perfect. Targeted campaigns are cleaner than legitimate internal email. Verdicts come from provenance and behavior — headers, origins, where links actually lead — not from prose quality.

Misconception

"Confirmed phish — delete it from the reporter's mailbox and close the ticket."

Reality

One report is a sample from a campaign, never the campaign. The mandatory follow-ons: who else received it, who clicked or opened, purge everywhere, block the infrastructure, and preserve the sample as evidence and intel. Deleting the report and stopping is closing your one open eye.

Misconception

"A user clicked — time for consequences and mandatory training."

Reality

The lure was engineered by professionals to be clicked; someone clicking is the expected failure mode the SOC exists to absorb. Blame produces exactly one outcome: the next clicker stays silent, and silence is how one compromised mailbox becomes a quarter-long intrusion. Reward reporting — especially post-click reporting — like the early-warning system it is.

Misconception

"I'll just open the link quickly to see where it goes."

Reality

On your workstation, with your session cookies, from your source IP — announcing the investigation to the attacker's analytics and risking self-infection in one move. Hostile artifacts get examined in sandboxes and isolated environments, indicators get defanged in notes, and "quickly checking" is how analysts become case numbers.

Misconception

"Phishing is a user-awareness problem — training will fix it."

Reality

Awareness helps and reporting culture is gold — but a defense that requires every human to be right every time is a defense designed to fail. The layers do the real work: gateway filtering, authentication enforcement, URL and attachment detonation, endpoint rules like R-2077 for what gets through, and a fast response pipeline for what runs anyway. Users are one layer, never the plan.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • Email is the front door because it delivers stranger-controlled content to humans — and the spectrum runs mass phish → spear phish → BEC, with credential-harvest and malware-delivery goals cutting across all of it.
  • The body is the forger's canvas; the headers are the postmarks. Analysis lives in the gap between what a message claims and what its provenance proves.
  • Header reflex: bottom Received = true origin; check From / Reply-To / Return-Path agreement — and which domain they agree on.
  • SPF (authorized sender IPs), DKIM (signed, unaltered), DMARC (policy + alignment) prove a message came from its claimed domain — a pass says nothing about whether that domain is hostile. Lookalikes authenticate perfectly.
  • Safe handling is rule zero: sandbox and isolated analysis only, defang every indicator you write down, never "quickly check" a link on your own machine.
  • The pipeline: triage → verdict → scope (who else received, who interacted) → contain (purge, block, reset, isolate) → feed the loops — and credential exposure starts the reset clock immediately, sessions included.
  • Blameless, always: reporters are a sensor network you're training, clickers are the expected failure mode, and layered controls — not perfect humans — are the actual defense.
11
Assessment

That .xlsm detonated in a sandbox and the report came back — now learn to read it like an analyst. Malware families and what each actually does, static versus dynamic analysis, persistence and C2 behaviors to recognize on sight, and how a SOC analyst extracts verdicts and IOCs from a sandbox report without being a reverse engineer.

SOC Foundations Module 12 — Malware Analysis Lesson 14 — Malware Fundamentals
Module 12 · Lesson 14

Malware Fundamentals:
Types, Behavior & Sandbox Literacy

Yesterday's phishing triage sent an .xlsm to the sandbox. Today the report is back. This lesson teaches you to read it like an analyst: what each malware family is actually for, the behavioral tells that survive every recompile, and how to extract verdicts and indicators from a detonation report — without reversing a single byte.

LEVELBeginner DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–13 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • Classify malware by its job: droppers install, RATs control, stealers harvest, ransomware extorts, worms spread.
  • Ask five behavior questions: does it persist, beacon, steal, spread, encrypt?
  • Static analysis first, sandbox second — and a clean sandbox run proves very little.
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Classify malware by its job

Recognize droppers, RATs, stealers, ransomware, and worms by what they're built to accomplish — not by their names.

Spot behavioral tells

Identify the persistence, beaconing, and staging behaviors that survive every recompile — top-of-pyramid thinking, applied to files.

Run static-first triage

Extract cheap verdicts from hashes, file types, strings, and structure before anything ever executes.

Read a sandbox report

Walk process trees, persistence entries, and network activity to a defensible verdict — and know the report's blind spots.

Extract and route IOCs

Pull hashes, domains, and artifacts from a detonation and feed them straight into scoping, intel, and detection.

Know your escalation line

Handle behavior-level analysis confidently — and recognize exactly when a specimen deserves a real malware analyst.

02
Orientation

Why malware literacy beats malware fear

Malware is the attacker's automation — code that does their work at scale: keeps their access alive between sessions, harvests what they came for, spreads where they haven't been, and detonates their endgame. Nearly every case in this course had malware in the chain: FIN-WS-042's macro payload, INC-0043's beacon and scheduled task, yesterday's .xlsm. The SOC meets malware constantly — in sandbox verdicts, EDR alerts, and intel reports — and the analyst who can't read malware behavior is triaging with a dictionary they can't open.

Here's the liberating part: Tier-1 malware work is literacy, not reverse engineering. You will almost never disassemble a binary — specialists do that, rarely and expensively. What you do daily is read behavior: what a specimen did when detonated, what it dropped, where it called, how it persisted — and convert that reading into verdicts, indicators, and scoping questions. It's the Pyramid of Pain from Lesson 11, applied to files: names and hashes are costumes that change per victim; behaviors are the job description, and the job barely changes.

Analogy — the customs officer

A customs officer doesn't dismantle every engine to find smuggling compartments — that's the forensic workshop's job, used for special cases. The officer works from behavior and profile: declared purpose versus actual contents, routes that make no sense, weight that doesn't match the manifest. Ninety-five percent of the job is pattern literacy at the inspection lane; five percent goes to the workshop. Tier-1 malware analysis is the inspection lane — and knowing when to send something to the workshop is part of the skill.

Where this sits. This lesson closes the loop Lesson 13 opened — the .xlsm's detonation report is section 06's centerpiece — and it arms the next two: EDR alerts (Lesson 15) are largely malware behavior seen live on endpoints, and network analysis (later) is malware's C2 traffic seen on the wire.

In plain words

Malware is software built to do the attacker's dirty work. A small dropper fetches the real payload; a RAT gives remote control; ransomware encrypts files for money. Most malware phones home to its C2 server on a steady rhythm (a beacon) and uses tricks to survive reboots (persistence). You study it safely by running it in a sandbox and watching what it touches.

03
Core concepts

Families by job description — and the modern realities

Malware taxonomy gets messy fast — vendors invent names, families blend capabilities, and marketing loves a scary label. Cut through it with one question: what is this code's job? The working set: droppers and loaders establish the beachhead — small, disposable first stages whose only task is fetching and launching the real payload. RATs and backdoors maintain interactive control — the attacker's remote hands, beaconing for orders. Infostealers grab credentials, cookies, and wallets, exfiltrate, and often vanish. Ransomware monetizes by denial — encryption plus extortion. Worms self-propagate. Classic labels like trojan (disguised delivery) and rootkit (concealment) describe traits that combine with any of the above. Real intrusions chain the jobs: yesterday's .xlsm was a trojan-delivered dropper installing a RAT — three words, whole story.

Three modern realities to install early. Commodity vs targeted: most malware is rented — malware-as-a-service kits sprayed by affiliates — which is why the same stealer appears in a thousand unrelated companies; targeted tooling exists but is the exception, and the distinction shapes severity calls. Fileless and living-off-the-land: plenty of "malware" is never a file on disk at all — it's PowerShell in memory, scheduled tasks, WMI, legitimate binaries doing illegitimate work (Lesson 12's LOLBins) — invisible to file scanning, loud in behavioral telemetry. Per-victim builds: automated repacking gives every campaign fresh hashes, which is why hash-only defense is the pyramid's floor.

The label matters less than the behavior. Whether intel calls it "AgentTesla" or "generic.trojan.xyz", your response keys on what it does: does it persist (survive reboots)? Does it beacon (attacker still connected)? Does it steal (credentials now burned)? Does it spread (scope just widened)? Does it encrypt (clock just started)? Five questions, and the answers — not the name — drive containment.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five working roles

Select a role, then work the tabs — "behavioral tells" is what the specimen looks like in a sandbox report or on an endpoint, and "SOC response notes" is what the verdict changes about your next hour.

05
Core concepts

Static first: cheap answers before anything runs

Two complementary lenses, always in this order. Static analysis examines the file without executing it: identity (hashes against intel — Lesson 11's thirty-second win), true file type versus claimed extension, embedded strings (URLs, IPs, suspicious commands hiding in plain text), structure and metadata, and packing — deliberate obfuscation that is itself a signal, because legitimate payroll spreadsheets aren't armored. Static is instant, safe, and free; it triages what deserves detonation. Dynamic analysis executes the specimen in an instrumented, isolated sandbox and records everything it does — the behavioral truth no obfuscation survives, because to work, malware must eventually act.

STATIC TRIAGE — salary_bands_2026.xlsm (30 seconds, nothing executed) sha256: 9f2c…41ab intel lookup: no match ← unknown ≠ safe: per-victim builds type: Office Open XML, macro-enabled (vbaProject.bin present) strings: "powershell -enc", hxxps://cdn-invoice-view[.]net/… ← commands in a spreadsheet macro: auto-exec trigger (Workbook_Open) · obfuscated string concat verdict: detonate in sandbox — high suspicion, zero ambiguity about next step

Note the division of labor in that block: static didn't prove malice — it proved enough suspicion to justify detonation, in half a minute, with the specimen never executed. That's the Tier-1 pattern: hash check → static triage → sandbox → read the report. Full manual reverse engineering — debuggers, disassembly — exists beyond this pipeline, owned by specialists, and reserved for specimens that matter: novel tooling, targeted attacks, evidence for attribution. Knowing that escalation path exists is part of the literacy; walking it is not your job.

Obfuscation is information. Packing, encoded commands, string concatenation gymnastics — attackers spend effort hiding because the content would convict them. When static analysis finds armor on something claiming to be mundane, the armor itself has already answered the question static couldn't read through.

06
Core concepts

Sandbox literacy: reading the detonation

Here it is — the report Lesson 13's triage queued. A sandbox report has four load-bearing sections, and you read them in this order: process tree (who spawned whom — Lesson 4's lineage, recorded), persistence (what survives reboot), network (where it called, what it asked for), and artifacts (files dropped, their hashes). The score at the top is a hint; the behaviors are the evidence.

SANDBOX REPORT — job 8841 · salary_bands_2026.xlsm · win11-x64 · score 92/100 PROCESS TREE excel.exe ← the lure opens normally: user sees salary bands └─ powershell.exe -enc JAB3AGMAPQBOAGUA… ← Workbook_Open macro fires ├─ GET hxxps://cdn-invoice-view[.]net/d.php → beacon.exe └─ writes %APPDATA%\WinDiag\beacon.exe (sha256 e3b0…991b) PERSISTENCE schtasks /create /tn "WindowsDiagnosticSvc" /tr %APPDATA%\WinDiag\beacon.exe /sc onlogon NETWORK beacon.exe → 198.51.100.34:443 · TLS · retry every 60s ← C2 beacon pattern CLASSIFICATION trojan dropper → RAT implant · T1566.001 · T1059.001 · T1053.005 · T1071.001 IOC HARVEST: 2 hashes · 1 domain · 1 IP · task name · %APPDATA%\WinDiag path

Read what that report just handed you. Scoping ammunition: every IOC becomes a fleet-wide question — has this hash, domain, or task name appeared anywhere else? (That's how Lesson 13's response found the second host.) Detection validation: the persistence line is exactly R-2077's trigger — the rule and the specimen confirm each other. Intel product: the harvest, with context and expiry, ships to enrichment and the ISAC. One detonation, three loops fed — and the analyst never touched a disassembler.

The sandbox's blind spot. Malware authors know their code will be detonated, so they build evasions: long sleeps to outlast analysis windows, checks for VM artifacts and missing user activity, geo- and time-fencing, payloads that require a click the sandbox never makes. The rule: a dirty run convicts; a clean run proves little. A clean report on a statically-suspicious file means escalate or extend the analysis — never "benign, release it."

07
Hands-on · Simulation

You're the analyst: name the role

Six behavior summaries, straight from sandbox reports and EDR timelines. Classify each specimen by its job — the role drives the response: a stealer means credentials are burned now, a RAT means the attacker is still connected, a dropper means the real payload is the next question.

Role-recognition drill

Specimen 1 / 6 · Score 0
08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

Job 8841: reading the report

Yesterday, 08:49: the .xlsm enters the sandbox queue. Here's the analysis, start to finish — static triage through IOC harvest — as the analyst experienced it. Twelve steps, zero bytes reversed.

Analysis replay — "from suspicious file to fed loops"

08:49 · IdentityHash first — thirty seconds, no executionSHA-256 computed and checked against intel: no match anywhere. Which proves nothing — per-victim builds mean fresh hashes are the norm — but the check is free, and a hit would have ended triage instantly. Cheap questions first, always.
08:50 · Static triageThe file argues against itselfMacro-enabled workbook with an auto-exec trigger, obfuscated string assembly, and — sitting in the strings dump — "powershell -enc" and a defanged URL. A payroll document carrying encoded commands has already told you what it is; the sandbox will just write it down.
08:51 · DetonationInstrumented, isolated, recordedJob 8841 opens the file on a disposable Windows VM wired with sensors: every process, file write, registry touch, and packet logged. The lure renders a perfectly convincing salary table — the user-visible half doing its job while the sensors watch the other half.
Process treeThe forbidden parent, on the recordexcel.exe spawns powershell.exe with an encoded command line. Lesson 4 taught this lineage as theory, Lesson 12 hunted it in history — here it is happening live, timestamped, in a report you can attach to a case.
Stage twoThe dropper does its one jobPowerShell fetches beacon.exe from cdn-invoice-view[.]net and writes it to %APPDATA%\WinDiag\. The macro was never the malware — it was the delivery driver. Role one identified: trojan-delivered dropper. The interesting question is what it delivered.
PersistenceThe scheduled task — an old acquaintanceschtasks creates "WindowsDiagnosticSvc" to launch beacon.exe at logon: the exact artifact pattern from INC-0043, the exact behavior R-2077 watches for. The specimen and the detection rule have just validated each other in a lab.
NetworkThe beacon starts asking for ordersbeacon.exe opens TLS to 198.51.100.34 and retries every 60 seconds — the metronome heartbeat of a RAT awaiting tasking. The sandbox's fake network answers just enough to record the pattern. Role two identified: RAT implant.
VerdictThree words, whole storyTrojan dropper → RAT implant. Score 92/100 — but the score is the headline, not the evidence: the process tree, the persistence entry, and the beacon are the conviction. Verdicts cite behaviors, and this report is thick with them.
ATT&CK mappingBehaviors, given their shared namesT1566.001 (spearphishing attachment), T1059.001 (PowerShell), T1053.005 (scheduled task), T1071.001 (web-protocol C2). Now the incident report, the detection rules, and the ISAC brief all speak the same four IDs. Lesson 11's grammar, in daily use.
IOC harvestThe report becomes ammunitionTwo hashes, one domain, one IP, a task name, a filesystem path — extracted, defanged, and immediately spent: fleet-wide scoping queries (clean), enrichment records with expiry, gateway and proxy blocks. The detonation's whole point was this list.
The honest caveatWhat the sandbox did NOT proveThe analyst's note: "beacon received no tasking — post-C2 capability unobserved; classification based on delivery and implant behavior." If this specimen ever needs courtroom-grade capability analysis, that's the specialists' workshop. Knowing the line is part of the literacy.
Loops fedFourteen minutes of reading, three systems smarterScoping answered, intel shipped, R-2077 validated against a live specimen — and the report attached to the case for whoever works this actor next. The analyst read behavior like a language. That's the whole skill, and it compounds.
Ready. Press Play to run the analysis, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: follow what each stage contributed. Static triage justified the detonation; the process tree named the delivery; persistence and network named the implant; the harvest armed three loops. No single stage proved everything — the sequence did. And notice the caveat in step 11: strong analysts state what their evidence doesn't cover. That habit is worth more than any tool.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Malware judgments gone wrong tend to fail in the same few directions. Pre-correct them:

Misconception

"The hash isn't in any threat feed — the file is safe."

Reality

Per-victim builds make fresh hashes the norm, not the exception — job 8841's specimen matched nothing and was dropper-plus-RAT. A hash hit convicts instantly; a hash miss says only "nobody has reported this exact byte sequence." Unknown means keep analyzing, never "release."

Misconception

"The sandbox run came back clean — file's benign."

Reality

Malware authors test against sandboxes the way developers test against browsers. Sleeps that outlast analysis windows, VM-artifact checks, geo-fencing, waiting for human interaction — all standard. A dirty run convicts; a clean run proves little. Clean-but-statically-suspicious means extended detonation or escalation, with the static findings deciding.

Misconception

"Real malware would have been caught by antivirus."

Reality

Signature AV is a floor, and attackers test their builds against every engine before shipping — evading day-one detection is a solved problem for them. The defense that works is behavioral and layered: lineage rules, persistence detection, beacon analytics. If AV silence meant safety, this course would be three lessons long.

Misconception

"Malware means .exe files."

Reality

Yesterday's specimen was a spreadsheet. Malware ships as macros, scripts, shortcuts, container images, and — increasingly — as no file at all: PowerShell in memory, WMI subscriptions, scheduled tasks, legitimate binaries repurposed (LOLBins). File-shaped thinking misses the fileless half; behavior-shaped thinking catches both.

Misconception

"Ransomware hit at 03:00 — so the attack happened at 03:00."

Reality

Encryption is the finale, detonated at the intrusion's end — the access, recon, privilege escalation, staging, and usually data theft happened days or weeks earlier. Response scopes backward from the blast: entry point, dwell activity, exfiltration evidence. Treating the detonation as the attack is investigating a fire by studying the ashes' final temperature.

Misconception

"Proper malware analysis means reverse engineering, so this is above my level."

Reality

The daily work is behavior literacy — reading process trees, persistence, and network patterns from reports — and it's fully within Tier-1 reach, as job 8841 showed end-to-end. Disassembly is a specialist craft for specimens that earn it. Know the escalation line, use it without embarrassment, and own everything on your side of it.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • Classify by job description: droppers establish, RATs control, stealers harvest, ransomware extorts, worms spread — and traits like trojan and rootkit combine with any of them. Real intrusions chain the roles.
  • Five behavior questions beat any label: does it persist, beacon, steal, spread, encrypt? The answers drive containment; the name is for the report.
  • Modern realities: commodity malware-as-a-service dominates, fileless and LOLBin tradecraft evades file scanning entirely, and per-victim builds make hash-miss meaningless.
  • Static first: hashes, true type, strings, macros, packing — instant, safe, free. Obfuscation on a "mundane" file is itself evidence. Static earns the detonation; dynamic records the truth.
  • Sandbox reports read in order: process tree → persistence → network → artifacts. The score is a hint; the behaviors are the conviction.
  • A dirty run convicts; a clean run proves little — evasion (sleeps, VM checks, fencing) is standard, so clean-but-suspicious means extend or escalate, never release.
  • Every detonation should feed the loops: IOCs to scoping and intel, behaviors to ATT&CK-tagged detection, the report to the case — and the honest caveat about what the evidence didn't cover travels with it.
11
Assessment

Test yourself

Eight questions, mixed formats — the literacy that turns sandbox reports into decisions.

Lesson 14 knowledge check

Question 1 / 8
12
Assessment · Mini-lab

The behavior verdict

Five lines from a sandbox report on a file that arrived as "Q3_budget_review.xlsx". Legitimate software does surprisingly suspicious-looking things, so most of these lines are explainable. One is verdict-grade. Click the behavior that convicts.

Thought exercise (no clicking required)

Then the design question: which of the five behaviors would you convert into a detection rule, and at which Pyramid of Pain level does it sit?

From antivirus to EDR's flight-recorder telemetry, working endpoint alerts with process trees at your fingertips, and the response actions — isolate, kill, quarantine — that make endpoints the SOC's strongest lever.

SOC Foundations Module 13 — Endpoint Security Lesson 15 — Endpoint Security & EDR
Module 13 · Lesson 15

Endpoint Security & EDR:
The SOC's Strongest Lever

Everything job 8841 recorded in a sandbox, EDR records live — on every host, all the time. This lesson covers the evolution from antivirus to flight-recorder telemetry, working endpoint alerts with the process tree at your fingertips, and the response actions that let one analyst reach into any machine in the fleet.

LEVELBeginner DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–14 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • EDR records endpoint activity continuously, so you can detect, investigate and respond — not just block files.
  • Work an alert: read the tree → walk the timeline → query the fleet → then respond, cheapest action first.
  • Know the blind spots: unmanaged hosts, dead or tampered agents, and everything that isn't an endpoint.
Hands-on:Lab 2 · Sysmon telemetry
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Place EDR in its lineage

Explain the road from signature AV to behavioral prevention to full detection-and-response — and what each layer still contributes.

Know the telemetry

Name what the agent records — processes, files, registry, network, scripts — and why that stream powers everything else.

Work an EDR alert end-to-end

Read the tree, walk the timeline, scope the fleet — Lesson 9's triage with the evidence pre-assembled.

Price response actions

Choose between isolate, kill, quarantine, and collect — weighing evidence, business impact, and speed like an IC in miniature.

Respect the blind spots

Know exactly where EDR doesn't see: unmanaged hosts, tampered agents, and everything that happens off the endpoint.

Pair EDR with the SIEM

Use endpoint depth and cross-source breadth as the complements they are — not the rivals vendors sell.

02
Orientation

Why the endpoint is where attacks become real

Follow any intrusion in this course to its decisive moment and you land on an endpoint: the macro executing on HR-WS-117, the beacon persisting on FIN-WS-233, the credential harvest rendering in someone's browser. Phishing, exploits, and stolen credentials are all delivery; the attack becomes real when code runs on a machine — and endpoints are where code runs. That makes them simultaneously the richest evidence source (Lesson 4's telemetry lives here) and the most direct point of intervention.

EDR — endpoint detection and response — is both of those things in one agent. It's a flight recorder: continuous capture of process activity, file operations, and network connections, kept whether or not anything alerts — which is why the sandbox report from Lesson 14 and an EDR timeline read like the same document. And it's remote hands: from one console, an analyst can isolate a host on another continent, kill a process, pull a forensic package. Visibility plus reach, on every managed machine, is why this lesson's subtitle isn't marketing — for a Tier-1 analyst, EDR genuinely is the strongest lever on the desk.

Analogy — the flight recorder with a remote copilot

Aviation didn't get safer by predicting every failure — it got safer by recording everything, so any incident could be reconstructed second-by-second, and every reconstruction improved the fleet. EDR is that black box on every endpoint. Then it adds what aviation can't: a copilot who can take the controls remotely — cut the network, stop the process, retrieve the evidence — from an ocean away. Recording plus reach; that combination is the product.

Where this sits. This lesson is the operational home of half the course: Lesson 4's process lineage is EDR's native language, Lesson 10's containment pricing governs its response buttons, Lesson 12's hunts run on its telemetry, and Lesson 14's sandbox behaviors are what its detections watch for — live. The scenario picks up FIN-WS-233, isolated at 09:05 in Lesson 13, and finishes that story properly.

In plain words

EDR is the modern security agent living on each computer. Old antivirus only matched known-bad files; EDR records all process, file, and network activity, spots bad behavior, and lets you isolate a machine from the network with one click while you investigate. It's your eyes and hands on the endpoint — and isolation is reversible, so you can act fast without breaking things forever.

03
Core concepts

From antivirus to EDR — what actually changed

The evolution is a story about one question getting harder. Traditional antivirus asked "is this file known-bad?" — signature matching against a database: fast, cheap, and defeated by per-victim builds (Lesson 14's whole point). Next-gen AV upgraded the question to "does this file or behavior look bad?" — machine-learning classifiers and behavioral heuristics that block never-before-seen samples, still fundamentally in the prevention business. EDR changed the question entirely: "record everything that happens, so anything can be detected, investigated, and responded to." Prevention still runs (EDR platforms include NGAV), but the defining capability is the telemetry stream and what it enables — because Lesson 8 taught you no prevention layer catches everything, and EDR is built for the everything it misses.

What the agent actually records, per host, continuously: process events (creation, termination, command lines, parent-child lineage — Lesson 4's Sysmon story, productized), file operations (writes, modifications, especially in interesting paths), registry changes (persistence's favorite home), network connections (which process talked to which address), script and memory activity (PowerShell content, injection attempts — the fileless tradecraft file-scanning can't see). This stream feeds four consumers: real-time behavioral detections on the endpoint, the console's investigation views, fleet-wide hunting queries, and — forwarded onward — the SIEM, where endpoint depth joins Lesson 5's cross-source breadth.

The acronym landscape, briefly. XDR extends the EDR model across sources (endpoint + identity + email + cloud) under one detection layer; MDR is EDR operated for you as a service. Useful terms, same fundamentals — telemetry, detection, investigation, response. Master the EDR core and the extended alphabet follows.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five capability pillars

Select a pillar, then work the tabs — "analyst moves" is how you use it on shift, and "limits & gotchas" is where each pillar quietly stops working if nobody's paying attention.

05
Core concepts

Working an EDR alert: triage with the evidence pre-assembled

Here's what R-2077's detection looked like in the EDR console when FIN-WS-233's attachment ran — the same event Lesson 13's scenario showed from the SIEM side. Notice what's different from a classic alert: the process tree, command lines, and network activity arrive already attached. Lesson 9's context-building phase — the entity timeline, the pivots — is largely pre-computed:

EDR ALERT — FIN-WS-233 · 09:02:11 UTC · severity HIGH · tactic: Persistence (T1053.005) DETECTION Scheduled task registered from user-writable path (rule R-2077-EP) TREE outlook.exe → excel.exe ("salary_bands_2026.xlsm") └─ powershell.exe -enc JAB3AGMA… ├─ net: GET cdn-invoice-view[.]net → beacon.exe ├─ write: %APPDATA%\WinDiag\beacon.exe (e3b0…991b) └─ exec: schtasks /create /tn "WindowsDiagnosticSvc" … NETWORK beacon.exe → 198.51.100.34:443 · 2 attempts · BLOCKED at proxy (intel feed) CONTEXT user: a.rahman (Finance) · asset: standard workstation · agent: healthy ACTIONS [Isolate] [Kill process] [Quarantine file] [Collect package] [Fleet query] the whole Lesson 9 investigation, pre-assembled — judgment is the only part left to add

The working pattern on any EDR alert, in order: read the tree — parent-child lineage and full command lines usually settle "malicious or not" in one look (Lesson 14's chained-behaviors rule, applied live). Walk the timeline — what did the host do in the minutes around the detection: other file writes, other children, other connections? Scope the fleet — every artifact becomes a one-click estate-wide question: this hash, this task name, this destination — anywhere else? Then, and only then, the response buttons. The tooling compresses hours into minutes, but note what it doesn't compress: the verdict is still yours. EDR alerts false-positive like every detection (admin scripts trip persistence rules constantly), and the console's confidence score is Lesson 9's severity label wearing new clothes — an input, not an answer.

The pre-assembled evidence cuts both ways. Because everything is one click away, anchoring accelerates too: the tree looks complete, so analysts stop looking. The discipline: the tree shows this host's lineage — it does not show the other host, the cloud session, or the mailbox rule. EDR depth still needs SIEM breadth for anything that crossed machines.

06
Core concepts

The response buttons — and what each one costs

EDR's response actions are Lesson 10's containment options, miniaturized and instant — which makes the pricing discipline more important, not less, because a mistake now takes one click too. The toolkit: network isolation — cut the host from everything except the EDR management channel, so investigation continues while the attacker's access dies; kill process and quarantine file — stop and neutralize specific malicious activity; collect forensic package — memory, key artifacts, and logs preserved before anything changes them (Lesson 10's capture-before-you-change, as a button); live response — a remote shell for surgical evidence gathering and cleanup; and fleet-wide blocking — a hash banned everywhere in seconds.

RESPONSE PRICING — the question each button must answer first isolate host stops: all attacker access costs: user/service downtime right when: active destruction, spreading, live C2 wrong when: low-confidence hunch kill + quarantine stops: this process/file costs: volatile evidence, tips the attacker right when: evidence captured or damage active wrong when: scoping unfinished collect package stops: nothing costs: minutes right when: almost always FIRST, unless those minutes are being spent encrypting fleet query stops: nothing costs: nothing right when: always — scope is never wasted ← the free action

Two structural notes that complete the picture. Coverage is a precondition: EDR sees exactly the hosts where a healthy agent runs — Lesson 7's lesson wearing an endpoint badge. Unmanaged machines, BYOD, appliances, and OT are dark; agent health monitoring and tamper protection (attackers try to kill the agent first — an agent going silent mid-incident is itself a high-severity signal) are what keep the flight recorder recording. And authority matters: isolating a workstation is a Tier-1 call in most SOCs; isolating a production server or an executive's laptop mid-meeting is Lesson 10's business-impact conversation — the button being available doesn't make it yours.

The default sequence, absent urgency: fleet query (free) → collect (cheap) → then contain and clean (priced). Urgency — encryption running, worm spreading, live hands-on-keyboard — inverts it: isolate first, apologize to the evidence later. Knowing which situation you're in is the skill; the drill ahead trains exactly that.

08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

FIN-WS-233: inside the isolated host

Lesson 13 ended with one host isolated at 09:05 "pending endpoint review." This is that review — the EDR-driven investigation that turns an isolation into a clean, evidenced, closed case. Twelve steps at the console.

Endpoint replay — "twenty minutes on the flight recorder"

09:12 · The alert, revisitedEverything is already on screenThe R-2077-EP detection sits in the console with its tree attached: Outlook → Excel → encoded PowerShell → beacon.exe → scheduled task. What Lesson 9 assembled through pivots, the agent recorded as it happened. Triage starts from evidence, not from questions.
Tree walkThe chain convicts in one readDocument spawns interpreter, interpreter fetches and stages a binary, binary persists — Lesson 14's chained-behaviors rule, live. Command lines are captured in full, including the encoded payload, decoded by the console with one click. Verdict confidence: total.
TimelineFour minutes of beacon lifetimeThe flight recorder answers the question that matters: beacon.exe ran from 09:01 to isolation at 09:05. Two C2 attempts, both blocked at the proxy — the intel feed from Lesson 11's loop did its job. No tasking ever arrived. The implant lived four minutes and spent them on hold.
Around the eventWhat else did the host do?Timeline scan of the surrounding hour: no other file writes to interesting paths, no additional children, no lateral connections, no credential access. The intrusion's footprint on this host is exactly the tree — small, early, and contained before it grew.
09:18 · Collect firstThe package, before anything changesOne click: memory capture, the beacon binary, the scheduled task definition, relevant logs — preserved into a forensic package and attached to the case. Lesson 10's capture-before-you-change, executed in ninety seconds without leaving the chair.
Fleet queryThe free action, spent generouslyHash, task name, %APPDATA%\WinDiag path, C2 address — queried across every agent in the estate in seconds. Result: FIN-WS-233 only. The same question that took HUNT-007 a structured hunt now costs one console query. Tooling compounds too.
09:24 · RemediateKill, quarantine, uprootBeacon process killed, binary quarantined fleet-wide (a ban, not just a deletion), scheduled task removed via live response, run-key sweep clean. Evidence was captured first, scope was confirmed first — so remediation is now just tidying, in the right order.
Credential checkWhat could four minutes have stolen?The timeline shows no credential-store access, no LSASS interaction, no token games — but a.rahman's sessions are revoked and password rotated anyway. Four minutes of implant lifetime buys a lot of doubt, and doubt about credentials is always resolved in one direction.
The prevention questionCould this have been blocked, not just detected?Review finding: the platform's attack-surface rules could block Office-spawning-interpreters outright on standard workstations — currently audit-only, feared breakage. The finance fleet has zero legitimate macro-to-shell usage in 90 days of telemetry. The data just paid for the policy change.
RestoreBack to work, watchedHost released from isolation after cleanup verification, agent healthy, elevated monitoring tag for 48 hours — Lesson 10's validation watch, scoped to one machine. a.rahman loses half a morning. The alternative timelines cost considerably more.
DocumentThe case file writes itself — almostTree screenshot, timeline export, forensic package, fleet-query results, actions log with timestamps — attached. The analyst adds the two things no tool generates: the verdict reasoning and the honest note that C2 was never tasked. Evidence assembled by machines; judgment signed by a human.
The lever, measuredTwenty minutes, one analyst, zero site visitsInvestigation, evidence, scoping, remediation, hardening recommendation — from one console, while the host sat isolated three floors away. Before EDR this was a day and a desk visit. The flight recorder plus remote hands: that's the lever, and now you know how to pull it.
Ready. Press Play to run the investigation, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: notice the order held even under comfort — collect, then scope, then remediate — and notice step 9's question: detection worked; could prevention have worked earlier? Mature endpoint programs climb that ladder constantly, using their own telemetry to prove hardening is safe. The best EDR alert is the one next quarter's policy makes impossible.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

EDR's power breeds its own failure modes — most of them varieties of overconfidence:

Misconception

"We have EDR now — the SIEM is redundant."

Reality

EDR is endpoint depth; the SIEM is cross-source breadth. The intrusion that touches a mailbox rule, a VPN login, a cloud API, and one endpoint is visible end-to-end only where those sources meet — and Lesson 13's campaign was scoped in mail and proxy logs before any endpoint fired. Depth and breadth are complements; vendors selling either as sufficient are selling half a picture.

Misconception

"Prevention mode is on — we're covered."

Reality

Prevention blocks what it recognizes; Lesson 8's lesson stands — no layer catches everything, which is why EDR's defining half is detection and response for what gets through. And prevention configs rot: exclusions accumulate ("the backup tool kept tripping it"), audit-mode rules never graduate to block, and each exception is a lane an attacker can drive through. Prevention is a layer to maintain, not a box to tick.

Misconception

"Something looks suspicious — isolate first, always."

Reality

Isolation is the right reflex for destruction, spread, or live C2 — and an expensive overreaction to a low-confidence hunch on a surgeon's workstation or a production server. The pricing discipline from Lesson 10 governs every button: free actions first (fleet query), cheap ones next (collect), disruptive ones when evidence or urgency justifies. One-click power demands more judgment, not less.

Misconception

"Threat confirmed — kill it immediately."

Reality

The kill-first reflex destroys the volatile evidence (memory, live sessions) that answers scope and root cause — and tips the attacker that you've seen them, before you know their full footprint. Absent active damage, the order is collect → scope → then kill, coordinated. Lesson 10's iron rule survives the convenience of the button.

Misconception

"EDR sees everything that happens."

Reality

EDR sees managed endpoints with healthy agents — nothing else. Unmanaged and BYOD machines, network appliances, OT, printers: dark. Tampered or crashed agents: dark (which is why an agent going silent is itself an alert). And whole categories of modern attack — SaaS sessions, cloud control planes, stolen tokens used from attacker infrastructure — never touch your endpoints at all. Know the map's edges.

Misconception

"EDR alerts are verdicts — the platform already decided."

Reality

EDR detections false-positive like all detections: admin scripts trip persistence rules, deployment tools look like lateral movement, and the confidence score is an input, not an answer. The pre-assembled evidence makes your triage faster — it doesn't make it optional. Lesson 9's discipline applies in full; it just starts three steps ahead.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • The evolution: AV blocks known-bad files, NGAV blocks bad-looking behavior, EDR records everything so anything can be detected, investigated, and responded to — prevention plus a flight recorder plus remote hands.
  • The telemetry: processes (with command lines and lineage), files, registry, network, scripts and memory — captured continuously, alert or no alert, feeding detections, investigations, hunts, and the SIEM.
  • Working an alert: read the tree → walk the timeline → fleet-query the artifacts → then respond. The evidence arrives pre-assembled; the verdict is still yours.
  • Response pricing: fleet query is free, collect is cheap, isolate and kill are priced — default order absent urgency; active destruction, spread, or live hands inverts it to isolate-first.
  • Isolation preserves the EDR channel — the host is cut off from everything except your investigation, which is exactly the point.
  • The blind spots are structural: unmanaged hosts, dead or tampered agents (a silence that is itself an alert), and everything off-endpoint — SaaS, cloud, identity. EDR depth needs SIEM breadth.
  • Climb the ladder: use your own telemetry to prove hardening is safe, and graduate detections into prevention — the best alert is the one policy makes impossible.

Module 14 · Lesson 16

Network Traffic Analysis:
Reading the Wire

A compromised endpoint can lie — rootkits hide, logs get wiped, agents get killed. But to matter, an attack must eventually cross the wire, and the wire keeps its own records. This lesson teaches you to read them: beacon rhythms, DNS as a covert channel, and how exfiltration betrays itself by shape when encryption hides everything else.

LEVELBeginner-plus DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–15 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • The network is ground truth: a compromised host can lie in its own logs, but not on the wire.
  • Encryption hides content, not shape — beacons show up as small, regular exchanges with one destination.
  • Flow, DNS, proxy and TLS metadata together expose command-and-control, tunneling and exfiltration.
Hands-on:Lab 3 · DNS & beacons
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Treat the wire as ground truth

Explain why network evidence survives endpoint compromise — and where it fits beside EDR depth and SIEM breadth.

Choose the right data source

Know what flow data, DNS logs, proxy logs, packet capture, and IDS/NDR each capture — and what each misses.

Spot C2 by rhythm

Recognize beaconing — interval, jitter, size consistency, destination fidelity — against the noise of human browsing.

Read DNS as an attack surface

Catch tunneling, DGA patterns, and first-seen domains in the protocol everyone forgets to watch.

Detect exfiltration by shape

Use volume, direction, timing, and destination rarity to convict data theft through unbroken encryption.

Cover the endpoint gaps

Aim network monitoring at exactly what EDR can't see: unmanaged hosts, appliances, IoT, and tampered agents.

02
Orientation

Why the wire never lies

Every other evidence source in this course lives on something an attacker can own. A rootkitted host lies to its own logs. A killed EDR agent records nothing (Lesson 15's tamper warning). Cleared event logs take their history with them. But network traffic is observed from vantage points the compromised host doesn't control — taps, span ports, firewalls, resolvers — and an attacker who wants to control anything, steal anything, or spread anywhere must send packets. They can encrypt what the packets say; they cannot make the packets not exist. That asymmetry is the entire discipline.

The modern twist is that encryption won — the overwhelming majority of traffic is TLS, and payload inspection is mostly a memory. But surrender was never required, because what encryption can't hide is shape: who talked to whom, when, how often, how much, in which direction. A beacon's metronome rhythm, an exfiltration's upload asymmetry, a tunnel's absurd DNS volume — all fully visible in metadata. Network analysis didn't die with plaintext; it became a discipline of traffic behavior, which — pyramid of pain — is exactly where you want to fight anyway.

Analogy — the postal ledger

Imagine you can't open anyone's mail — every envelope is sealed. You'd still catch the smuggler with the post office's ledger alone: who sends to whom, how often, how heavy, at what hours. A resident mailing one identical small envelope to the same foreign address every hour, all night? A house that suddenly ships forty kilograms to an address nobody in town has ever used? You don't need the contents — the pattern is the confession. Flow data is that ledger, and this lesson is learning to read it.

Where this sits. Lesson 2's networking and Lesson 3's protocols are the grammar; this lesson is reading comprehension. It completes the sensor triad — EDR depth (15), SIEM breadth (5–6), and now wire truth — and its scenario pays off two old debts at once: Lesson 7's silent hosts and Lesson 15's forty unmanaged machines, one of which is about to matter.

In plain words

Network analysis reads traffic metadata — who talked to whom, when, how much. Even when content is encrypted, the shape of traffic gives attacks away: a first-ever connection to a strange destination, or a big outbound flow (exfiltration — data being stolen). Watching machine-to-machine (east-west) traffic catches attackers moving sideways inside the network, which many teams forget to monitor.

03
Core concepts

Vantage points, data types, and the two directions

Network visibility comes in layers of decreasing volume and increasing detail. Flow data (NetFlow/IPFIX-style) is the postal ledger: per-connection records — source, destination, ports, byte counts, timing — tiny to store, retainable for months, and sufficient for most behavioral questions. DNS logs record every name lookup: cheap, universal, and disproportionately valuable, because almost every attack phase asks DNS a question first. Proxy logs add URL-level detail and user attribution for web traffic. TLS metadata — certificate details, SNI (the requested hostname), handshake fingerprints — lets you characterize encrypted sessions without decrypting them. Full packet capture is everything, byte for byte: forensically priceless, economically brutal, and therefore deployed selectively. And IDS/NDR platforms sit across these layers, applying signatures and behavioral analytics — Lesson 8's detection engineering, running on wire data.

Two directions organize everything. North–south — traffic crossing your perimeter — is where C2, exfiltration, and initial delivery live, and where monitoring traditionally concentrated. East–west — host to host, inside — is where lateral movement, staging, and worm spread live, and where visibility is historically thinnest: exactly why attackers love the interior. A mature program watches both, and the scenario ahead turns on an east–west observation most estates would have missed.

The baseline is the instrument. None of these sources yields verdicts alone — a 2 GB transfer is exfiltration or a backup depending entirely on what's normal for that host, that hour, that destination. Every technique in this lesson is Lesson 12's baselining applied to traffic: normal is boring, deviation is interesting, and context converts deviation into verdict. Network analysis without baselines is just staring at numbers.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five wire sources

Select a source, then work the tabs — "analyst moves" is what you actually query, and "what it misses" is the blind spot that sends you to the next source over.

05
Core concepts

C2 on the wire: the rhythm gives it away

Lesson 14 taught the beacon from the malware's side; here's what it looks like from the wire's. Human network activity is bursty and chaotic: a page load explodes into dozens of connections, then silence, then another burst — irregular sizes, irregular gaps, dozens of destinations. Machine C2 is the opposite: patient and regular — the same destination, on a timer, exchanging small and consistent payloads, running through lunch breaks and midnight because nobody's at the keyboard. Attackers add jitter (randomized delay, ±10–20%) precisely to blur the metronome, so detection looks for statistical regularity — tight distributions of interval and size — rather than perfect clockwork.

FLOW EXCERPT — FIN-WS-233 · 09:01–09:05 (the four minutes from Lesson 15) 09:01:12 ws-233 → 198.51.100.34:443 out 312B in 168B ← small, consistent 09:02:13 ws-233 → 198.51.100.34:443 out 309B in 168B ← +61s 09:03:11 ws-233 → 198.51.100.34:443 out 315B in 168B ← +58s: jittered metronome 09:04:14 ws-233 → 198.51.100.34:443 out 311B in 168B ← same dst · same shape · no human is this boring — versus the same host, one browsing minute — 09:00:02 ws-233 → 23 destinations out 4-380KB bursts, irregular gaps ← human chaos

DNS runs a parallel racket. Because almost everything is allowed to ask DNS questions, it makes a superb covert channel: tunneling encodes data into query labels and responses — betrayed on the wire by absurd volume to one domain, long high-entropy subdomain labels, and unusual record types (TXT everywhere) — and DGA (domain generation algorithms) lets malware compute thousands of candidate rendezvous domains, betrayed by streams of random-looking lookups that mostly fail to resolve. Two cheap, high-yield DNS habits: domain age (first-seen-recently is Lesson 13's registration signal, automated) and NXDOMAIN rates (legitimate software rarely guesses names; DGAs do little else).

The four choke points, revisited. Lesson 12 named the grounds where attackers must walk: auth, persistence, process creation, beaconing. The first three live in endpoint telemetry; this is the fourth — and it's the one that still works when the endpoint has no agent to betray it.

06
Core concepts

Exfiltration: convicted by shape alone

Data theft through encrypted channels is invisible to content inspection and glaring in metadata, because stealing data changes traffic shape in ways attackers struggle to hide. The tells, in rough order of power: direction asymmetry — workstations and most servers are download-heavy by nature; a host suddenly uploading gigabytes has inverted its personality. Volume against baseline — not "3 GB is a lot" but "3 GB is 40× this host's nightly norm." Destination rarity — first-seen domains, personal cloud storage, residential IPs: places this estate has never sent data before. Timing — 02:00 transfers from a host whose user sleeps. Protocol misuse — megabytes moving through DNS, or uploads over a port that should carry heartbeats. And the strongest pattern of all is the pair: an east–west staging pull followed by a matching north–south push.

FLOW SUMMARY — LAB-SRV-09 · overnight (the scenario ahead, previewed) 01:10-01:38 FILES-02 → LAB-SRV-09 1.9 GB SMB ← east-west: the staging pull 01:52-02:41 LAB-SRV-09 → cdn-sync[.]example 1.8 GB TLS ← north-south: the matching push context dst first seen by estate: EVER · host baseline upload: ~40 MB/day payload: encrypted, unreadable — verdict needs none of it pull ≈ push · rare destination · 45× baseline · 2 a.m. — the shape IS the evidence

Note what convicted that transfer: five metadata facts, zero decrypted bytes. This is also where Lesson 11's feed hygiene echoes — rarity is a signal, not a verdict: first-seen destinations and volume spikes are leads that context confirms or clears (the drill ahead includes a 3 GB transfer that's a backup, because real estates are full of them). And operationally, exfil findings carry unique weight: the quantified answer to "what left, and how much" feeds Lesson 10's legal and notification obligations — one more reason flow retention, cheap as it is, earns its keep for months.

East–west is where exfil is born. The staging pull — data massing on the host that will ship it — happens inside, before any perimeter sensor gets a vote. Estates that only watch north–south see the push with no context; estates that watch both see the pair, and the pair is the conviction. Interior visibility isn't a luxury tier; it's half the pattern.

08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

LAB-SRV-09: the wire never lies

Lesson 15 counted forty hosts without EDR agents and called them dark. One of them wasn't dark to everything — the flow sensors could still see it. This is the investigation that runs entirely on wire evidence: no agent, no process tree, no endpoint logs. Twelve steps.

Network replay — "conviction by metadata"

07:40 · The deviationA quiet server stops being boringThe NDR's baseline model flags LAB-SRV-09 — a lab server that averages 40 MB of outbound traffic a day — for periodic outbound connections to a destination the estate has never contacted. Score 87. No endpoint alert accompanies it, because no agent lives there to raise one.
Validate the rhythmThe metronome testInterval histogram over six hours: outbound connections clustering tightly around 300 seconds, ±8% jitter, payloads 280–340 bytes each way, one destination. Human traffic is chaos; this is a heartbeat. The analyst has seen this shape before — in Lesson 15's flow excerpt, wearing a different address.
DNS contextThe domain is twelve days oldPassive DNS: the destination hostname first resolved twelve days ago, registered nine days before that — Lesson 13's registration-age signal, automated into enrichment. Estate-wide DNS logs show exactly one host has ever asked for it. Rarity isn't a verdict, but rarity plus rhythm is getting hard to explain.
The coverage realizationThis host is dark everywhere elseNo EDR agent — it's on Lesson 15's list of forty. Server segment traffic doesn't traverse the proxy. Local logs, if any survive, can't be trusted from a suspect machine. Every investigative tool from the last three lessons is unavailable. What remains is the wire — and the wire has been recording all along.
East-west pivotThe staging pullFlow history for LAB-SRV-09, interior first: two nights ago, 01:10–01:38, it pulled 1.9 GB from FILES-02 over SMB — a file server it contacts for kilobytes, normally. The data massed here before it moved. East-west visibility just earned its budget line.
North-southThe matching pushFourteen minutes after the pull completed: 1.8 GB outbound over TLS to the twelve-day-old domain, 01:52–02:41. Pull ≈ push, rare destination, 45× the host's baseline, deep in the sleeping hours. The payload is encrypted and unreadable — and unnecessary.
VerdictExfiltration, convicted by shape aloneFive metadata facts — rhythm, rarity, the pair, the volume ratio, the hour — and zero decrypted bytes. This is the lesson's thesis made operational: the endpoint had no agent to lie or confess, and it didn't matter. Traffic must cross the wire, and the wire keeps its own records.
08:20 · Declare and containIncident, IC, and a firewall ruleDestination blocked at the perimeter, LAB-SRV-09 cut from the network at the switch — no EDR isolation button exists for it, so containment happens the old way, at the infrastructure. The beacon dies mid-interval. Lesson 10's machinery spins up around a case built entirely from flow records.
Scope what leftWhich 1.9 gigabytes?FILES-02 has an agent and audit logging: the SMB session maps to a service account reading the engineering archive share. Now the exfil has a name, a scope, and an owner — the quantified answer legal and notification decisions require. Flow found the theft; the covered neighbor identified the goods.
Entry pointHow they got in — also on the wireFlow history backward: three weeks of inbound connections to a management service LAB-SRV-09 exposed to a partner network segment — a service two patch cycles behind, because unmanaged hosts miss those too. First contact, first foothold, first beacon: all reconstructed from connection records.
OutputsFour fixes, one lessonAn NDR detection for the staging-pull-then-push pair. Proxy enforcement extended to the server segment. The EDR deployment ticket for the lab fleet, suddenly unblocked by executive attention. And the exfil volume documented for counsel. Every output existed because flow retention reached back far enough — cheap data, kept long, wins again.
ReflectionThe triad, completeEDR gives depth where agents live; the SIEM gives breadth across sources; the wire gives truth that survives endpoint compromise — and covers the hosts the other two can't reach. LAB-SRV-09 was invisible to two of the three and convicted by the third. That's not redundancy. That's the design.
Ready. Press Play to run the investigation, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: count what this case ran on — flow records and DNS logs, the two cheapest sources in the stack — and what it never had: an agent, a process tree, a readable payload. The expensive question ("what exactly left?") was answered by pivoting to a covered neighbor. Sensor strategy in one sentence: deep where you can, wide where you can't, and always keep the ledger.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Network analysis attracts a specific set of wrong conclusions — most involve giving up too early or trusting a single signal too much:

Misconception

"Everything is encrypted now — network monitoring is dead."

Reality

Encryption hides content, not behavior — and this lesson's entire scenario convicted an exfiltration through unbroken TLS using shape alone: rhythm, volume, direction, rarity, timing. Metadata analysis isn't the consolation prize; it's behavior-level detection, which the pyramid says is the better fight anyway.

Misconception

"We have EDR everywhere — network monitoring is redundant."

Reality

"Everywhere" means everywhere an agent runs — and Lesson 15 counted forty exceptions in one estate, before mentioning printers, cameras, appliances, and OT. The wire covers what agents can't reach and survives what tampers with them (an attacker can kill the agent; they can't kill the switch's view of their packets). LAB-SRV-09 is the argument, settled.

Misconception

"A big transfer means exfiltration."

Reality

Estates are full of legitimate gigabytes: backups, OS updates, media, replication. Volume convicts only against context — baseline for that host, destination reputation and age, hour, direction, and above all the staging pair. The drill's backup case exists because real analysts clear more big transfers than they escalate; the skill is knowing which facts separate them.

Misconception

"DNS is boring plumbing — not worth logging."

Reality

DNS is the cheapest high-yield telemetry in the stack: tunneling betrays itself in label entropy and volume, DGAs in NXDOMAIN storms, new C2 infrastructure in first-seen ages — and nearly every attack phase asks DNS a question before acting. One caveat growing yearly: encrypted DNS (DoH) can bypass your resolvers, so estates increasingly force internal resolution precisely to keep this ledger readable.

Misconception

"Rare destination — alert on it."

Reality

First-seen domains number in the hundreds per day in any living estate — every new SaaS tool, CDN edge, and marketing site qualifies. Rarity is an enrichment signal that raises priority when it co-occurs with rhythm, volume, or odd hours — Lesson 11's feed-hygiene rule in wire form. Alert on the combination, or drown.

Misconception

"Serious shops capture full packets everywhere."

Reality

Full PCAP at estate scale is a storage bill measured in days of retention — while flow data costs a rounding error and keeps for months, which is exactly what let this lesson's scenario reach back three weeks to the entry point. The mature pattern: flow and DNS everywhere and long, PCAP selectively and short — triggered captures at choke points when investigations need bytes.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • The wire is ground truth: compromised hosts can lie to their own logs and kill their own agents, but traffic is observed from vantage points they don't control — and attacks must eventually send packets.
  • Encryption hides content, not shape: who, whom, when, how often, how much, which direction — sufficient for beacons, tunnels, and exfiltration, no decryption required.
  • The source ladder: flow data (the cheap, long-retention ledger), DNS logs (cheapest high-yield telemetry), proxy logs (URL and user detail), TLS metadata, and selective PCAP — with IDS/NDR analytics across them all.
  • C2 betrays itself by rhythm: tight interval and size distributions to one destination, running through the night — statistical regularity that jitter blurs but can't erase. Human traffic is chaos; implants are metronomes.
  • DNS deserves its own watch: tunneling (volume, label entropy, TXT), DGA (NXDOMAIN storms), and domain age as automated enrichment.
  • Exfiltration converts to a verdict through shape against baseline — direction asymmetry, volume ratio, destination rarity, timing — and the strongest pattern is the pair: east-west staging pull, then matching north-south push.
  • Aim the wire at the gaps: unmanaged hosts, appliances, IoT, tampered agents. EDR depth, SIEM breadth, wire truth — the triad is the design, and every estate needs all three.
11

Lesson 17 — Cloud Security Monitoring: When the Perimeter Is an API

LAB-SRV-09 at least had a wire to watch. Your cloud estate doesn't — no switch, no tap, no perimeter in the old sense. Next: control-plane logs, identity as the attack surface, misconfigurations as the new vulnerability class, and how SOC fundamentals translate to infrastructure where the perimeter is an API and identity is the new network.
