Module 18 · Lesson 20

Metrics, Reporting & SOC Maturity:
Proving the Invisible

The playbook that saved four hours at 03:00. The virtual patch that bounced the probes. The forty alerts tuned away before they fired. The SOC's best work is invisible by definition — incidents that never happened — and invisible work gets defunded. This lesson is measurement done honestly: the metrics that mean something, the vanity numbers that lie, and how to report the invisible in the only language the business hears.

LEVELBeginner-plus DURATION50–60 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–19 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • Measure speed, quality, coverage, load and outcomes — and define exactly when every clock starts and stops.
  • Goodhart's law: a target stops measuring. Pair every speed metric with a quality metric.
  • Report your own gaps, keep evidence of prevented incidents, and give leadership narrative, trend and ask.
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Define the core metrics honestly

MTTD, MTTA, MTTR — with clock definitions that survive scrutiny, medians per severity tier, and endpoints that mean "verified," not "ticket closed."

Spot the lies in a dashboard

Recognize vanity metrics, blended averages, cherry-picked windows, and unfalsifiable claims — in others' reporting and your own.

Pair metrics against gaming

Apply Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, pair it with the second measure that exposes the gaming.

Place a SOC on the maturity ladder

Grade a program from ad-hoc to optimizing by its processes and measurement — never by the tools on its shelf.

Evidence the invisible

Turn prevented incidents into defensible claims — blocked probes, closed doors, near-misses with logs attached.

Report upward

Build the executive one-slide — narrative, trend, ask — in business language, and answer "are we secure?" without lying in either direction.

02
Orientation

Why measurement is the SOC's survival skill

Consider what this course's SOC accomplished lately, and who saw it. The Friday advisory: probes bounced off a WAF rule six hours before they arrived — nobody noticed, because nothing happened. The 03:00 phishing wave: contained in nine machine minutes — the on-call slept through the SOC's best night of the quarter. The detection backlog, the tuned false positives, the doors closed by the vulnerability program: all of it invisible, because the product of good security operations is the absence of events. Now put that team in a budget meeting opposite departments that ship features, close deals, and show revenue. The SOC that cannot measure and narrate its value competes for funding armed with anecdotes — and anecdotes lose to spreadsheets every fiscal year.

But measurement cuts both ways, and the second edge is sharper: what gets measured gets managed — including wrongly. Reward alerts-closed-per-shift and analysts close fast instead of right; the queue empties while real intrusions get two-minute glances (Lesson 9's triage quality, sacrificed to a leaderboard). Celebrate a green dashboard and nobody mentions the forty unmanaged hosts making it green by not reporting (Lesson 7's silence, laundered into success). This is Goodhart's law — when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — and it operates in every SOC that measures carelessly. So this lesson teaches two skills as one: measuring what matters, and measuring it in ways that survive being aimed at.

Analogy — the fire department's annual report

A fire department that reports "we sprayed 4 million liters of water this year" has said nothing — that's activity. "Average response time" is better, until you learn they blend downtown's four minutes with the rural district's forty and call it twenty-two. The honest report says: response time by district, trended; fires prevented by inspections, with the violation records to prove it; and the neighborhoods still beyond the four-minute line — the coverage gap, stated plainly, with a costed plan. Note the twist: the inspections that prevented fires are the hardest number to sell and the most valuable work they did. The SOC has exactly this report to write, every quarter.

Where this sits. This lesson is the course measuring itself: Lesson 6's fatigue math becomes load metrics, Lesson 7's silent sources become coverage metrics, Lesson 8's tested detections become quality metrics, Lesson 18's remediation clocks become the flagship outcome metric, and Lesson 10's business-translation skill graduates into executive reporting. The scenario is the meeting every SOC lead eventually faces: proving the invisible, at budget time, to people who count.

In plain words

Metrics only help if they're honest. Time-to-detect/respond (MTTD/MTTR) matter, but the moment a number becomes a target, people game it (Goodhart's law) — rewarding “alerts closed” makes people close fast, not right. The fix is pairing: attach a truth-teller to every target (closure speed plus reopen rate). Big activity numbers that measure nothing are vanity metrics.

03
Core concepts

The metric families, and the clocks inside them

SOC metrics organize into families, each answering a different question. Speed: MTTD (mean/median time to detect — from when the malicious event happened to when the SOC knew), MTTA (time to acknowledge — detection to a human engaging), MTTR (time to respond/remediate — and everything hangs on where that clock stops). Quality: false-positive rate, escalation accuracy, reopen rate, and Lesson 19's auto-closure error rate — the measures of whether fast work was also right. Coverage: log sources onboarded and healthy (Lesson 7), ATT&CK techniques with tested detections (Lesson 8), EDR agent and scan coverage (Lessons 15 and 18) — the measures of what the SOC can even see. Load: alerts per analyst, queue depth, after-hours pages — Lesson 6's fatigue math, quantified before it becomes resignation letters. And outcome: time-to-verified-remediation for exploited-and-exposed findings, incidents prevented with evidence, loop outputs shipped — the family that budget meetings are actually about.

Every speed metric is secretly a pair of clock definitions, and the definitions are where dashboards lie. When does MTTD start — at the attacker's first event, or at the alert (flattering, and wrong)? When does MTTR stop — at containment, at ticket closure (the classic dodge), or at verified remediation, Lesson 18's standard? Blend severities into one average and the thousand routine alerts drown the three incidents that mattered; report means instead of medians and one weekend outlier rewrites the quarter. The honest defaults: medians and percentiles, per severity tier, with clock definitions published next to the number, trended over time — because a trend survives arguments that a snapshot never does.

One sentence to keep: a metric you can't define the clocks for is an anecdote with decimal places. Ask "when does the timer start, when does it stop, and who decided?" of every number on every dashboard — including yours.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five metric families

Select a family, then work the tabs — "how to use it" is the practice, and "how it lies" is the failure mode that turns each family against you.

05
Core concepts

Honest measurement: the same SOC, two dashboards

Here is one quarter of one SOC, reported twice. The first dashboard is what dishonest defaults produce — technically true, engineered to please. The second is the same data with honest clocks, tiers, and pairings. Read them as the board would:

DASHBOARD A — technically true, engineered to please MTTR down 40% (mean · all severities blended · clock stops at ticket closure) alerts 1.4M processed, +22% ← activity dressed as achievement auto-close 98% of alerts resolved by SOAR ← no error sampling attached breaches zero successful compromises ← unfalsifiable where coverage is dark — DASHBOARD B · same SOC, same quarter, honest defaults — speed median MTTD, sev-high: 4 min (was 41) — driver: auto-triage (L19) · clocks published outcome KEV-listed + exposed → verified fixed: median 22h (was 9 days) quality FP rate −18% from tuning · reopen rate flat — speed gains are real, not gamed coverage EDR: 94% of estate · 40 hosts dark — plan and cost attached B is less flattering and infinitely more fundable: honest numbers build the only currency that compounds

Three disciplines separate B from A. Publish the clocks: every speed number carries its start, stop, and tiering — "median, sev-high, event-to-verified" — so the number survives the first hard question. Pair against gaming: every metric that could be aimed at gets a partner that exposes the aiming — closure speed pairs with reopen rate, auto-closure volume pairs with sampled error rate, alert reduction pairs with detection coverage (deleting detections also reduces alerts). State the dark honestly: coverage gaps reported by the SOC, with a costed plan, are a funding argument; the same gaps discovered by an incident are a credibility funeral. Lesson 16's LAB-SRV-09 taught that arithmetic — this section is where it becomes policy.

Goodhart's law is a standing threat, not a trivia fact. Any number attached to performance reviews, bonuses, or leaderboards will be optimized — the measure, not the mission. The defenses: measure teams over individuals where gaming hurts most, pair every target with its truth-teller, rotate scrutiny, and treat a metric improving suspiciously fast as an investigation, not a celebration. The analysts aren't dishonest; the incentive is doing exactly what incentives do.

06
Core concepts

Maturity, and the one slide that funds it

Maturity models grade the program, not the toolshed, on a ladder of roughly four levels. Ad hoc: heroics — response depends on who's on shift, procedures live in heads, nothing is measured (Lesson 19's automation prerequisite, failed). Defined: written runbooks, consistent triage, an incident process that survives personnel changes — Lessons 9 and 10, institutionalized. Measured: the disciplines of this lesson — honest metrics with published clocks, coverage tracked, quality paired against speed. Optimizing: the loop runs on the numbers — Lesson 10's improvement machinery, Lesson 8's detection factory, and Lesson 19's automation, all steered by measurement, each quarter's metrics setting next quarter's engineering. The tell at every level is the same question: can you show me, or only tell me? Tools appear nowhere in that ladder; a SOC with world-class platforms and undocumented processes is an ad-hoc SOC with an expensive shelf.

THE EXECUTIVE ONE-SLIDE — narrative, trend, ask (in the audience's language) NARRATIVE one sentence: "Detection-to-containment for high-severity threats is now minutes, and this quarter that speed provably prevented a data breach." EVIDENCE the file-transfer save: patched + virtual-patched 6h before first exploit probes (WAF logs attached) · finance-exports exposure: $0 vs. disclosure-scale cost TREND 3 numbers, 4 quarters each: sev-high median MTTD ↓ · KEV-exposed fix time ↓ · FP rate ↓ THE DARK stated by us, not found by attackers: 40 unmanaged hosts · 7 of 9 stores unlogged ASK EDR completion + data-plane logging: cost X vs. LAB-SRV-09's incident cost 4X no tool names · no alert counts · nothing the CFO can't repeat to the board unaided

The translation rules, distilled from Lesson 10's IC craft: business language only — risk reduced, obligations met, revenue protected, never EPS-per-second or rule counts; evidence over adjectives — the blocked probes in the WAF log are worth a thousand "robust postures"; trends over snapshots — three quarters of direction beat any single quarter's number; and the ask ties to the dark — the stated gap, its incident-shaped cost (you have LAB-SRV-09's receipts), and the price of closing it. And when the board asks the inevitable question — "so, are we secure?" — the mature answer is never yes: it's posture, coverage, trend, and the honest dark, because the leader who says "yes" owns the next incident personally, and the one who shows the map gets funded to shrink it.

The prevented incident has evidence — collect it as you go. Lesson 18's WAF logs caught the probes that bounced; Lesson 19's audit trail timed the 03:00 save; the intel-fed proxy block gave FIN-WS-233's beacon four useless minutes. Near-misses with logs attached are the SOC's proof of the counterfactual — start a "saves file" now, because at budget time, the difference between "we prevent incidents" and "here are three we provably prevented, with timestamps" is the budget.

07
Hands-on · Simulation

Six metrics from real dashboards. Diagnose each — the questions from section 05: what are the clocks, what's the pairing, does it measure outcome or activity, and would it survive a hard question?

08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

The budget meeting: proving a quarter of invisible work

Quarter-end. The SOC lead has thirty minutes with the executive committee, one ask on the table — completing the EDR rollout and the logging gaps — and a quarter of mostly invisible success to prove. Twelve steps from raw logs to a funded program.

Reporting replay — "the case for the invisible"

Two weeks out · The askStart from the decision, not the dataThe ask is written first: fund EDR completion for the 40 dark hosts and data-plane logging for 7 unlogged stores — cost X. Every number in the deck will exist to support that one decision. Reports that start from "what data do we have" end as tours; reports that start from the ask end as outcomes.
The incident reelA quarter of stories, receipts attachedThe raw material: the file-transfer emergency, the 03:00 phishing wave, LAB-SRV-09's exfil, the AKIA…Q7 takeover — each with timelines, actions, and outcomes already documented, because Lessons 9 and 10 made documentation non-optional. The case file discipline of the whole course is about to pay its dividend.
The counterfactualThe breach that provably didn't happenThe crown jewel: WAF logs showing exploitation probes at 23:10 Friday, bouncing off the virtual patch deployed at 17:30 — six hours of margin, timestamped. Paired with what the appliance moves (finance exports) and what disclosure costs, "we prevent incidents" becomes "here is one we prevented, with logs." The saves file earns its keep.
Speed, honestlyTiered medians, published clocksSev-high median MTTD: 4 minutes, down from 41 — driver named (auto-triage playbooks), clocks published (event-to-detection, not alert-to-detection). KEV-exposed remediation: 22 hours median, down from 9 days. No blended averages anywhere. Every number carries its definition like a passport, ready for inspection.
Quality, pairedThe truth-tellers ride alongSpeed claims arrive pre-paired: reopen rate flat (the fast closures are real closures), auto-closure error sampling at 0.4% (the SOAR isn't silently eating true positives), FP rate down 18% from tuning (the queue shrank because detections improved, not because detections were deleted). Every gaming vector, answered before it's asked.
The dark, statedForty hosts, seven stores, one mapThe coverage slide the SOC writes about itself: 94% EDR coverage — and the 6% named, with LAB-SRV-09 as exhibit A of what dark costs. Data-plane logging on 2 of 9 stores — and AKIA…Q7's scope answer as exhibit B of what the ticked checkbox bought. The gaps aren't confessed; they're presented, priced, and owned.
TranslationEvery number becomes business languageThe exfil becomes "engineering IP exposure, legal review costs, and the notification analysis it triggered." The Saturday patch window becomes "Monday settlement files, protected." The four-minute MTTD becomes "threats contained before spread, most quarters of the year." Not one EPS count, rule total, or tool name survives the translation pass.
The one slideNarrative, trend, askEverything compresses to one slide: the sentence ("this quarter, speed provably prevented a breach"), the evidence (the WAF save), three trend lines across four quarters, the dark with its map, and the ask with its arithmetic — gap cost X, LAB-SRV-09's incident cost 4X. The thirty-page appendix exists; nobody will need it. The slide can be repeated by a CFO, unaided, to a board.
The meetingTwelve minutes of numbers, eighteen of questionsThe presentation lands in twelve minutes because every claim was pre-hardened: clocks published, pairings attached, evidence linked. The questions are the good kind — about the plan, not the numbers. A dashboard that survives contact with a skeptical CFO is the product of every honest choice made two sections ago.
The question"What else is dark that you haven't found?"The CFO's closer — and the maturity test. The honest answer: "Here's our discovery process, here's its cadence, and here's what it surfaced last quarter that we didn't know the quarter before. The map grows at the edges; that's why discovery is a standing line item, not a project." No "we're covered." The room notices the difference.
The outcomeFunded — and something betterThe ask is approved in full. But the durable win is the precedent: the SOC that states its own gaps, prices them, and proves its saves has become a team the board extends credit to — next quarter's ask starts from trust, not from zero. Credibility compounds exactly like the improvement loop does: quarter over quarter, or not at all.
ReflectionMetrics are the SOC's own telemetryEverything this course said about logs applies to the SOC measuring itself: honest sources, defined clocks, baselines before verdicts, and no dashboard trusted past its coverage. The team that instruments itself the way it instruments the estate gets better on purpose — and can prove it. That's maturity; the tools were never the point.
Ready. Press Play to run the budget meeting, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: nothing in this meeting was produced for this meeting. The timelines came from case discipline, the save from the WAF's ordinary logs, the trend lines from clocks defined quarters ago, the dark map from coverage tracking that never stopped. Executive reporting isn't a quarterly art project — it's the exhaust of a SOC that measures itself honestly all year. Build the habits; the slide builds itself.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Measurement failures are quiet — the dashboard stays green while the program drifts. The recurring ones:

Misconception

"Big numbers impress: 1.4 million alerts processed."

Reality

Activity is not achievement — 1.4 million alerts processed says nothing except that the SOC was busy, and might mean the detections desperately need tuning (Lesson 6 would read that number as a fatigue emergency). Executives fund outcomes: threats contained, doors closed, breaches prevented with evidence. Every count of things-done should face the question "and what did that change?"

Misconception

"One MTTR number keeps it simple for leadership."

Reality

One blended number keeps it false for leadership: the thousand routine alerts drown the three incidents that mattered, means let outliers rewrite quarters, and "resolved" quietly means "ticket closed" instead of "verified fixed" (the gap where LAB-SRV-09's stale service lived). Simple done honestly is tiered medians with published clocks — still three numbers, still one slide, actually true.

Misconception

"The dashboard is green — the SOC is healthy."

Reality

Green measures what's instrumented; it says nothing about the dark. Forty unmanaged hosts keep a dashboard green by not reporting; a dead log source keeps detections "passing" against silence (Lesson 7's oldest trap). Every dashboard needs its coverage statement attached — "green, across the 94% we can see" — or it's an instrument panel with the fuel gauge painted on.

Misconception

"The team's metrics are fine for the board deck."

Reality

Different audiences, different languages: the team needs queue depths, FP rates, and per-rule performance; the board needs risk reduced, obligations met, and money — protected or asked for. Sending EPS counts upstairs wastes the meeting; sending only vibes downstairs wastes the team. Translation is a deliverable (Lesson 10's IC skill), and it runs in both directions.

Misconception

"A little metric gaming is harmless hustle."

Reality

Goodhart's law compounds: the closure leaderboard produces two-minute triage on real intrusions; the auto-closure celebration hides eaten true positives; the alert-reduction target invites deleting detections. Gaming doesn't just corrupt the number — it corrupts the behavior the number was supposed to protect. Pair every target with its truth-teller, and treat suspiciously fast improvement as an investigation.

Misconception

"We bought the top platforms — we're a mature SOC."

Reality

Maturity is graded on process and measurement, never inventory: written runbooks that survive personnel changes, honest metrics with published clocks, a loop that turns each quarter's numbers into next quarter's engineering. A world-class platform running undocumented heroics is an ad-hoc SOC with an expensive shelf — and the maturity question that exposes it is always the same: can you show me, or only tell me?

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • The SOC's best work is invisible by definition — and invisible work gets defunded. Measurement and narration are survival skills, not paperwork.
  • Five families: speed (MTTD/MTTA/MTTR), quality (FP, reopen, auto-closure error), coverage (sources, detections, agents), load (fatigue math), outcome (the family budget meetings are about).
  • Every speed metric is its clock definitions: when the timer starts, when it stops, who decided. Honest defaults — medians and percentiles, per severity tier, definitions published, trended.
  • Goodhart's law is a standing threat: a measure aimed at becomes a target and stops measuring. Pair every target with its truth-teller — speed with reopen rate, auto-closure with error sampling, alert reduction with coverage.
  • State the dark yourself: coverage gaps reported with a costed plan are a funding argument; the same gaps found by an incident are a credibility funeral.
  • Prevented incidents have evidence — blocked probes, bounced beacons, near-misses with timestamps. Keep a saves file; at budget time it's the difference between claims and proof.
  • Maturity is process and measurement, never inventory: ad hoc → defined → measured → optimizing — and the executive one-slide is narrative, trend, ask, in business language, honest about the dark. "Are we secure?" is never answered "yes."

Assessment · Mini-lab

The dashboard review

Five claims from five different SOC dashboards. Four are vanity, gaming bait, or dishonest framing. Click the one claim that is honest and meaningful — the number you'd put in front of a skeptical CFO.

Thought exercise (no clicking required)

Repair the four rejects: give M-1 an outcome it could support (what would ingest growth plus which paired number tell a real story?), rewrite M-2 with honest clocks and tiers, attach the guard M-4 needs to become trustworthy, and replace M-5 with the falsifiable claim a mature SOC would actually make. Then the design question: draft the three trend lines you'd put on your own one-slide — and for each, name the clock definitions and the truth-teller pairing that make it survive a hard question.

Career Capstone:
The Analyst's Path

Twenty lessons ago, this course opened with a triad and a promise: one continuous campaign, start to finish. You've since watched a password spray become an exfiltration, a leaked key become an identity surgery, a Friday advisory become six hours of margin, and a playbook run the night shift. This finale reassembles the whole saga, maps the careers it prepares you for, and covers the last mile — certifications, portfolios, interviews, and the first ninety days. The knowledge is yours; this lesson is about earning the seat.

LEVELBeginner-plus DURATION55–65 minutes PREREQUISITESLessons 1–20 FORMATInteractive · offline
soc-analyst@foundations:~
The 60-second versionread this first — the lesson unpacks every line
  • Hiring runs on evidence: labs, tested detections and honest writeups an interviewer can inspect.
  • One foundational certification opens doors; a portfolio keeps you in the room.
  • In interviews, reason out loud — clarify, baseline, pivot, verdict — and be honest at the edges of what you know.
Hands-on:Lab 10 · Portfolio writeup
01
Orientation

What you will be able to do

By the end of this capstone, you will be able to:

Tell the whole saga

Walk the campaign end-to-end — spray to exfil to key to patch to playbook to funding — and name the discipline each chapter taught.

Choose a direction

Map the five main career paths out of the SOC seat — analyst, detection engineer, DFIR, hunter, leadership — and what each actually rewards.

Plan certifications honestly

Know which credentials open which doors, in what order, and why evidence of thinking outranks any badge wall.

Build a portfolio that hires

Stand up a home lab, write and test real detections, and publish investigation writeups — the proof interviewers can inspect.

Interview with evidence

Answer scenario questions with structured walkthroughs, handle the unknowns honestly, and evaluate the SOC across the table right back.

Win the first ninety days

Learn the estate, respect the baselines, and ship a first improvement — arriving as a contributor to the loop, not just a seat filler.

02
Orientation

Why knowledge and the seat are two different problems

Here is the uncomfortable arithmetic of entering this field: SOC hiring managers see hundreds of résumés listing the same certifications and the same tool names — and almost none demonstrating the thing the job actually is: structured investigative thinking under uncertainty. You now own twenty lessons of exactly that. You've priced containment against a CFO's laptop, convicted an exfiltration on wire shape alone, refused to trust a green dashboard, and gated a bot's hands at 03:00. The gap between you and the seat is no longer knowledge — it's evidence: artifacts an interviewer can inspect, stories you can walk through under questioning, and the judgment to present both honestly. That's a smaller gap, and it closes with deliberate work this lesson maps.

The second thing to internalize: the SOC seat is a beginning, not a destination. Tier 1 triage is where the field's instincts are forged — the baselines, the pivots, the discipline of writing down what you did — and every senior role in security operations is built on someone who did that apprenticeship well. The paths out of the seat diverge fast (you'll explore five in section 04), but they share one currency: the improvement loop, applied to yourself. The analyst who treats every shift as training data — what did I miss, what would I tune, what will I automate — is promotable in every direction at once. The one who just closes alerts is Goodhart's law with a chair.

Analogy — the flight hours problem

Airlines don't hire pilots for memorizing the aircraft manual; they hire logged hours, checkrides, and how a candidate talks through an engine-out scenario — evidence of judgment under pressure, accumulated deliberately. A student pilot who can't afford jet time builds hours in small aircraft and simulators, logs everything, and walks into the interview with a logbook. Your home lab is the simulator, your writeups are the logbook, and the scenario interview is the checkride. Nobody hands over an aircraft — or an estate — on the strength of a manual read. Build the logbook.

Where this sits. This is the only lesson in the course about you rather than the estate. Section 03 replays the entire saga as one timeline — the review that makes everything portable. Sections 04–06 are the map: paths, credentials, portfolio, interviews. The drill and scenario put you in the interview chair. And the door out of this file leads to a shift schedule.

In plain words

To get hired, prove you can do the work — don't just collect badges. One entry cert (like Security+) opens doors; after that, a portfolio beats certificates. Build a home lab, run investigations, and write them up honestly (mistakes included — they read as credible). The ladder goes Tier 1 → 2 → 3, with paths into detection, hunting, and DFIR. The labs in this course are your starting portfolio.

03
Core concepts

The saga, reassembled: one campaign, twenty disciplines

Everything this course taught, it taught inside one continuous story. Read it now as a single timeline — because this reassembly is the most valuable interview asset you own: a complete incident lifecycle you can narrate from first log line to funded program, naming the discipline at every turn.

THE CAMPAIGN — as the case files tell it the spray 203.0.113.77 walks the login endpoints · caught by a tested detection (L5–8) R-2041 → triaged, not trusted: baselines first, verdicts second (L9) the case CASE 2041-118 → INC-0042: evidence, timeline, chain of custody (L10) the loop IOCs shipped to intel · ISAC enriched · detections tuned (L11) the hunt HUNT-007 assumes the miss → finds HR-WS-117 · INC-0043 · ships R-2077 (L12) the wave salary_bands_2026.xlsm lands · FIN-WS-233 isolated 09:05 (L13) sandbox job 8841: dropper → RAT · C2 198.51.100.34:443 / 60s (L14) the beacon EDR closes it: 4-minute beacon, C2 pre-blocked by the intel feed (L15) 40 unmanaged hosts noted — a debt with a due date the wire LAB-SRV-09: 1.9GB to a first-seen dst · convicted on wire shape alone (L16) entry: exposed mgmt service, two patch cycles stale — the debt collects the key AKIA…Q7, public for 6 days · 214 GetObject · identity surgery, not re-image (L17) the patch CVE-2026-31337, KEV day one · virtual patch 17:30 · probes bounce 23:10 (L18) the bot phish-triage-v4 runs the 03:00 wave: 41→1 case · 9 min · the gate holds (L19) the meeting honest clocks + the WAF save + the dark, priced → EDR completion funded (L20) one attacker infrastructure, one estate, one team getting better on purpose — that's the job

Now notice the shape of the whole. The campaign was never a straight line — it was a loop closing on itself: the spray's IOCs armed the intel feed that later strangled the RAT's C2; the hunt that assumed the miss found the host triage never saw; the forty dark hosts noted in one lesson became the exfil's entry point two lessons later, and the budget that fixes them was won by honestly reporting exactly that failure. Every discipline fed every other. That interconnection — telemetry feeding detection feeding triage feeding response feeding intel feeding hunting feeding back into telemetry — is the actual subject of this course, and the thing that separates security operations from a pile of tools. You didn't learn twenty topics; you learned one system, twenty ways in.

Make it yours before the interview: practice narrating this timeline aloud in under three minutes, then in ninety seconds. Every scenario question you'll ever face — "walk me through a phishing response," "how would you catch exfiltration," "what makes a detection trustworthy" — is a doorway into some chapter of a story you already know cold. Candidates with a rehearsed, honest, end-to-end narrative are unforgettable, because they are rare.

04
Core concepts · Interactive

Explore the five paths out of the seat

Select a path, then work the tabs — "how to get there" is the route from where you sit now, and "the trap" is the failure mode that stalls people on that road.

05
Core concepts

Credentials, honestly: what opens doors and what keeps you in rooms

The truth about certifications, from the hiring side of the table: they are HR filters and vocabulary proofs — necessary at the entry, insufficient everywhere after. A foundational credential (CompTIA Security+ is the near-universal baseline; a blue-team-specific one like CySA+ or Blue Team Level 1 signals direction) gets your résumé past the first screen and proves you share the field's vocabulary. What it cannot prove is the thing interviews exist to find: whether you can think through an incident. So the honest sequencing is: one foundational cert to open the door, then every subsequent hour into the portfolio and the craft — with deeper credentials (the SANS/GIAC track like GCIH for incident handling, or hands-on blue-team certs with practical exams) earned later, ideally employer-funded, when a specialization justifies them. A wall of entry-level badges signals test-taking budget; one badge plus twelve tested detections signals a hire.

THE SKILLS-TO-EVIDENCE MAP — what you know → how you prove it triage baselines, pivots, verdicts (L6, L9) → writeup: one alert investigated end-to-end telemetry log sources, silence, coverage (L5, L7) → home lab: endpoint telemetry into a free SIEM detection rules, testing, tuning (L8) → 12 Sigma rules, tested vs replayed attacks response containment pricing, IR flow (L10, L15) → tabletop narrative: the ransomware 02:00 call hunting hypothesis → evidence (L12, L16) → writeup: a hunt in your own lab's data cloud identity, control plane (L17) → lab: audit-log detection for a leaked-key play judgment gates, metrics, honesty (L19, L20) → the way you talk — this one can't be faked every row is a weekend project · the whole table is a hiring case no badge wall can match

Two notes on the wider credential landscape. First, degrees: helpful, decreasingly mandatory — this field promotes demonstrated capability faster than most, and a strong portfolio routinely beats a generic degree at the SOC entry level. Second, vendor certifications (the certification tracks from firewall, EDR, and SIEM vendors): genuinely valuable once you know which stack you'll operate, because SOCs hire for their tooling — but learn the concepts first. This course deliberately taught concepts over consoles, because the analyst who understands why beaconing looks like beaconing can learn any vendor's screen in a week; the reverse is not true.

The cert trap has a Goodhart shape. When "get certified" becomes the target, people optimize exam technique instead of capability — braindumps, cram-and-forget, badge collections — and the measure stops measuring. Interviewers know this, which is why scenario questions exist: they're the paired metric that exposes the gaming. Study for the knowledge; let the cert fall out as a side effect, exactly like the honest dashboards of Lesson 20.

06
Core concepts

The portfolio, the interview, and the questions you ask back

The portfolio is three artifacts, all buildable on a free hypervisor and open-source tools. The home lab: one Windows VM generating endpoint telemetry (Sysmon is the standard instrument), one collector VM running a free SIEM stack — then attack yourself with well-documented techniques and watch what the logs show. Tested detections: write rules (Sigma is the portable, vendor-neutral format) for what you just did, run them against your captured data, document the false positives you had to tune out — that last part is what separates you from everyone who copied rules off the internet. Investigation writeups: two or three, each walking one scenario from first signal to verdict with your reasoning visible — screenshots, dead ends included, honest about what you'd do differently. Publish them anywhere inspectable. This is the logbook; interviewers read maybe one page, and that page does more than every bullet on the résumé.

THE SCENARIO ANSWER SKELETON — "walk me through a suspicious login alert" clarify "What tier of asset, and do we have identity logs?" ← scoping before acting (L9, L15) baseline "First: is this normal for THIS user — hours, geo, device history?" pivot "Then the entity timeline: what did the account do AFTER auth — new inbox rules, MFA changes, token grants?" ← the pivots, named (L9, L17) price "Cheap reversible steps first — force re-auth — while evidence builds; account disable is staged, not fired, on one weak signal" ← L15's pricing, L19's gate verdict "Escalate with a timeline attached, or close WITH the reasoning documented" honesty "And if the logs can't answer it — I say so, and log the coverage gap" ← L7, L20 structure beats speed · reasoning beats tool names · honesty beats bluffing · every time

Handling the two hard moments: when you don't know the tool they use, say so in one sentence and bridge to the concept — "I haven't operated that EDR, but an isolation-and-timeline workflow is an isolation-and-timeline workflow; here's how I'd run it" — because bluffing fails in thirty seconds and honesty-plus-concepts is exactly what mature teams hire. And when the interview ends, ask your questions — they evaluate the SOC right back, using Lesson 20's instruments: "What's your log coverage like, and who owns the gaps?" "Do analysts have authority to tune detections, or does that go elsewhere?" "What's gated versus auto in your response playbooks?" "What does the on-call load actually look like?" A team that answers those honestly is a team worth joining; a team that bristles just told you about its dashboards.

The first ninety days, in one line per month. Month one: learn the estate and the baselines — ask questions, close alerts carefully, document like Lesson 9 is watching. Month two: find your corner of the noise — the recurring FP, the manual toil — and understand it deeply. Month three: ship the improvement — a tuning proposal with data, a runbook draft, an enrichment automation — because the fastest way to stop being the new analyst is to feed the loop everyone else lives in. Arrive as a contributor; the seat becomes yours.

07
Hands-on · Simulation

You're in the chair: what is each question really testing?

Six real interview questions. Before answering any question well, diagnose it — every scenario question is a doorway into one competency. Identify which.

Interview-decoder drill

Question 1 / 6 · Score 0
08
Hands-on · Real-world scenario

The interview: sixty minutes to earn the seat

A Tier 1 SOC analyst interview, replayed. Watch how every answer draws on a chapter of the saga — and how the candidate evaluates the team right back. Twelve steps to an offer.

Interview replay — "evidence of thinking"

The night before · PrepThe evidence file, assembledThe candidate preps like an analyst works a case: three writeups printed, the lab detection repo link tested, the saga narrative rehearsed to ninety seconds, and — Lesson 20 thinking — three questions prepared that will measure the SOC across the table. Interviews are incidents: the prepared responder wins.
Minute 0 · The opener"Tell me about yourself" — answered as a narrative arcNot a résumé recital — a story with direction: "I trained by working one continuous campaign end-to-end — a password spray that became an exfiltration, a cloud key leak, an emergency patch — and I built a lab to practice every phase. I can walk you through any of it." The interviewer sits up. Nobody says that.
Minute 8 · Scenario one"A suspicious PowerShell alert fires. Your first fifteen minutes?"The skeleton runs: clarify the asset, baseline the user and host — is encoded PowerShell normal for this admin? — then the entity timeline: parent process, what spawned it, network connections after. Cheap reversible steps while evidence builds. The interviewer notes the structure; most candidates lead with a tool name.
Minute 18 · The pricing question"When do you isolate versus watch?"Straight from Lesson 15: "Containment has a price — isolation costs the business the asset, watching costs risk of spread. Ransomware behavior: isolate immediately, seconds matter. One weak signal on an executive's laptop: cheap reversible steps and a human decision, because a wrong disruption spends the SOC's credibility." The interviewer writes something down.
Minute 26 · The depth probe"Tell me about an investigation that impressed you"The candidate tells LAB-SRV-09: an exfiltration convicted purely on wire shape — volume baselines, first-seen destination, the transfer's rhythm — with zero payload visibility, then the pivot to root cause: a management service two patch cycles stale. "What impressed me is that the evidence was traffic metadata alone. Encryption hides content, not behavior." Depth, demonstrated.
Minute 34 · The engineering probe"How do you know a detection actually works?"Lesson 8, verbatim conviction: "Because it's been tested against replayed attack data, not because it compiled. And because its log sources are monitored for silence — a detection over a dead source passes forever. In my lab I broke my own rules twice that way; now I test the pipeline, not just the logic." Lab receipts, offered unprompted.
Minute 41 · The cloud question"An access key leaks in a public repo. First three moves?"Lesson 17's surgery, compressed: "Control-plane logs first — what did the key DO: reads, and any persistence like new keys or grants. Rotate and revoke, then hunt everything the key created. Re-imaging a server doesn't help; the perimeter is the credential itself." The interviewer, who has lived this incident, nods slowly.
Minute 47 · The curveball"We use a SOAR platform you've never touched. Problem?"One honest sentence, then the bridge: "I haven't operated it — but I know what I'd look for: where the human gates sit, what the circuit breakers cap, and how auto-closures get sampled for errors. The console I can learn in a week; the judgment about what machines should never do alone, I'm bringing with me." Honesty plus concepts. No bluff.
Minute 52 · The reversalThe candidate's questions measure the SOC"What's your log coverage, and who owns the gaps? Do analysts get authority to tune detections? What's gated versus fully automated in response?" The panel exchanges a look — these are the questions their own maturity review asked. Teams worth joining light up at them; the candidate is watching for exactly that.
The debriefWhat the panel says when the door closes"Third candidate today with the same cert. First one who walked in with tested detections and asked about our coverage gaps." The differentiator was never the badge — it was inspectable evidence and structured thinking under questioning. The offer goes out Thursday.
Day 1–90 · The seatArrive as a contributor to the loopMonth one: the estate and its baselines, alerts closed carefully, everything documented. Month two: adopt a corner of the noise — the recurring FP everyone sighs at. Month three: the tuning proposal, with data, in the format Lesson 8 taught. The new analyst stops being new the day their first improvement ships.
ReflectionThe seat is earned by evidence of thinkingTwenty-one lessons, one campaign, one method: baselines before verdicts, evidence before conclusions, price before action, honesty before polish. The interview rewarded the same discipline the SOC floor does — because it was never a separate skill. You've been practicing for the seat since Lesson 1. Go take it.
Ready. Press Play to run the interview, or Step to advance manually.

Key insight: nothing in this interview was improvised. The narrative was rehearsed, the writeups pre-existed, the questions-to-ask were drafted the night before, and every scenario answer was a chapter of a story practiced end-to-end. Interviews reward preparation shaped like the job: evidence gathered in advance, structure under pressure, honesty at the edges of knowledge. That's triage. You already know how.

09
Consolidate

Misconceptions to unlearn early

Career mistakes compound quietly, like unmonitored automation. The recurring ones:

Misconception

"Collect enough certifications and the job follows."

Reality

One foundational cert opens the door; after that, badges hit diminishing returns fast while portfolios compound. The hiring question is never "how many certs" — it's "show me how you think." A lab, tested detections, and honest writeups answer it; a badge wall doesn't. Study for knowledge and let credentials fall out as side effects — the Goodhart lesson, applied to yourself.

Misconception

"Tier 1 is beneath me — I'll skip straight to threat hunting."

Reality

Hunting is triage instincts pointed at the unalerted — there is nothing to point without the apprenticeship. Tier 1 is where you internalize baselines, learn what normal looks like at volume, and build the pattern library every senior role runs on. The path out of the seat runs through doing the seat well; the analysts who resent the queue learn the least from it.

Misconception

"Memorize the tools — that's what they screen for."

Reality

Tools churn; concepts transfer. The analyst who understands why beaconing has a rhythm, why identity is the cloud perimeter, why detections need tests, can operate any vendor's console within weeks — and says so honestly in interviews. The reverse — console fluency without concepts — collapses at the first scenario question. This course taught concepts on purpose.

Misconception

"Security rewards lone heroes."

Reality

Every chapter of the saga was a team sport: triage escalated with timelines attached, IR ran on roles and communication rhythms, the hunt briefed detection engineering, the budget case was built on everyone's documentation. The analyst who documents clearly, hands off cleanly, and asks for help early is worth two brilliant hoarders. Interviews probe for this; so does every on-call rotation.

Misconception

"Once hired, the studying is over."

Reality

The field's half-life is short: techniques evolve, estates migrate, yesterday's playbook rots like unmaintained automation. The working analyst's edge is the improvement loop turned inward — what did I miss this week, what will I learn from it, what do I ship next. Careers in this field compound exactly like SOC credibility does: quarter over quarter, or not at all.

Misconception

"Everyone else knows more — I'm a fraud waiting to be found."

Reality

Every honest professional's knowledge map has dark regions — the mature ones state theirs plainly and attach a plan, exactly like Lesson 20's coverage slide. "I don't know, here's how I'd find out" is a senior answer, not a confession. The imposters are the ones claiming green dashboards; you were trained to distrust those. Report your dark honestly, keep shipping, and the map shrinks.

10
Consolidate

What to remember

  • The gap between you and the seat is evidence, not knowledge: artifacts an interviewer can inspect, stories you can walk under questioning, honesty at the edges.
  • The saga is your master asset: one campaign, narratable end-to-end — spray → case → loop → hunt → wave → beacon → wire → key → patch → bot → meeting — every scenario question is a doorway into a chapter you know cold.
  • Five paths out of the seat — analyst mastery, detection engineering, DFIR, hunting/intel, leadership — all built on the same Tier 1 apprenticeship, all rewarding the improvement loop turned inward.
  • Certifications honestly: one foundational badge opens the door; portfolios keep you in rooms. Deep certs come later, funded, when specialization justifies them. Concepts over consoles, always.
  • The portfolio is three weekend-buildable artifacts: a telemetry-generating home lab, detections tested against your own attacks, and honest investigation writeups — the logbook no badge wall can match.
  • Interview with the skeleton — clarify, baseline, pivot, price, verdict, honesty — bridge unknown tools with concepts, and ask the questions that measure the SOC right back.
  • First ninety days: learn the estate, adopt a corner of the noise, ship one improvement. You stop being the new analyst the day you feed the loop. Then keep feeding it — that's the whole career.

Hands-On Lab Track:
From Reading to Doing

The lessons build your mind; these labs build your hands. Eleven free, safe exercises: one runs right here in your browser, the rest on a single throwaway virtual machine. Together they take you from your first log line to a tested detection, a working SIEM, an attack simulation, and a portfolio an interviewer can open.

COST$0 · free tools onlySAFETYSandboxed VM · snapshotsTIME20–60 min eachPAYOFFA portfolio that hires

How to use this track. Do Lab 0 first — it builds the sandbox the VM labs need. Lab 5 needs nothing at all: it is a SIEM sandbox inside this page, so you can start querying today. Then do each lab when you reach the lesson it names. Commands were checked against current tool documentation (November 2026); tools change, so if a step differs, the tool's own docs win.

Hands-on · pairs with Lesson 1 · ~45 min

Build your free practice lab

Before you can defend anything, you need a safe place to break things. This lab stands up a throwaway Windows machine on your own computer — free, isolated, and resettable in one click. Every VM lab below runs inside it.

1

Install a free hypervisor

A hypervisor runs a whole computer inside a window on your computer. Pick one (all free for personal use):

  • VirtualBox 7+ (Windows, Intel Mac, Linux) — supports the virtual TPM Windows 11 needs.
  • VMware Workstation Pro / Fusion Pro — free for personal use since 2024.
  • UTM (Apple-Silicon Macs) — use an ARM build of Windows or the Ubuntu option below.

Download from the vendor's official site and install with defaults.

2

Get a free Windows 11 evaluation ISO

Microsoft's Evaluation Center offers a 90-day Windows 11 Enterprise evaluation as an ISO: search for “Windows 11 Enterprise evaluation” on microsoft.com, register, and download the ISO for your language. Create a new VM from it with at least 2 vCPUs, 4 GB RAM (8 GB if you'll do Lab 6), and 64 GB disk, and enable TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot in the VM settings.

Older guides point to Microsoft's ready-made “Windows 11 development environment” VMs. Those downloads were pulled in October 2024 — use the evaluation ISO instead.

During setup, create a local account with a password (Lab 1 needs one): when asked how you'd like to set up the device, choose Set up for work or school, then Sign-in options → Domain join instead — you won't actually join a domain. When the evaluation expires, simply rebuild from the ISO — that's what snapshots and notes are for.

No Windows option for your hardware? A free Ubuntu Desktop VM works for the concepts in most labs — only the log names differ (/var/log/auth.log, journalctl, auditd).

3

Snapshot it — your undo button

Once the VM boots to the desktop, install guest additions/tools if offered, then take a snapshot (VirtualBox: Machine → Take Snapshot; name it clean). After any lab — especially Lab 7 — you restore it and you're instantly back to clean.

Golden rule of every lab here: run tests and untrusted things only inside the VM, never on your real computer, and restore clean when you finish. Never point attack tools at systems you don't own.

You did it if…
  • A Windows 11 (or Ubuntu) VM boots inside a window on your computer.
  • Your local account has a password you know.
  • You can restore a snapshot called clean and watch the VM reset.
1
Hands-on · pairs with Lesson 4 · ~20 min

See your first security logs

Every investigation in this course starts with a log line. Here you'll generate real Windows security events with your own hands and read them — the exact events an analyst sees on day one.

1

Generate a failed and a successful logon

Inside the VM, lock the screen (Win+L) and sign back in with a wrong password once, then the right one. You just created Event 4625 (failed logon) and 4624 (successful logon).

2

Find them in Event Viewer

Open Event Viewer → Windows Logs → Security → Filter Current Log… and enter:

4624,4625

Open your 4624 and find Logon Type: 2 = at the keyboard, 3 = over the network, 10 = Remote Desktop. Because you unlocked a session, Windows may record it as 7 (Unlock) or 11 (cached credentials) — same person at the same keyboard.

You'll also see many 4624 events with Logon Type 5 for SYSTEM — services starting. Noise is normal; filter to your own account name.

3

Query the same events from PowerShell

Analysts script what they repeat. In an Administrator PowerShell:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625} -MaxEvents 5 |
  Format-List TimeCreated, Id, Message

Find the account name, the failure reason, and the logon type in the message. Note that TimeCreated is shown in local time — real SOCs normalize everything to UTC (Lesson 5).

You did it if…
  • You found your own 4625 and 4624.
  • You can explain why your unlock showed the Logon Type it did.
  • You pulled the same failure with Get-WinEvent and can state who / when / how.
2
Hands-on · pairs with Lessons 4 & 15 · ~25 min

Turn on rich telemetry with Sysmon

Default Windows logging is thin. Sysmon is a free Microsoft Sysinternals tool that records process trees, command lines, hashes, network connections and DNS queries — the telemetry EDR is built on.

1

Install Sysmon with a community config

Download Sysmon from Microsoft Sysinternals, then a maintained starter config: either sysmonconfig.xml (the “Balanced” profile) from the latest release of Olaf Hartong's sysmon-modular on GitHub, or sysmonconfig-export.xml from SwiftOnSecurity's sysmon-config. Put Sysmon64.exe and the config in one folder and, in an Administrator PowerShell in that folder, run (use your config's file name):

.\Sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig.xml

Check it's running:

Get-Service Sysmon64

Sysmon without a config file logs process creation but not network connections (Event 3) or DNS queries (Event 22) — Labs 3 and 6 need those, so use a community config.

2

Create a suspicious-looking process chain

Make a harmless chain with the shape of many attacks — a shell spawning another shell:

powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command "Start-Process cmd.exe -ArgumentList '/c whoami'"
3

Read the process tree

Event Viewer → Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational, filter Event ID 1. Find your cmd.exe and read ParentImage — it points back to powershell.exe. Or from PowerShell:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'; Id=1} -MaxEvents 10 |
  Where-Object { $_.Message -match 'cmd.exe' } |
  Format-List TimeCreated, Message
You did it if…
  • Sysmon is running and writing to its Operational channel.
  • You found a Process Create (ID 1) event for your cmd.exe.
  • You traced ParentImage back to PowerShell — a real process tree.
3
Hands-on · pairs with Lessons 3 & 16 · ~25 min

Watch DNS and spot a beacon

Malware resolves domains and checks in with its controller on a schedule. Here you'll generate real DNS and HTTPS traffic with a beacon's rhythm — and see why regularity gives it away.

1

Look up names and read the DNS cache

In PowerShell inside the VM:

Resolve-DnsName example.com
Resolve-DnsName microsoft.com
Get-DnsClientCache | Select-Object Entry, Data | Format-Table -Auto
2

Send a beacon-shaped check-in

This loop makes a real DNS lookup and a real HTTPS request every 5 seconds, six times — the metronome shape of command-and-control traffic, aimed at a harmless test site:

1..6 | ForEach-Object {
  $t = (Get-Date).ToString('HH:mm:ss')
  Resolve-DnsName example.com -DnsOnly | Out-Null
  try { $null = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://example.com' -UseBasicParsing -TimeoutSec 5 } catch {}
  "$t  check-in sent"
  Start-Sleep -Seconds 5
}
3

Find the rhythm in your telemetry

With a community Sysmon config (Lab 2), each check-in left a DNS query (Event 22) and a network connection (Event 3):

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'; Id=3,22} -MaxEvents 60 |
  Where-Object { $_.Message -match 'example.com|powershell' } |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id | Sort-Object TimeCreated | Format-Table -Auto

Read the TimeCreated column: near-perfect five-second spacing. Human browsing is bursty; this regularity is exactly what network analysts hunt for (Lesson 16) — and what Challenge 7 in Lab 5 finds at scale.

Nothing listed? Your Sysmon config may exclude these events. Live view works too: Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established | Select-Object LocalPort, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, OwningProcess | Format-Table -Auto while the loop runs.

You did it if…
  • You read lookups back from the DNS client cache.
  • You generated a fixed-interval check-in and found its events.
  • You can explain why regular timing to one destination is suspicious.
4
Hands-on · pairs with Lesson 8 · ~45 min

Write and test your first detection

This is the lab that gets you hired. You'll write a real Sigma rule, run it against the telemetry you generated with an actual detection engine, convert it into a SIEM query, and name its false positive — the build → attack → detect → tune loop in miniature.

1

Create a lab folder and write the rule

In PowerShell:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\lab\rules, C:\lab\evtx | Out-Null
[guid]::NewGuid()   # copy this into the rule's id field

Save this as C:\lab\rules\proc_susp_powershell_cmd.yml (replace the id with your GUID):

title: PowerShell Spawning Cmd
id: 6f1c3b2e-8a4d-4c1e-9b7a-2d5e0f3a9c11
status: experimental
description: Detects PowerShell launching cmd.exe (home-lab rule).
author: your-name
date: 2026-11-01
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
    Image|endswith: '\cmd.exe'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Admin and installer scripts that call cmd.exe from PowerShell
level: medium

Read it in plain English: alert when a process whose parent ends in powershell.exe creates a process ending in cmd.exe. The tags map it to ATT&CK; falsepositives is the note to your future self.

2

Generate the attack, then export the evidence

Trigger the behavior (as in Lab 2), then export the Sysmon log to a file the detection engine can read:

powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command "Start-Process cmd.exe -ArgumentList '/c whoami'"
wevtutil epl Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational C:\lab\evtx\sysmon.evtx
3

Run the rule for real with Chainsaw

Chainsaw (free, open source, by WithSecure Labs) runs Sigma rules directly against .evtx files. From its GitHub releases page, download chainsaw_x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip — it contains chainsaw.exe and the mappings folder. Extract it into C:\lab so you end up with C:\lab\chainsaw\chainsaw.exe (if Windows adds an extra folder level, move the chainsaw folder up). SmartScreen may warn about an unsigned download — expected in a lab VM. Then:

cd C:\lab\chainsaw
.\chainsaw.exe hunt C:\lab\evtx -s C:\lab\rules --mapping .\mappings\sigma-event-logs-all.yml

Chainsaw prints a table with your rule's title and the matching event. That is a tested detection: real rule, real telemetry, real engine. No hit? Check the event exists (Lab 2), then the field names and backslashes in the rule — debugging a silent rule is the job.

4

Convert it into a SIEM query (optional)

Sigma is portable because tools translate it. With Python installed in the VM:

python -m pip install sigma-cli
sigma plugin install splunk
sigma convert -t splunk -p splunk_windows C:\lab\rules\proc_susp_powershell_cmd.yml

Output:

ParentImage="*\\powershell.exe" Image="*\\cmd.exe"

That's Splunk SPL, ready for Lab 6. sigma plugin list shows other backends (Elastic, Microsoft KQL, and more). If PowerShell says sigma isn't recognized, reinstall Python with Add python.exe to PATH ticked and open a new window.

5

Name the false positive and the tune

Plenty of admin scripts launch cmd.exe from PowerShell. Write one sentence: “This rule would false-positive on ________, so I'd tune it by ________.” (Hint: Challenge 8 in Lab 5 shows a real one — and the right fix is that exact script path, not the whole admin host.)

That sentence — the false positive and the tune — is what separates you from everyone who copied a rule off the internet. Put it in your writeup (Lab 10).

You did it if…
  • Chainsaw matched your rule against your own exported Sysmon log.
  • You converted the rule to a SIEM query with sigma-cli (or know how).
  • You named one realistic false positive and a specific tune.
5
Hands-on · pairs with Lessons 6, 8 & 12 · ~40 min · runs in this page

Query a SIEM in your browser

No VM, no install. Below is a working mini-SIEM loaded with one synthetic day of telemetry from the course's fictional company: authentication, Sysmon process creation, DNS and proxy logs — with a password spray, a brute force, an approved scanner, an Office-macro intrusion, a DGA burst and a beacon hidden inside. Its language is a small subset of Splunk's SPL; every challenge also shows the same idea in Microsoft's KQL.

Indexes & fieldsindex=auth EventCode, action, user, src_ip, logon_type, reasonindex=sysmon EventCode, user, parent_image, image, command_lineindex=dns src_ip, query, qtype, answerindex=proxy src_ip, dest_host, dest_port, method, status, bytes_out, bytes_inEvery event also has _time and host. Commands: search where stats (count, dc, sum, avg, min, max, values, range) sort head tail table dedup rename bin top rare. Values accept * wildcards; NOT, OR and != work.
Try:Enter runs · Shift+Enter adds a line

This sandbox teaches the shape of SIEM work — filter, aggregate, pivot — on a fixed dataset. Real platforms add time pickers, data models and far more commands; Lab 6 puts you in one.

6
Hands-on · pairs with Lessons 5–7 · ~60 min

Stand up a real SIEM: Splunk + Sysmon

Lab 5 taught the grammar; now run the real thing. You'll install Splunk Enterprise in your VM, onboard Security and Sysmon logs the way Lesson 7 describes, prove the source is usable, and run your Lab 4 rule as a search.

1

Install Splunk Enterprise (free)

Create a free account on splunk.com and download Splunk Enterprise for Windows (.msi) inside the VM. Install with defaults, set the admin password, and open http://localhost:8000.

You start on a 60-day Enterprise trial. Afterwards switch to the perpetual Free license (Settings → Licensing → Change license group → Free): up to 500 MB/day, single user, and no scheduled alerting — plenty for a home lab.

2

Onboard Security and Sysmon logs

From Splunkbase (Apps → Find More Apps) install the free Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows and Splunk Add-on for Sysmon — they parse the events into fields. Then add the inputs: create (or edit) C:\Program Files\Splunk\etc\system\local\inputs.conf with:

[WinEventLog://Security]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
source = XmlWinEventLog:Security
index = main

[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
source = XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational
index = main

Restart Splunk (Settings → Server controls → Restart).

3

Run the acceptance checks (Lesson 7)

Prove the source is usable, not just connected — liveness and field population:

index=main source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational"
| stats count, latest(_time) as last_seen by EventCode
| eval last_seen=strftime(last_seen, "%F %T")

You want recent events for EventCode 1 (and 3, 22 with a community config). Then check that the fields your rule needs exist:

index=main source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=1
| table _time, host, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine

Empty ParentImage / Image columns mean the add-on isn't parsing — searchable but not detectable, exactly Lesson 7's warning. Fallback that works without add-ons: | rex "Name='ParentImage'>(?<ParentImage>[^<]+)" | rex "Name='Image'>(?<Image>[^<]+)"

4

Run your Lab 4 detection as a search

Generate the behavior again (Lab 2's command), then paste the sigma-cli output behind the source filter:

index=main source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=1
    ParentImage="*\\powershell.exe" Image="*\\cmd.exe"
| table _time, host, User, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine

Then try the spray logic from Lab 5 on your own failed logons (fail a few logons first):

index=main source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4625
| stats dc(TargetUserName) as users, count by IpAddress
| sort - count

Save the first search as a report (and, during the trial, as a scheduled alert) — your first production-style detection.

Prefer another stack? The same steps work with Elastic Security (free basic license, Elastic Agent) or the open-source Wazuh — only the query language changes.

You did it if…
  • Splunk receives Security and Sysmon events with fresh timestamps.
  • ParentImage and Image are populated as fields — the source is usable.
  • Your Lab 4 rule returns your own test event as a search.
7
Hands-on · pairs with Lessons 8, 11 & 12 · ~60 min

Validate detections with an attack simulation

A detection you never tested is a guess. Atomic Red Team (free, by Red Canary) is a library of small, ATT&CK-mapped tests that reproduce one technique each. You'll run one, prove a rule catches it, and record your coverage in the ATT&CK Navigator.

Take a fresh snapshot first and run this only in your lab VM. Some tests may be blocked by Microsoft Defender — that's a detection too, and worth noting. Never weaken protection on a real machine.

1

Install the framework

In an Administrator PowerShell inside the VM:

Set-ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope Process -Force
IEX (IWR 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redcanaryco/invoke-atomicredteam/master/install-atomicredteam.ps1' -UseBasicParsing)
Install-AtomicRedTeam -getAtomics

In a new session, load it with:

Import-Module "C:\AtomicRedTeam\invoke-atomicredteam\Invoke-AtomicRedTeam.psd1" -Force
2

Pick the saga's persistence technique and read it first

The course's intrusion persisted with a scheduled task — ATT&CK T1053.005. Always read a test before running it:

Invoke-AtomicTest T1053.005 -ShowDetailsBrief
Invoke-AtomicTest T1053.005 -TestNumbers 1 -ShowDetails
Invoke-AtomicTest T1053.005 -TestNumbers 1 -CheckPrereqs
3

Write the rule, attack, detect

Save this rule as C:\lab\rules\proc_schtasks_create.yml:

title: Scheduled Task Created With schtasks
id: 2a6b1f0c-3d5e-4b7a-9c8d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
status: experimental
description: Detects scheduled task creation via schtasks.exe (home-lab rule).
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Software installers and admin tooling that register tasks
level: medium

Run the test, export the evidence, hunt, then clean up:

Invoke-AtomicTest T1053.005 -TestNumbers 1
wevtutil epl Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational C:\lab\evtx\sysmon-t1053.evtx
C:\lab\chainsaw\chainsaw.exe hunt C:\lab\evtx -s C:\lab\rules --mapping C:\lab\chainsaw\mappings\sigma-event-logs-all.yml
Invoke-AtomicTest T1053.005 -TestNumbers 1 -Cleanup

Did it fire? If not, find out why (wrong field? the test used a different binary or API?) and fix the rule — that debugging is detection engineering. Keep the exported .evtx: it's now a regression test for the rule.

4

Map your coverage in ATT&CK Navigator

Open the MITRE ATT&CK Navigator (search “ATT&CK Navigator” — it runs in the browser), create a new Enterprise layer, and search for each technique you have a tested rule for: T1059.001, T1059.003, T1053.005 (and T1110.003 if you built the spray search in Lab 6). Color them green, add a comment naming the rule and test, and export the layer as JSON and SVG for your portfolio.

Coverage means tested detections, not tagged rules. An all-green heatmap of untested tags is a vanity metric (Lesson 20) — three honest green cells beat three hundred hopeful ones.

You did it if…
  • You ran an ATT&CK-mapped atomic test and cleaned it up.
  • Your rule fired on the test's telemetry (or you fixed it until it did).
  • You exported an ATT&CK Navigator layer showing only tested coverage.
8
Hands-on · pairs with Lesson 13 · ~30 min

Dissect a phishing email's headers

Headers are the postmarks; the body is the forger's canvas. Below is a fictional phish reported by the finance user from the course saga (all domains and IPs are reserved documentation values). Work through the questions before opening each answer.

Reported message — raw headers and body (text only, safe to read)
Return-Path: <it-support@companv-helpdesk.example>
Received: from mail.companv-helpdesk.example (mail.companv-helpdesk.example [198.51.100.77])
        by mx1.company.example (Postfix) with ESMTPS id 4F2A1C0
        for <m.haddad@company.example>; Tue, 4 Aug 2026 08:52:11 +0000 (UTC)
Received: from [10.0.0.5] (unknown [203.0.113.200])
        by mail.companv-helpdesk.example with ESMTPSA id 77A1
        for <m.haddad@company.example>; Tue, 4 Aug 2026 08:52:09 +0000 (UTC)
Authentication-Results: mx1.company.example;
        spf=pass (sender IP is 198.51.100.77) smtp.mailfrom=companv-helpdesk.example;
        dkim=pass header.d=companv-helpdesk.example;
        dmarc=fail (p=none dis=none) header.from=company.example
From: "IT Service Desk" <it-support@company.example>
Reply-To: <servicedesk-reply@companv-helpdesk.example>
To: <m.haddad@company.example>
Subject: [Action required] Mailbox storage full - verify your account within 24h
Date: Tue, 4 Aug 2026 08:52:03 +0000
Message-ID: <20260804085203.77A1@companv-helpdesk.example>

Your mailbox has exceeded its quota. Verify your account to avoid suspension:
https://companv-helpdesk.example/sso/verify?u=m.haddad
1 · Where did this message really come from?

Read Received headers bottom-up: the lowest one is closest to the origin. The sender submitted it from 203.0.113.200 to mail.companv-helpdesk.example, which relayed it from 198.51.100.77 to your gateway. Nothing in that path is your company's infrastructure.

2 · Do From, Reply-To and Return-Path agree?

No. The visible From claims company.example, but Return-Path and Reply-To point to companv-helpdesk.example — a lookalike with v for y. Replies and bounces go to the attacker.

3 · SPF and DKIM passed. Doesn't that make it legitimate?

They passed for the attacker's own domain — they prove the lookalike domain sent it, nothing more. DMARC checks alignment with the visible From domain, and it failed. The message was still delivered because the policy is p=none (monitor only): a finding for your email team — move toward quarantine / reject.

4 · Record the indicator safely

Defang before you write it anywhere: hxxps://companv-helpdesk[.]example/sso/verify?u=m.haddad. Note the personalised u= parameter — this is targeted credential harvesting, and the parameter tells you who clicked when you search proxy logs.

5 · What do you do next?

Verdict: malicious — credential phishing impersonating internal IT. Then scope and contain (Lesson 13): search the mail gateway for the same sender domain, subject and URL to find every recipient; search proxy/DNS logs for companv-helpdesk.example to find who clicked; purge the messages; block the domain at gateway, proxy and DNS; for anyone who submitted credentials, reset the password and revoke sessions immediately; thank the reporter.

1

Write the verdict like an analyst

Use this skeleton in your notes — it doubles as a portfolio writeup (Lab 10):

Verdict: malicious / suspicious / benign  -- and confidence
Evidence: origin (Received), alignment (From vs Return-Path/Reply-To), auth results
Indicators (defanged): sender domain, URL, sending IPs
Scope: recipients found, clicks found
Actions: purge / block / reset + revoke / user comms
Follow-ups: DMARC policy, lookalike-domain monitoring
You did it if…
  • You identified the true origin from the bottom Received header.
  • You explained why SPF/DKIM passing did not make it legitimate.
  • You wrote a defanged indicator and a five-line verdict with next actions.
9
Hands-on · pairs with Lessons 9 & 12 · ~30 min

Run a full triage on your own activity

Now combine everything into the core SOC skill: triage. You'll treat your own lab activity as an alert, build an entity timeline from three sources, and reach a documented verdict — the Lesson 9 workflow.

1

Create the “incident”

Run this small burst:

whoami
powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command "Start-Process cmd.exe -ArgumentList '/c ipconfig /all'"
Resolve-DnsName example.com
2

Build the entity timeline

Pull together, in time order, everything that just happened for your user: process creations (Sysmon 1), the DNS lookup (Sysmon 22 or the DNS cache), and the logon you're running under (4624). If you built Lab 6, one search does it:

index=main host=<your-vm-name> earliest=-15m
| table _time, source, EventCode, User, ParentImage, Image, QueryName
| sort _time

Write it as a timeline — timestamp (UTC), source, what happened:

HH:MM:SS  Security/4624  logon type 2 (you)
HH:MM:SS  Sysmon/1       powershell.exe -> cmd.exe (ipconfig /all)
HH:MM:SS  Sysmon/22      example.com resolved
3

Reach a verdict, with reasons

Escalate or close — and why. The honest verdict here is benign: it was you, running diagnostic commands, from an interactive logon, with no unexpected destinations. Write the one-paragraph verdict, then ask the Lesson 12 question: if this had been an attacker, what one extra thing would I look for? (e.g., a connection to a never-before-seen external IP right after.)

You did it if…
  • You built a time-ordered timeline from three different log sources.
  • You wrote a one-paragraph verdict that says escalate/close and why.
  • You named one thing you'd hunt for if it had been a real intrusion.
10
Hands-on · pairs with Lesson 21 · ~45 min

Publish the writeup that gets interviews

Knowledge is invisible until you prove it. This capstone turns the track into the artifact hiring managers stop for: an honest investigation writeup with tested detections attached.

1

Use the analyst-writeup skeleton

Create a public GitHub/GitLab repository with your rules (rules/), test evidence (evtx/), Navigator layer, and a README using this structure:

# Investigation: Suspicious PowerShell -> cmd chain (home lab)

## Summary
One paragraph: what I saw, what I concluded.

## Environment
Windows 11 evaluation VM + Sysmon (community config) + Splunk Free. Free tools only.

## Timeline
(the time-ordered table from Lab 9, in UTC)

## Analysis
What each event meant and how I read the process tree.

## Detection
My Sigma rule (Lab 4), how I tested it (Chainsaw / Atomic Red Team, Lab 7),
the false positive I found, and how I tuned it.

## Coverage
ATT&CK Navigator layer (Lab 7) - only tested techniques are green.

## What I'd do differently
Honest reflection. Dead ends included.
2

Make it honest — that's the point

Include a dead end or a mistake: “I first thought X, then the timeline showed Y.” Admitting an instructive mistake reads as more credible than a flawless story, because it proves you did the work.

Do this three times — one endpoint investigation (Labs 2 & 9), one network one (Lab 3), one detection one (Labs 4, 6 & 7) — and you have the three-writeup portfolio Lesson 21 recommends.

3

Rehearse the ninety-second story

Out loud: “I built a lab, generated a suspicious process chain, wrote a Sigma rule, proved it fires with Chainsaw and an Atomic Red Team test, onboarded the logs into Splunk, and documented the false positive and my tune.” Delivered calmly, that beats any list of certifications.

Never publish anything from a real employer or real incident. Portfolio work uses only your own lab.

You did it if…
  • Your repository has rules, test evidence, a Navigator layer, and a README writeup.
  • The writeup honestly includes at least one dead end or correction.
  • You can tell the whole story out loud in about ninety seconds.
Track complete

You now have hands, not just a head

You built a lab, read real logs, installed Sysmon, caught a beacon's rhythm, wrote a Sigma rule and proved it fires, queried a SIEM, onboarded logs into a real one, validated a detection with an attack simulation, dissected a phish, ran a triage, and published an honest writeup. That is a working analyst's — and a junior detection engineer's — starter portfolio. Return to Lesson 21 for the career map that turns it into a job.

Who made it, and how it was checked

Author

Created by Yousef, a cybersecurity engineer working on SIEM, SOAR and detection engineering. Built as a free resource for students and junior analysts who want to understand how a SOC actually works. Live site: yousefelshetry.github.io/SOC-Foundations · source: GitHub.

Technical review (v1.1)

Event IDs, Sysmon IDs, ATT&CK technique IDs, Sigma syntax, CVSS / EPSS / KEV and incident-response frameworks were checked against the primary sources below. Sigma rules in Lesson 8 and the labs were validated and converted with sigma-cli. Lab steps were cross-checked against each tool's own documentation and source — Chainsaw's release packaging, CLI and field mappings; the Atomic Red Team test definition used in Lab 7; sysmon-modular's release files; Splunk's Sysmon input settings.
